title: A Prayer for Home: A Comprehensive Study — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: A Prayer for Home
description: A close reading of the novella A Prayer for Home — the Lady Jane Angel of Death scene, the Assumption staged on a public beach, and the origin of Molly Bonamici's clinical detachment.
text: A Prayer for Home: A Comprehensive Study — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon A Close Reading · On the Novella A Prayer for Home A full-length study of the novella that first gave Molly Bonamici her voice, her nickname, and her clinical detachment — a storefront faith healer, a widow's timed death, and a public beach standing in for the Assumption. Abstract A Prayer for Home (Silver Current Press, 2016) is a novella narrated by a teenage Molly Bonamici, built around her family's widowed, alcoholic neighbor Mrs. Muldoon, who plans a literal trip “home” to Ireland and instead dies of a deliberate overdose timed to her wedding anniversary. This essay argues that the novella is the direct textual origin of the “Angel of Death” designation and the clinical detachment later explored at full novel length in Molly Bonamici — tracing the designation to a storefront psychic named Lady Jane, whom Nonna deceives with a fabricated leukemia diagnosis to jump a healing line, and reading the novella's central beach scene, in which Mrs. Muldoon seeks the “Blessed Mother's cure,” as a comic, embodied rehearsal of the Marian Assumption that the novella's ending will invert into its opposite: not a body raised, but a body consumed. Contents I. A Title Borrowed from a Drinking Song II. Nonna's Moral Economy III. Lady Jane and the Origin of the Angel of Death IV. The Beach as a Staged Assumption V. Two Kinds of Home: Ireland and the Grave VI. Mr. Scarfone and the Graduation VII. The Corpse Scene and the Limits of Innocence VIII. The Conqueror Worm IX. Conclusion: The Moon Too High, the River Too Wide I. A Title Borrowed from a Drinking Song The novella opens not with narration but with an epigraph — the old music-hall song “Show Me the Way to Go Home,” sung by a drunk looking for his bed after “a little drink about an hour ago.” 1 The choice creates a small misdirection: a title that sounds devotional, A Prayer for Home , is in fact drawn from a maudlin drinking song about being lost and tipsy, and the novella spends its length working out the distance between those two registers — the sacred request implied by the title and the boozy, undignified reality of how “home” actually gets sought by the adults in Molly's world. Mrs. Muldoon, introduced on the first page as a woman “drunk as a skunk,” wandering the street “looking for her husband Jim,” 2 is the novella's first literal enactment of the epigraph's stumbling, sung request to be shown the way home. II. Nonna's Moral Economy Much of the novella's early comedy is built from Nonna's casual, unbothered amorality, delivered in the same warm, grandmotherly register she uses for affection. She steals Christmas ornaments off Mrs. Muldoon's tree while visiting her — “She won't notice them missing. And it's a shame not to have them appreciated” 3 — and dismisses her own late husband with the same breezy indifference she applies to organized religion: “Men are a pain in the ass,” she says, and of her lover Mr. Scarfone, “he's just a good fuck.” 4 Her single most important piece of instruction to Molly is explicitly a lesson in performed rather than felt faith: “Of course I don't” believe the Bible is the literal word of God, she admits, “But that's not the point. Most people do. And you gotta fit in.” 5 Nonna is teaching Molly the exact operating principle the later novel will diagnose in Molly herself: that belief is a social performance layered over a private skepticism. III. Lady Jane and the Origin of the Angel of Death A central scene, later alluded to in descriptions of Molly Bonamici on this site, takes place at a storefront psychic's parlor on Tremont Street, where Mrs. Muldoon has brought Nonna and Molly to be “cured” before her trip. Nonna secures a place at the front of a long line by lying outright to a stranger: she tells an Indian couple that Molly “had leukemia ‘very bad’ and the doctors gave me three months at most,” instructing Molly to perform the part — “I tried to appear sick. I started shaking a little and drooled… I managed to create a string of saliva that dropped like the thread of a spider's web hanging off the bottom of my chin.” 6 The scene demonstrates the novella's moral world: a fabricated terminal illness, staged convincingly enough to move strangers to pity, deployed casually to skip a line, with no consequence and no remorse from either grandmother or granddaughter. The healer, “Lady Jane,” delivers her verdict on Molly directly and without preamble: “I hate to tell people things like this… but I see gruesome deaths in your future… You have the unlucky fortune of being someone who will either find dead people or be near them when they die in violent situations. I guess you might say, ‘You're an Angel of Death.’” 7 The scene deliberately declines to resolve whether Lady Jane possesses any real gift or is simply a competent showman reading a room — she then giggles “like a little girl,” a detail that undercuts her own pronouncement's gravity even as the novella's plot will spend the rest of its length seeming to confirm it. 7 Nonna's furious reaction, dragging Molly out while cursing in Italian, and the family's own competing theories in the car afterward — police officer, doctor, murderer 8 — establish the designation as contested and uncertain from its very first appearance, exactly the interpretive posture a companion essay on this site identifies in the fuller novel, where Molly's “Angel of Death” status is treated as “more a curiosity than an obsession.” 9 IV. The Beach as a Staged Assumption The novella's other major scene sends Molly, Nonna, and Mrs. Muldoon to the beach on the Catholic feast of the Assumption, ostensibly so Mrs. Muldoon can seek “the Blessed Mother's cure” in the water. Molly's characteristically literal-minded interrogation of the doctrine — “What do you mean raised? She just flew into the air?” 10 — produces a striking image: as Mrs. Muldoon removes her housedress to reveal a swimsuit, her “round hard belly” makes her look “almost… pregnant,” and Molly, for a moment, “imagined she was going to demonstrate the Assumption and fly away.” 11 An aging, alcoholic widow's ordinary, unglamorous body becomes, for one absurd beat, a stand-in for the doctrine of a body raised bodily into heaven — a technique the site's essay on “Assumptions” identifies elsewhere in Mulhern's fiction as granting “a flawed, ordinary body the imagery reserved for the sinless one.” 12 Nonna's own gloss on the scene redirects the theology into the novella's real creed: “Who gives a damn if Mary flew into the sky or not?… The world is made up mostly of sheep. You have the good fortune… of being a lion in a world full of sheep.” 13 V. Two Kinds of Home: Ireland and the Grave What the Lady Jane scene establishes, and the beach scene deepens, is that Mrs. Muldoon's “going home” is, for most of the novella, meant and understood literally: she is planning an actual trip back to her family in Ireland, donating her furniture to Goodwill, and telling Nonna, when asked about her flight, “I'm going the third week of August.” 14 The novella tracks a real softening in her toward Molly over these middle chapters — at Molly's graduation party she is, in the narrator's own words, no longer “so bitchy” but “genuinely excited” to see her, singing “Moon River” softly across the table and offering an old Irish proverb as a parting gift: “Your feet will take you where your heart is… you must follow yours, too.” 15 The novella's title and its central irony both depend on this literal Ireland trip existing as a real, planned, believed-in future, so that when Mrs. Muldoon's actual departure turns out to be a deliberate overdose timed to her wedding anniversary rather than a flight to Shannon, the narrator's retrospective correction lands with its full weight: “I did think it was a bit silly to believe that she would be ‘going home’ to her husband Jim, when she was, in fact, going home to the earth, to her ‘conqueror worm.’” 16 The novella's whole architecture turns on this substitution of one home for another — Ireland, then the grave — and the reader is made to feel the substitution exactly when Molly, characteristically, does not. VI. Mr. Scarfone and the Graduation Molly's high school graduation party, held at her family's restaurant, gathers the novella's secondary cast for its fullest scene of family dysfunction and introduces Mr. Scarfone directly rather than by rumor. Nonna, drunk on whiskey, needles her son-in-law about the restaurant's failing finances in front of the whole party — “If you had managed the restaurant wisely… you wouldn't have to ask your wife's mother for money” 17 — while simultaneously appraising Mrs. Muldoon's hidden cash as a solution to the same problem, telling Mr. Scarfone she keeps “a stack of cash… in her bread box” and speculating about what remains of her belongings before she leaves. 18 Mr. Scarfone's single direct scene with Molly is brief but ominous, delivered with his hand “firmly” on her shoulders and his eyes fixed on hers: “If you ever need anything, and I mean anything… call me,” a line the narrator reports as spoken “almost menacingly.” 19 The scene establishes, in a single gesture, both his protective utility to the family (confirmed later when Nonna invokes his connection to the police chief) and the low-grade menace that makes the site's essay on the corpus's benign mafiosi describe such figures as sources of “domestic comfort rather than menace” only from a certain angle 20 — from Molly's angle, in this scene, the comfort and the menace arrive in the same handshake. VII. The Corpse Scene and the Limits of Innocence The novella's discovery scene is unsparing in what it reports and precise about what it withholds. Molly catalogues Mrs. Muldoon's decomposing body with the same clinical precision she brought to Lady Jane's parlor and the beach — “I kneeled and pressed my finger against a dark purple spot above her right ankle; the skin was so cold. The flesh broke, and blood trickled slowly” 21 — and her curiosity is explicit rather than displaced onto some other object, as it will be with the toad in the later novel: “I guess you could say I was mesmerized.” 21 When the responding officer asks whether touching the maggot-infested corpse “bothered” her, Molly's answer is characteristically literal and characteristically undisturbed: “No. A maggot is just a baby fly.” 22 This is the scene a companion essay on this site cites directly as evidence for the corpus-wide pattern of childhood affect withheld rather than perception failed 23 — and reading it here, in its original context, clarifies that the trait is not an invention of the later novel but a documented, textually prior feature of the character. Nonna's anxious aside that “it's a good thing Mr. Scarfone knows the chief of police” and can supply an excuse for Molly's behavior 24 closes the loop the graduation scene opened, confirming Mr. Scarfone's utility exactly when the family needs it. VIII. The Conqueror Worm Molly's own interpretive frame for the death arrives not from Catholic doctrine but from Poe, whose “The Conqueror Worm” she has been assigned to recite for English class and recalls, unprompted, while riding in the patrol car: “A crawling shape intrude!… The mimes become its food… Its hero the Conqueror Worm.” 25 The citation lets Molly resolve the day's theology on her own terms, converting Mrs. Muldoon's chosen death into a private, literary Assumption: “She had created her own Assumption and I thought, ironically, consumption” 26 — the pun turning the Marian miracle of a body raised whole into its precise physical opposite, a body consumed by rot and by the insects Molly examined with her own hands an hour earlier. IX. Conclusion: The Moon Too High, the River Too Wide The novella's closing movement returns to song, as its title did, but shifts from the comic drinking ballad of its epigraph to “Moon River,” the same song Mrs. Muldoon sang at Molly's graduation, now recalled with its promise inverted: “We're after the rainbow's end,” the song promises, “But there was no rainbow's end for her. Her end was several days of rot and decay in a hot, humid room.” 27 Nonna's offered comfort — “Everything will be all right, Molly” — is met with the novella's direct admission of unresolved despair: “I would like to say that I was comforted, but I wasn't… prayers for home, wherever we believed we were going, would never be answered.” 28 The novella's final sentence borrows the song's own geography to deliver its verdict — “The moon was too high, the river was too wide, and our hearts would be broken after all” 28 — refusing the genre convention that would let a coming-of-age narrative close on hard-won consolation. Read with Lady Jane's storefront prophecy and Mrs. Muldoon's real, believed-in trip to Ireland in view, A Prayer for Home establishes early versions of the “Angel of Death” designation, the family's casual moral economy of theft and performed illness, and the narrator's calm in the presence of death; the later novel develops those elements further. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. title: About James Mulhern — Novelist, Poet, Professor Emeritus
heading: About the Author
description: Biography, awards, and teaching life of James Mulhern, Kirkus-starred novelist, Pushcart-nominated poet, Oxford writing fellow, and educator.
text: About James Mulhern — Novelist, Poet, Professor Emeritus ← Back to The 2601 Salon A Life in Letters About the Author Author of fiction, poetry, and nonfiction. Professor emeritus. Founder of Silver Current Press. Biography More than three hundred journal and anthology appearances James Mulhern is a Philadelphia-based novelist, poet, essayist, and professor emeritus of English. His writing in fiction, poetry, and nonfiction has appeared in international literary journals and anthologies more than three hundred times. His novels and short story collections — among them Give Them Unquiet Dreams , Molly Bonamici , A Prayer for Home , and Assumptions and Other Stories — have earned favorable critiques from Kirkus Reviews , including a starred review. In 2015, Mulhern was awarded a fully paid Creative Writing Fellowship to the University of Oxford in the United Kingdom, graduating with “Highest Distinction,” the university's highest designation. That same year, a story of his was longlisted for the Fish Short Story Prize . In 2017, he was nominated for a Pushcart Prize . He has been shortlisted for the Aesthetica Creative Writing Award for poetry, nominated for Best of the Net , and named a Finalist for the Tuscany Prize in Catholic Fiction. His work received Honorable Mentions for the Short Story America Prize , and two of his novels were Finalists — one a Red Ribbon Winner — for the United Kingdom's Wishing Shelf Book Awards . His novel Give Them Unquiet Dreams is a Readers' Favorite Book Award winner and was named one of the Best Books of 2019 by Kirkus Reviews , which awarded it a starred review. His poetry collection Crossings: Selected Poems was published by Silver Current Press in August 2026. Forthcoming titles include The Collected Stories and Poems , the first gathering of his fiction and poetry into a single volume; the story collection The Weight of Small Mercies ; the second edition of his textbook How to Analyze Literature ; and a separately planned illustrated edition of Crossings . He is the founder of Silver Current Press , a Philadelphia imprint devoted to literary fiction, poetry, and the art of the well-made book. After three decades teaching creative writing, literary analysis, and the craft of the short story to undergraduate and graduate students, he writes and publishes full time as professor emeritus. View All Books on Amazon Life & Background From Boston to Oxford to Philadelphia James Mulhern was raised in a Boston Irish Catholic family whose rhythms — the church bells and the family kitchen, the rosary and the radio, the silences kept and the secrets passed down — supply the moral atmosphere of his fiction. The 1970s Boston of Give Them Unquiet Dreams is not a tourist's Boston; it is the city as it was lived by working-class families on tree-lined streets where the past was always close enough to touch. He entered a teaching life that would last more than three decades — working principally with inner-city high school and college students, many of them children of immigrants and immigrants themselves. Their lives, voices, and resilience would, over time, enter his fiction as deeply as his Irish-Catholic inheritance ever had. "As a teacher of American literature," he has written, "I want my students to use the literature as a way to make connections and find meaning. Explore the circumference of your life. Write about your experience. Celebrate yourself." The literature he taught — Whitman, Dickinson, Emerson, Thoreau, Hughes, O'Connor, Joyce — is the same literature that quietly informs his prose: a faith that the well-made sentence is a moral instrument, that the right line of poetry can hold a life. That same Oxford fellowship — awarded in 2015 — would mark the last major milestone of his teaching years. He now makes his permanent home in Philadelphia — a city he has come to love for its history, its museums, its green space, and, most of all, its character. Having spent time in cities around the world, he finds a particular gratitude in living among Philadelphians, whose everyday warmth keeps faith with the city’s old name. In Philadelphia he founded Silver Current Press , an independent imprint devoted to literary fiction, poetry, and craft writing — including his own work and that of writers whose voices he wishes to bring to a wider readership. He is now professor emeritus, dividing his days between writing, editing, and the work of Silver Current Press — a small literary press devoted to fiction, poetry, and the craft of writing well. He continues to mentor writers, teach the occasional seminar, and read widely in the tradition that shaped him. The sentences continue. The Art of Telling A study of narrative craft — voice, point of view, scene construction, and the architecture of meaning across the modern short story. A Working Credo "Literature is one of the great moral instruments of the human race. The work is to keep faith with it — sentence by sentence." — James Mulhern Silver Current Press family: Silver Current Press · The 2601 Salon · For Program Partners See James Mulhern’s full body of work — fiction, courses, and publishing — in The Gathering Room →

title: All We Ever Needed: The Architecture of Mercy in the Fiction of James Mulhern
heading: All We Ever Needed
description: An essay on James Mulhern's short story collection All We Ever Needed — tracing its themes, motifs, character archetypes, allusions, and craft techniques, with close readings and direct quotation.
text: All We Ever Needed: The Architecture of Mercy in the Fiction of James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On the Short Story Collection All We Ever Needed The Architecture of Mercy in the Fiction of James Mulhern Abstract This essay offers a sustained critical reading of James Mulhern’s short story collection All We Ever Needed (Silver Current Press, 2026), tracing the book’s recurring themes (inheritance, faith and its counterfeits, care disguised as cruelty, the porousness between comedy and horror), its central motifs (salt water and the “cure,” candy and food as vehicles of love and poison, the useless object that turns out to be sacred, the recurring Feast of the Assumption), its character archetypes (the profane grandmother-confessor, the charlatan-healer, the watchful child-witness, the disintegrating institution), its network of literary and religious allusion (Scripture, Emerson, Thoreau, Poe, Hunter S. Thompson, Titian), and the craft techniques that bind them: free indirect discourse braided with unreliable first-person retrospection, the comic-grotesque register, and a prose rhythm built on accretive, catalog-like sentences. It argues that Mulhern’s abiding subject is the indistinguishability, at close range, of love from harm, and that his sentences are built to keep both possibilities alive at once. I. The Governing Idea: Mercy Without Innocence James Mulhern states the aim of All We Ever Needed in the closing author’s note: “I write from mercy rather than judgment, and I extend that mercy to every character I make.” The statement offers one way to read the collection, rather than treating its author as a satirist delighting in the grotesqueries of drunk grandmothers, con-artist psychics, and homicidal narrators. The stories often seek tenderness toward people who do genuinely terrible things, while withholding the comfort of a clean moral distance from them. That concern helps organize the book. Nearly every story pairs an act of care with an act of harm so tightly that they become one gesture. In “Assumptions,” the opening and title-anchoring story, a boy pours whiskey sours for a widow who has just been institutionalized by grief; the same scene that establishes his tenderness toward “Lovely Peggy” also shows the family degrading her for sport, “puffing on Lucky Strikes and Parliaments” while likening her features “to a bulldog’s.” Care and cruelty are administered by the same hands, in the same breath. The title phrase itself becomes the thesis, delivered at the close of “A Bath”: after a fraught reckoning between a battered daughter, her evasive mother, and a watching grandson, all three retreat into an ordinary intimacy — “There was no conversation. I heard splashing and my grandmother’s sighs as my mother rubbed her back… For a few moments, the three of us had all we ever needed.” The sentence does not resolve the story’s violence; it simply sets beside it the modest, bodily fact of people tending to one another. This unresolved juxtaposition recurs throughout the collection. II. Recurring Themes A. Inheritance as Both Blessing and Contamination Mulhern’s people inherit almost everything — faith, cruelty, appetite, wit, even crime — the way one inherits a family recipe. Molly Bonamici, the narrator who anchors five of the eight stories, absorbs her grandmother Nonna’s moral logic wholesale, including its most monstrous extension. Nonna’s creed is domestic and reasonable on its surface — “You’ve got to have compassion for her, Molly. She’s been through a lot” — yet the same Nonna easily justifies petty theft (“She won’t notice them missing… Don’t ya agree, Molly?”) and eventually, in “Mia Bambina,” supplies the poison that kills a roommate, delivered with the chilling domesticity of a woman baking for a beloved grandchild: “Sure, mia bambina. What’s one more ingredient? Not a problem.” The horror of the collection’s darkest turn is not that Molly becomes a murderer; it is that we can trace, story by story, exactly how she was raised into the capacity. Inheritance, in Mulhern’s hands, is never a metaphor for gentle continuity. It is a mechanism, and it transmits damage as efficiently as it transmits love. B. Faith and Its Counterfeits Religion in this collection is rarely a source of stable comfort; it is a live wire that runs through kitchens, beaches, and church basements, connecting genuine devotion to superstition, grift, and cruelty. The Feast of the Assumption — “when Jesus’s mother… was taken to her heavenly home” — recurs across two separate stories (“Assumptions” and “Useless Things”) as the occasion for a “cure in the water,” and each time the ritual produces the same three-part rhythm: comic bickering, an accidental baptism by wave, and an undertone of real, if inarticulate, spiritual hunger. Alongside this sincere folk-Catholicism, Mulhern sets a rogues’ gallery of religious counterfeits: the storefront healer “Lady Jane,” whose fake British accent slips into “a Georgia twang,” and who tells a teenager she will become “an Angel of Death” while “giggling like a little girl”; the New Age shopkeeper Myra Bocca, who activates a customer’s “forehead chakra” while planning to steal her credit card. Mulhern’s target is not faith itself but the commercial and psychological uses to which faith and its imitations are put — a theme he makes explicit in his own gloss on the collection’s title story in the companion essay “Altogether Beautiful” , where the doctrine of the Assumption is read against Peggy Fleming’s grotesque and holy body. The epigraph to “Assumptions,” drawn from the Song of Solomon — “You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you” — is not incidental decoration; it is a deliberate, almost defiant, act of scriptural reassignment, draping the language of divine perfection over a woman the narrator’s own family calls “the homeliest damn woman” anyone had ever seen. C. The Comedy That Precedes Horror Several stories behave like farce until, without changing their voice, they become something closer to horror. “Useless Things” is a clear instance: two-thirds of the story is broad comedy — a fake-cancer scam to jump a line, a healer with a “Georgia twang,” slapstick beach-wave pratfalls — and then, on the same porch where the comic set pieces occurred, the narrator discovers Mrs. Muldoon’s decomposing corpse, rendered in unflinching clinical detail: “Her skin was green, purple and black... A bloody maggot emerged from her right ear.” Mulhern does not signal the shift with a change in diction or pacing. Comedy and death therefore share a register in the prose because, in this account of experience, they share a world. “Myra Bocca” repeats the pattern: broad comedy (a stolen credit card charged for a television and pornographic DVDs titled Debbie Does Dallas ) resolves into a graphically described traffic fatality, complete with a bystander directing chest compressions by silently counting the beat of “Stayin’ Alive.” The stories draw on the American and Irish grotesque, including Flannery O’Connor’s violent grace and Synge’s black comedy, while using pacing to withhold an advance warning of the turn. D. Watching as a Form of Complicity Several stories turn on children or adolescents who watch adult suffering with a clinical, sometimes erotic, curiosity that implicates them in what they observe. The boy in “Assumptions” studies Peggy’s dying voice and calls it his first encounter with “death’s glower.” Molly, throughout the linked stories, catalogs bodily decay with the eye of a coroner — “I kneeled down and pressed my finger against a dark purple spot above her right ankle; the skin was so cold” — and admits flatly, of Mrs. Muldoon’s corpse, “I guess you could say I was mesmerized.” This is not simple childhood insensitivity; Mulhern is dramatizing the particular ethical peril of the writer’s own instrument — attentiveness itself — when it is turned on suffering without the mediating protection of adult tact. The watching child becomes, by the collection’s end, an adult who acts on what she has learned to observe without flinching. III. Motifs A. Salt Water and the Cure Water is a recurring motif. Its appearance across two separate stories in the same collection suggests authorial design rather than coincidence. The Feast of the Assumption beach scene in “Assumptions” and the nearly identical scene in “Useless Things” (same beach, same “cure,” an almost identical description of “the waves beyond glimmer[ing] like sparks from an unquenchable fire”) can be read as a diptych: two women, two summers, the same ritual, the same collapse into an accidental baptism by “a spirited breaker” that “razed them in its wake.” The repetition is examined at length in the companion essay “Unquenchable Fire” . In his author’s note, Mulhern explicitly defends this kind of return: “This is why, across my work, I return again and again to the same scenes, the same symbols, the same faces. I do it deliberately… What looks like repetition is recurrence, and recurrence is how the spirit comes to know itself.” Water in these stories cures nothing in a literal sense — Peggy dies delusional, Mrs. Muldoon dies within weeks of her “cure” — yet it produces a moment of unguarded joy and touch, “kneeling forward, laughing so hard that they cried.” Water washes nothing clean; it makes contact briefly possible. B. Food and Candy as Vectors of Love and Poison Mulhern repeatedly makes food the medium through which love is expressed and, twice, through which death is delivered. Peppermint candy appears first as an innocent childhood pleasure — “enjoying the deliciousness of peppermint candy, swinging our legs together” in “Assumptions” — and then becomes, in the story that bears its name, a murder weapon: a teacher poisons a peppermint with Visine “to lightly rub” onto a student’s candy, in retaliation for classroom humiliation. Chocolate chip cookies undergo an identical transformation across two stories: in “Mia Bambina,” Nonna’s cookies begin as an act of grandmotherly love (“Nonna loves mia bambina”) and end as the delivery vehicle for the cyanide that kills a hated roommate — “Not a problem,” Nonna says, agreeing to bake “the special cookies” as though asked for an extra egg. The pattern asks readers to receive food as affection before showing it as a vehicle for harm. C. The “Useless Thing” That Is Secretly Sacred The collection’s title-adjacent phrase, “useless things,” operates as an ironic motif that inverts itself by the end of nearly every story that deploys it. Nonna dismisses the possessions of the aging and dying as clutter — “When you get old you accumulate a lot of useless things, Molly. And then you become one of them” — and the story ends with Molly holding a gold necklace from the dead woman’s final gift, pronouncing it, in the story’s closing line, “A useless thing.” But the story has just spent its final pages proving the opposite: that even a corpse, even a cheap piece of costume jewelry, carries unbearable weight. The irony recurs in “A Bath,” where sea lettuce scraped from the rocks of Clew Bay — “’Twasn’t the best food, but it was all we needed” — becomes, decades later and an ocean away, the emotional key that unlocks the entire story’s meaning, quoted almost verbatim in the collection’s own title. Mulhern’s motif work depends on this kind of long-distance echo: a phrase planted in one story’s margin becomes, chapters later, the frame for the whole book. D. The Body in Decay Mulhern does not flinch from physical decomposition, and he uses it with unusual frequency as a motif rather than a shock effect. Two separate corpses in this collection — Mrs. Muldoon and Myra Bocca — are described with near-identical clinical attention to skin discoloration, fluid, and insect activity, a repetition that cannot be accidental. Mrs. Muldoon: “Her skin was green, purple and black… a bloody maggot emerged from her right ear.” Myra Bocca, struck by a car: “the skin from her nose had ripped off revealing the cartilage… Her dentures lay on the street, smeared with blood and phlegm.” The doubling suggests that Mulhern is not interested in any single character’s death so much as in death itself as a recurring visitor to these communities — an idea he makes explicit through Hunter S. Thompson’s line, quoted directly in “Useless Things”: “We are all alone, born alone, die alone… we shall all someday look back on our lives and see that, in spite of company, we were alone the whole way.” The corpse, appearing twice in near-identical language, becomes less a plot event than a structural refrain — a memento mori embedded in the architecture of the book itself. IV. Character Archetypes A. The Profane Grandmother-Confessor Nonna (also called Helen in “Assumptions” and “A Bath”) is a central archetype in the collection: a foul-mouthed, whiskey-drinking matriarch who dispenses both moral instruction and moral corruption in the same sentence, often the same breath. She can say, with total sincerity, “You’re a beautiful, smart woman... Who needs them anyway? Men are not so great,” and, moments later, casually reveal she stole silverware for her mobster boyfriend. She resists a simple reading: readers may not decide whether she is the collection’s moral center or its original corrupting force. She recurs, with variations, as Nana in “A Bath” and Nonna throughout the Molly Bonamici stories, functioning as a kind of stock figure — in the mode of a commedia dell’arte type rather than a conventionally “rounded” character — while speaking in sharply specific dialogue: “Cause she’s rotten, Molly... She had the gall to tell one of the judges that she filed divorce simply because she wanted to find out how much money Lazarus had.” B. The Charlatan-Healer Lady Jane, Myra Bocca, and (in a lower key) the faith healer subplot of “Useless Things” collectively establish a recurring type: the woman who performs spiritual authority for profit and validation, often while being, herself, in genuine psychological or financial distress. Myra’s introduction — “I’m a bit psychic... I’m activating your forehead chakra” — is immediately undercut by Gabe’s deflating observation that her “psychic” perception of Massachusetts origins was simply an accent, and later fully demolished by Alexander Michaelis’s testimony that she is “evil... a sociopath.” Yet Mulhern denies the reader an uncomplicated villain: Myra dies moments after being unmasked, in a grotesque accident that briefly restores her humanity — “However dishonest she was, she didn’t deserve to die that way.” The charlatan-healer archetype exists in this collection to be exposed, and then, immediately, to be grieved. C. The Watchful, Precociously Clinical Child Molly Bonamici, the boy narrator of “Assumptions,” and Billy in “A Bath” all share a defining trait: a preternatural verbal and observational intelligence that alienates them from the adults meant to be shaping them, and that eventually curdles (in Molly’s case, explicitly) into something dangerous. Molly’s IQ of “148, almost genius level” is mentioned twice by other characters, always as a kind of warning label. This archetype allows Mulhern to narrate scenes of adult depravity through a voice too young to have the moral vocabulary to condemn what it sees, producing the book’s characteristic flatness of affect around horror: “I turned, accidentally stepping on one of Mrs. Muldoon’s bare feet. The skin cracked; a clear fluid oozed…” The sentence continues in the same register as any other observation in the story. That flatness is not authorial insensitivity; it is a rendering of a child’s-eye view in which moral horror has not yet been taught, only cataloged. D. The Institution in Slow Collapse Schools, in “Peppermint Candy” and “Drenched to the Bone,” function as a collective archetype: bureaucratic structures that perform concern (incident reports, I.E.P. meetings, security cameras) while failing, structurally and repeatedly, to protect the people inside them. The vending machine looting, the broken surveillance cameras (“Evidently, she screwed up. She didn’t have the damn camera on”), the tar dust falling from an unmaintained vent, and the near-strangling of one student by another in a classroom — all in a single story — build a portrait of institutional entropy that mirrors, at a civic scale, the domestic entropy of the Molly Bonamici stories. Principal Jackson, revealed late in “Drenched to the Bone” to be quietly overwhelmed by a mother with dementia and an unemployed brother, exemplifies Mulhern’s insistence that institutional failure is not incompetence but exhaustion — another instance of the collection’s refusal to separate cruelty from suffering. V. Allusion and Literary Lineage The collection draws on a range of literary and religious references, using them less as ornament than as part of its argument. The epigraph from the Song of Solomon (“You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you”) frames the entire title story as a meditation on how scripture’s language of perfect beauty might be extended to a woman conventionally regarded as monstrous — an interpretive move elaborated in “Altogether Beautiful.” Titian’s Assunta receives a full ekphrastic treatment in the same story — “A startled Mary, arms spread above her upturned face, is being lifted on a cloud toward heaven... It is difficult to tell whether the crowd of apostles below is reaching to pull her down or to push her upwards” — and that ambiguity (rescue or restraint?) offers a visual parallel to the collection’s treatment of care and harm as indistinguishable gestures. Poe appears twice, doing double duty: Helen Thano vomits during a classroom reading of “The Pit and the Pendulum” in “Peppermint Candy,” linking Gothic dread to the mundane cruelty of adolescence, and is later invoked (mistakenly, by a character who confuses him with Shakespeare) in “Mia Bambina” — a small, very funny piece of characterization-through-misattribution that also gently reminds the reader how casually literary knowledge is possessed, half-possessed, or performed by Mulhern’s people. Thoreau and Emerson anchor “Drenched to the Bone” as the occasion for an explicit meditation on conscience versus institution — “Nothing is at last sacred but the integrity of your own mind” — and Mulhern extends this Transcendentalist frame into his own authorial voice in the closing “Note from the Author,” where he names Emerson, Thoreau, and Whitman directly as writers who taught him “to trust the inner light,” “to look long and closely at the near and the small until they open,” and that “a single life, honestly told, contains multitudes.” The note provides a statement of influences, connecting a book about grandmothers, faith healers, and grotesque deaths to nineteenth-century American Transcendentalism. Hunter S. Thompson’s dictum on solitary death, quoted verbatim in “Useless Things,” and Karl Marx’s “opium of the people” (misquoted by a student as “the oxycodone of the masses” in “Drenched to the Bone,” then corrected by the teacher-narrator) round out a pattern: Mulhern likes to let his characters half-remember or garble the tradition they are inheriting, dramatizing at the level of a single misquotation the same process of imperfect transmission that structures his plots. VI. Craft Technique and Style A. The Accretive, Catalog-Driven Sentence Mulhern’s prose style, particularly in scenes of sensory abundance or decay, favors long accretive sentences built from serial appositives and lists, a technique that mimics the overwhelming, undifferentiated flood of memory itself. Describing Peggy Fleming in the collection’s opening paragraph: “Her face was swollen and pasty, with broken capillaries that sloped down the sides of her nostrils, flooding the arid plain of her skin, like some dreary river and its tributaries eking over a delta of nasolabial folds to terminate in the red seas of two droopy cheeks.” The sentence extends an anatomical description into a full topographical metaphor — face as riverine landscape — without pausing for breath, and this expansive, clause-stacking method recurs at moments of both beauty (the Nantasket Beach passages) and horror (the corpse descriptions), suggesting that for Mulhern, intensity of any kind — comic, erotic, grotesque, sacred — demands the same syntactic strategy: accumulation rather than compression. B. Free Indirect Discourse Braided with Retrospective Irony Mulhern’s first-person narrators consistently blend the voice and vocabulary of their past, younger selves with the interpretive hindsight of an adult narrator, often within a single paragraph, without typographic signal. In “Assumptions,” the boy who “shook my head, wondering... what a jinnit must be” is the same narrator who, sentences later, delivers a fully adult reading of the Assumption dogma’s theological history and Pope Pius XII’s 1950 declaration. This is a controlled anachronism, not a lapse: it allows Mulhern to hold childhood’s innocent literalism and adulthood’s ironic knowledge in permanent, unresolved tension — formally enacting the book’s thematic obsession with inheritance and its long-delayed comprehension. C. Dialect, Malapropism, and Comic Diction as Characterization Mulhern renders working-class Boston Irish and Italian-American speech through phonetic and idiomatic details — “Terties” for “thirties,” “cazzone” mistaken for “calzone,” “squash rot” for alcohol-induced dementia, “knackered” and “crikey” marking the Scottish-inflected Evy — and uses these malapropisms for warmth and comic release, often when a scene threatens to become sad. Nonna’s insult, delivered mid-argument, that Mary Muldoon should ask for money because “she keeps a stack of cash in her bread box,” interrupts a scene of real cruelty with comedy. The shifts between comic and darker material are an important part of the collection’s tonal pattern. D. The Deadpan Ending Mulhern regularly closes his stories on a single flat, unembellished line that reframes everything preceding it without any authorial comment. “A useless thing” ends “Useless Things”; brief, deadpan closing lines of this kind recur across the collection, most devastatingly in “Peppermint Candy,” which ends not with confession or consequence but with chilling procedural calm: “I retrieved the peppermints from my desk drawer and placed them in my satchel. I would share them again another day.” The refusal to editorialize at the exact moment the reader most wants editorial guidance is a deliberate withholding, and it is what gives these stories their unusual, lingering unease — Mulhern trusts the juxtaposition of the plain sentence against the preceding horror to do the moral work no character will do explicitly. E. Stylistic Range Across the Collection The collection moves among several registers. “Assumptions” and “A Bath” work in a lyrical-elegiac register built for memory and grief. “Useless Things,” “A Nun’s Arse,” and “Myra Bocca” shift into a broader comic-picaresque mode, dense with dialect and incident. “Peppermint Candy” and “Drenched to the Bone” move into a spare, present-tense, almost clinical realism suited to institutional settings and slow-burning despair. Titian, cyanide-laced cookies, Thoreau, and a joke about calzones sit beside one another in this mix; the collection connects them through its recurring concern with care and harm. VII. Conclusion: What the Book Insists On All We Ever Needed asks readers to consider whether the people who love us may also be the people who damage us. The book’s closing “Note from the Author” supplies the theological frame explicitly: “The sacred, I believe, is not far off but here — in a kitchen, a sickroom, a stretch of shoreline, the face of someone loved and lost.” Read against the stories, that sentence can be taken literally: the sacred, in this book, is in the kitchen — in Nonna’s poisoned cookies as much as her chocolate-chip ones, in the bathwater as much as the bruise that precedes it. The collection returns to a version of mercy that acknowledges its own capacity for harm, using sentence rhythms, recurring motifs, and a limited amount of editorial comment to hold that tension in view. — Silver Current Press Works Quoted James Mulhern, All We Ever Needed (Philadelphia: Silver Current Press, 2026). All quotations are drawn from the collection’s stories “Assumptions,” “A Bath,” “Useless Things,” “Peppermint Candy,” “A Nun’s Arse,” “Myra Bocca,” “Mia Bambina,” and “Drenched to the Bone,” and from the collection’s “Introduction” and “A Note from the Author.” Related essays on this site: Altogether Beautiful reads “Assumptions” against the Catholic dogma; Unquenchable Fire follows the fire and water imagery in the same story; The Sacred in the Shabby traces the governing method across the fiction; and The Quiet Cartographer of Irish-American Memory situates the whole body of work within the Irish-American literary tradition. title: Altogether Beautiful — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: Altogether Beautiful
description: A close reading of James Mulhern's 'Assumptions': its epigraph, the Assumption feast, and the story's images of stain, care, and mortality.
text: Altogether Beautiful — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On Religious Interpretation Altogether Beautiful Reading “Assumptions” against the Catholic dogma of the Assumption — and asking what it means to grant a flawed, ordinary body the imagery reserved for the sinless one. “Tota pulchra es, amica mea, et macula non est in te.” — Song of Solomon 4:7 in the Vulgate; epigraph to “Assumptions” The title carries two meanings at once. “Assumptions” names the small cruelties of a family that has already decided, before the beach trip even starts, what Peg is worth — “the homeliest damn woman” in the family, good for a joke, not much else. But capitalized, in Catholic usage, an Assumption is a specific doctrine: the teaching, defined by Pope Pius XII in the 1950 apostolic constitution Munificentissimus Deus , that the Virgin Mary was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory at the close of her earthly life, spared the ordinary corruption of the grave. The story explores the tension between these senses of its title, asking whether the second sense — a body received into glory rather than left to decay — can be imagined in relation to a body that has already failed every test implied by the first. The epigraph is the antiphon of the feast The verse that opens the story is not chosen for its sweetness. In the Vulgate, Song of Solomon 4:7 reads Tota pulchra es, amica mea, et macula non est in te . From the fourth century onward that verse, with Mary’s name substituted for the beloved’s, has been sung as Tota pulchra es, Maria — one of the oldest Marian prayers in the Latin Church. In the older chant books it is assigned to two feasts. One of them is August 15: the Feast of the Assumption, which is the day on which the story takes place. So the epigraph is not a poetic flourish laid over a summer outing. It is the proper chant of the liturgical day the plot occupies. And it supplies the story’s single most important word. Macula means stain. Immaculate means unstained. Now read the first close description of Peggy’s body on the morning of that feast: “Her housedress, which had a pattern of tiny roses, shrouded a pair of small black boots; there were red stains at the end of her sleeves from where she had spilled some juice.” — “Assumptions” The epigraph promises a body without stain. The body arrives marked — in red, at the ends of the sleeves, which is to say at the wrists, which is where the nails go. The dress that carries the stains is patterned with roses, the flower of the Litany of Loreto and of the Passion. And the dress does not cover the boots; it shrouds them, three pages before the woman wearing it will need a shroud. None of this is announced. The narrator supplies an innocuous explanation in the same clause — spilled juice — and moves on. One possible reading is that the story places sacred associations in the language of the shabby without having a character point them out. The sacramental sequence disguised as a day at the beach Once the pattern is visible, the Nantasket excursion reads as a sequence of sacraments performed by people who would be astonished to hear them called that. Tanning oil is rubbed into a bald scalp, forehead, and neck — and oil poured on the head is what makes a king, a priest, an anointed one ; it is also what the woman with the alabaster jar did at Bethany, of which Christ said she had done it beforehand for his burial. Peggy dies within days. A gust lifts her wig; a child catches it and holds it up “like the head of John the Baptist”; the narrator smooths it and buries it in a paper bag with a stone he has found near the water. A head, a shroud, and a stone: an entombment, performed as play, on the morning of the feast. What is buried is the false hair. What comes out of the sea an hour later is the true head, anointed and shining. A mourning dove starts from a cleft in the rocks, rises, and then descends over the water at the exact spot where two women are wading in. That is the Baptism of the Jordan, and the cleft in the rock is Song of Songs 2:14. A wave nobody asked for knocks both women flat and leaves them kneeling in the surf, laughing until they cry — a total immersion administered by force, arriving at the posture of prayer by accident. And when a boy reaches down and she takes his hand, the sentence reads: she rose from the sea . Judgment’s imagery, reissued to mercy One striking element of the story is not simply its use of religious imagery but its altered emphasis. Nothing abject is removed; images of condemnation can be reread in the light of mercy or glory. Unquenchable fire , the Gospels’ own phrase for hell, becomes sunlight glittering on the water as two women walk into the sea. Baldness, a curse in Isaiah, becomes “a laurel of peach-fuzz hair” garlanded at the temples — a crown, and behind it the Coronation that follows the Assumption. The stigmata become spilled juice on a housedress sleeve. Chrism becomes suntan lotion; the entombment becomes a paper bag; the purple robe of the mocked king becomes a beach towel spread over two children so they will not burn. And the Cross appears in the final sentence as a Father’s “crossed arms” in the act of cradling a dead woman’s head and kissing her cheek — the instrument of death disclosed as the shape of an embrace. Not one story: a body of work The pattern is not confined to a single story, though its extent remains open to interpretation. A line-by-line survey of the whole corpus — two novels, three story collections, the poems, and twenty-eight pieces published in literary magazines — has catalogued 1,096 passages associated with scripture, liturgy, hagiography, iconography, and a literary line running from Yeats and Joyce through Dante to Flannery O’Connor. Four kinds of evidence hold the case together. The doctrine is quoted, not gestured at. The text of the 1950 constitution appears inside a short story. Mark 15:33–34 and 16:6 are read verbatim over two caskets in Molly Bonamici . John 1:1, Matthew 7:6, Romans 6:23, and Genesis 1:26–28 all appear directly. The same images recur for three decades. The Feast of the Assumption. A seawater cure at Nantasket. A wet silvery scalp and a crown the boy will not touch. A mourning dove out of its cleft. “Up you go. On the count of three.” Twenty-four such repetitions have been documented across the books, sometimes in identical sentences — a private liturgy, returned to on a cycle the way a missal returns to the same propers every August. Revision runs toward the sacred, not away from it. A poem was changed from “At dawn, he was gone” to “When I wake, I find that he has gone,” moving the resurrection parallel off objective paschal dawn and onto the mourner’s own waking. Another draft sharpens into the grammar of Psalm 130. A third swaps embers for paper and keeps the smoke rising. A magazine reprint cut the Lughnasadh material and the line about hell; the book keeps them. The pattern may also be absent. One story in The Weight of Small Mercies lacks the transfiguring apparatus entirely — no ghost, no holy object, no cure, no scriptural frame — and has a notably bleak tone within the cycle. The contrast offers a useful check on this interpretation. An Irish Catholicism of the small mercy There is no functioning priest anywhere in these books who does what a priest is for. A grandmother invents a nickname after a sermon on the power of names and thereby confers a grace that reaches, by the last page, into the Trinity. Another leads the blessing. Another absolves on a park bench. Another administers a counterfeit Eucharist to a woman in an institution. The men are dead, absent, silent, drunk, or at work. The Church in this fiction is a matriarchy operating without a license, and it works. And characters who deny God outright may still grieve in Catholic language. The stories suggest people for whom Catholicism has stopped being true without ceasing to be an available language. Canonization, not catharsis Catharsis purges. This work converts. The stain stays and becomes a wound; drunkenness stays and becomes Pentecost; a gold crucifix is dismissed as “a useless thing,” which is Saint Paul’s own doctrine — God chose the foolish things, and the despised things, and the things which are not. In 1950 a pope closed a document with the words we pronounce, declare, and define . The story closes: Completely awake—laughing, altogether beautiful, and divine—she rises once again to sing her favorite song . Glory, for Peggy Fleming, is a Friday night set in a Back Bay dive with her husband at a table near the front. The closing language recalls the pope’s formulation, spoken by a boy about a woman others have treated unkindly. Tota pulchra es. There is no flaw in you. What makes that ending land is partly what the story never says. Set on the Feast of the Assumption, it withholds almost the entire vocabulary of the thing it performs. There is no altar , no amen , no rosary , no mercy , no sacrifice , no resurrection , no veil , no baptism , no canonization . Even grace and spirit never appear as nouns — the story allows only “gracious” and “spirited,” the adjectives, kept down at the level of manners and temperament. In their place stand folk substitutes and plain speech: “Mary’s blessing,” “a cure,” “miracles,” “Lovely Peggy,” and a repeated practical vocabulary of getting wet, helping, and rising. A story that stages a canonization refuses the nouns that would declare one. The ordinary words carry the weight instead, and they arrive in the compromised sense first. Body is a judged physical body long before it is “body and soul.” Cure begins as a folk rite and slides into joints, bowels, and wet boots. Cross is mostly a verb for getting across a street or a threshold. Wine is never consecrated; it is a smell in a kitchen. White does five different jobs, and the first is a white lie — so that by the time clothing is “white as snow,” the reader is being asked to hold the harmless deception inside the exalted image rather than replace one with the other. That is the story’s actual method: not sacred language applied to a shabby life, but household language put under pressure until it will bear a sacred reading without ever announcing that it has. title: The Architecture of Attention: Craft, Motif, Theme, and Allusion in James Mulhern — An Essay
heading: The Architecture of Attention
description: A survey of James Mulhern's craft signature, recurring tropes, thematic architecture, and allusive practice across his fiction, poetry, and teaching.
text: The Architecture of Attention: Craft, Motif, Theme, and Allusion in James Mulhern — An Essay ← Back to The 2601 Salon A Close Reading · On the Whole Body of Work The Architecture of Attention Craft, motif, theme, and allusion across the fiction, poetry, and teaching of James Mulhern — a synthesis of the techniques that make his recurrences a coherent, disciplined vision rather than a set of habits. Abstract Mulhern has written, of his own method, that he “place[s] the ordinary and the unspeakable in the same paragraph” and trusts that a detail, “watched closely enough and long enough,” will “tell me what it is actually for.” 1 This essay reads that stated method against the demonstrable evidence of the corpus, synthesizing findings developed in greater depth across the site's other essays into a single account of four interlocking systems: a sentence-level and structural craft signature (missing dialogue tags, action-beat attribution, second sight as a licensed point-of-view exemption, genetic revision visible across published texts); a set of recurring tropes (fire, water, thresholds, sacred objects hidden inside shabby ones); a six-part thematic architecture (faith and doubt, family as fortress and prison, the sacred ordinary, inherited guilt, the ethics of listening, the persistence of the dead); and a disciplined allusive practice in which names, scripture, and canonical texts are deployed as compressed, load-bearing citations rather than ornament. Taken together, these systems constitute what this essay calls an architecture of attention — a body of work organized less around plot mechanics than around the sustained, disciplined act of looking hard at what most fiction considers beneath its notice. Contents I. A Stated Method, Tested Against the Text II. Craft Signature: The Sentence-Level Techniques III. Structural Craft: Second Sight, Compression, and the Point-of-View Exemption IV. Recurring Tropes: Fire, Water, and the Sacred Hidden in the Shabby V. The Thematic Architecture: Six Pillars VI. Allusive Practice: Names, Scripture, and Citation as Compression VII. Genetic Evidence: Revision as a Visible Process VIII. Conclusion: Devotion as a Working Method I. A Stated Method, Tested Against the Text Critics writing about a living author have an advantage rarely available to critics of the dead: the author has, in this case, described his own method directly, and that description can be checked against the work rather than merely inferred from it. Mulhern's introduction to All We Ever Needed states that “I take language to be a sacred inheritance and the act of naming to be a kind of devotion”; 2 his essay on craft states that his habit is “to place the ordinary and the unspeakable in the same paragraph — a teacup poured, a lie confessed; a hand laid on a bald scalp, a body quietly dying under it,” and that he trusts a closely watched detail to “tell me what it is actually for,” adding that “it is very rarely only what it appears to be.” 1 He describes revision not as correction but as “listening harder to a draft that already knows more than I did when I wrote it,” 1 and his credo names attention itself, rather than any particular belief, as the discipline his work is built to practice: “Our failure, then, is not principally a failure of faith but of attention.” 3 These statements of method offer a useful lens for the work. This essay considers whether the missing dialogue tags, recurring fire and water, thematic concerns, and citational names might be read together as related habits operating at the scales of the sentence, scene, book, and broader body of work. II. Craft Signature: The Sentence-Level Techniques At the level of the individual sentence, Mulhern's fiction often favors a small set of techniques that a companion essay on this site discusses in detail: limited use of explanatory dialogue tags, physical action beats in place of “he said”/“she said,” and the em dash for self-interruption and withheld speech. 4 In stories including “A Bath” and “Myra Bocca,” these choices can make dialogue feel closer to overheard exchange, leaving the placement of a dash or the length of a line to carry information that adverbs and commentary might otherwise provide. 4 The approach resembles the author’s stated preference for allowing material to stand without immediate interpretation. A related withholding appears in Mulhern's handling of first-person confession and justification. A companion essay identifies a recurring narrative posture the site calls the unreliable confession: a first-person narrator — the poisoner of “Peppermint Candy,” the killer in “Mia Bambina” — who reports morally catastrophic action in the same flat, procedural diction used for filing paperwork or pouring orange juice, offering justification without a narratorial signal that the justification should be doubted. 5 Rather than declaring their unreliability, these narrators can sound reasonable, leaving readers to register the gap between the calm register and the content being described. III. Structural Craft: Second Sight, Compression, and the Point-of-View Exemption In Give Them Unquiet Dreams , the device of second sight provides a sustained way of managing access to information. A companion essay reads it not primarily as theme but as narrative technology: a feature of the novel’s world that permits foreshadowing, brings three generations and two continents of family history into scenes a fourteen-year-old narrator can plausibly witness, and connects a supernatural premise to the plot concerning a mother’s psychiatric commitment. 6 The device addresses a familiar challenge of first-person narration — how a temporally bound consciousness can encounter information beyond ordinary realistic access — through material that draws on Irish folk cosmology rather than flashback chapters or omniscient narration. 6 Related questions arise in Mulhern's child and adolescent narrators. A companion essay argues that Molly Bonamici and the young Aiden Glencar may be unreliable less because their perception fails than because their affect is withheld: they report what they see while lacking, or declining, the interpretive frame to say what it costs them. Because both novels are narrated from an adult retrospective vantage, this withholding can work on two temporal tracks — what the child did not understand in the moment, and what the adult narrator, looking back, still leaves unexplained. 7 This approach lets a coming-of-age narrative remain unsettled between childhood innocence and retrospective understanding. IV. Recurring Tropes: Fire, Water, and the Sacred Hidden in the Shabby Across the fiction and poetry, a small set of images recur with enough consistency that the site's essays treat them as a compositional system rather than coincidence: fire, which moves in Mulhern's work from a scriptural register of damnation into “the shimmer over a baptism”; 8 water, which carries “tears, rain, tide pools, and the unglamorous water of the sickroom” as the element that transmits mercy across the corpus; 9 and thresholds — doorways, crosswalks, the border between sleep and waking — that recur so often across the poetry and fiction that a companion essay reads them as a governing structural device rather than incidental staging. 10 Underneath all three tropes runs a single governing conviction the site's essays call the sacred in the shabby: “the holy in James Mulhern's work always arrives disguised as the ordinary — a housedress, a bottle of suntan oil, a classroom of restless teenagers.” 11 This is not merely a thematic preference; it is, per the author's own account of his working method, the actual mechanism by which his images are generated — he does not begin with an intended symbol and search for an object to carry it, but returns obsessively to a concrete image (a housedress, a beach, a bottle of oil) until, in his words, “the language underneath the language declared itself.” 1 V. The Thematic Architecture: Six Pillars A full-length comparative study on this site identifies six thematic pillars running through the corpus: faith and doubt; family as both fortress and prison; the ordinary understood as sacred; the persistence of the dead among the living; inherited guilt passed forward across generations; and the ethics of unauthorized confession — who is granted the authority to hear what cannot otherwise be said, and what that authority costs the listener. 12 These six pillars are demonstrably not independent thematic preoccupations that happen to recur in the same author's work; they are structurally interdependent, each pillar supplying the conditions the others require. Family functions as prison specifically because it is also fortress — the same intimacy that protects a character from the outside world (Aiden shielding Laura from psychiatric scrutiny, Billy shielding his mother's silence in “A Bath”) is what makes betrayal from within the family so costly. Inherited guilt persists specifically because the dead persist — Sinead's death by the well does not resolve into the past tense because Catherine's guilt, and later Aiden's inherited obligation to close the account with Rita, keep it structurally present across three generations. 13 And the ethics of confession matter specifically because none of Mulhern's confessors — grandmothers, children, a boy speaking for his dead grandmother — hold institutional warrant for the power they exercise, which is what makes each confessional scene a live moral question rather than a settled sacrament. 14 VI. Allusive Practice: Names, Scripture, and Citation as Compression Mulhern's allusive practice operates chiefly through naming, and a companion essay on this site demonstrates that his character names function as compressed citations rather than euphonious labels: Molly Bonamici imports Defoe's Moll Flanders, a survivor narrating her own moral compromises in flat, unsentimental first person, into a surname that means “good friends” and is worn by a woman who kills, calmly, out of family loyalty. 15 Myra Bocca imports Fitzgerald's Myrtle Wilson — killed by a car in The Great Gatsby — through near-homophony, so that a reader who catches the echo has effectively been told the plot in advance, while “Bocca” (Italian for “mouth”) literalizes the character's compulsive talkativeness before she speaks a line. 16 Peggy Fleming imports the 1968 Olympic figure skater's name into a body devastated by disease and alcoholism, a cruelty the text names explicitly, while quietly preserving in the character one faculty — performed grace under difficult conditions — that the allusion's source figure was famous for. 17 This is allusion functioning as the author's own stated principle of naming as devotion made technical: each name is a promise the narrative goes on to keep, ironize, or literalize, and the promise is legible only to a reader willing to hear names as citations rather than sounds. A second allusive register operates through direct citation of religious and canonical material: the Marian dogma of the Assumption structuring “Assumptions”'s religious architecture, 18 the Emerson-and-Thoreau classroom scene in Give Them Unquiet Dreams naming Mulhern's Transcendentalist inheritance directly, 19 and W. B. Yeats's Celtic Twilight supplying the folkloric taxonomy — banshees, second sight, the porousness of the dead and the living — that Mulhern relocates from rural Sligo into Irish-American Boston. 20 In every register, allusion in Mulhern's work does compression's job: it lets a single name or a single borrowed image carry a weight of inherited meaning the text itself does not have to spell out, precisely the same economy his stated method claims for the ordinary object watched closely enough to reveal what it is actually for. VII. Genetic Evidence: Revision as a Visible Process Because Mulhern's fiction and poetry have been published, republished, and adapted across multiple texts over more than a decade, the corpus offers something most contemporary fiction does not: visible genetic evidence of the author's own revision process. A companion essay on this site documents a bath scene redrafted from poem to story and a jetty passage duplicated within a single collection, arguing that these are not oversights but evidence of the same recursive attention the author describes in his own account of craft — a writer who returns to an image across forms and years because, in his words, revision means “listening harder to a draft that already knows more than I did when I wrote it.” 21 A separate bibliographic essay traces “Assumptions” across its four published texts — a 2015 web publication, a 2016 collection, a 2020 journal printing, and a 2026 return to book form — documenting the specific textual variants introduced at each stage. 22 Read together, this genetic record confirms that the recurrence critics observe across Mulhern's corpus — the same image, the same family, the same theological question returning in a new form — is not merely thematic preoccupation observed from outside the work. It is a documented, textually verifiable compositional practice: the author himself keeps returning to redraft the same material until, by his own account, it tells him what it was for. VIII. Conclusion: Devotion as a Working Method The four systems this essay has traced — sentence-level craft, structural invention, recurring trope, and allusive citation — do not operate independently of one another; they are different resolutions of the same instrument. The missing dialogue tag and the second-sight narrator are both refusals to let narratorial mediation stand between a reader and material the author trusts to speak for itself. The recurring fire and water and the citational names are both methods of compression, letting a single image or a single borrowed name carry inherited meaning the prose does not need to state outright. And the genetic evidence of redrafted scenes confirms that this is not simply a set of finished techniques deployed once and left alone, but an active, ongoing practice of return — the same discipline of attention the author names directly when he writes that imagination is “a gift on loan from something larger than myself” and that to write, therefore, “is not self-expression. It is stewardship.” 23 What this essay has called an architecture of attention is, finally, that stewardship made visible at every scale of the work: a body of fiction and poetry organized not around what happens, but around what a writer is willing to keep looking at until it tells him what it is actually for. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. title: Book Club Companions — James Mulhern
heading: Book Club Companions
description: Reading-group guides for every book by James Mulhern: Crossings, Give Them Unquiet Dreams, Molly Bonamici, Assumptions and Other Stories, and A Prayer for Home.
text: Book Club Companions — James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon For Reading Groups Book Club Companions Discussion guides for every Silver Current Press title by James Mulhern. Reading-group guides for every Silver Current Press title by James Mulhern — a poetry collection, two novels, a story collection, and a novella. Facilitators are encouraged to select a handful of questions from each guide rather than working through every one in a single sitting. Jump to a Companion Crossings (Poetry) Give Them Unquiet Dreams Molly Bonamici Assumptions and Other Stories A Prayer for Home Poetry Collection · 2026 Crossings Twenty poems of family, inheritance, and threshold. This companion has its own full page, with questions grouped by Voice, Themes, and Line Breaks, plus a critical essay on sensory imagery. Open the full Crossings Companion · View on Amazon Novel · 2019 · Kirkus Starred Review Give Them Unquiet Dreams A novel about the haunted territory of family — what we inherit, what we conceal, and what eventually surfaces — set in 1970s Irish Catholic Boston. The novel is set in 1970s Irish Catholic Boston. How does the historical and religious setting shape what characters are able to say to each other directly, versus what stays unspoken? Kirkus described the novel as “a luminous, beautifully told fairy tale grounded in history and elevated by spirit.” Where do you see the fairy-tale register enter a story otherwise grounded in realistic family history? The book concerns what a family inherits, conceals, and eventually cannot keep hidden. Choose one secret in the novel and trace how its concealment shapes the people around it, not just the person keeping it. How does memory function as a structural device in the novel — is the past treated as settled, or as something still being negotiated by the present-day characters? Discuss the novel’s pacing. Where does Mulhern let a scene breathe, and where does he compress years into a paragraph? What determines that choice? What role does Catholic faith and ritual play for the characters — comfort, obligation, or something more ambiguous? How does the novel handle grief across generations? Do older and younger characters grieve differently, and if so, how? By the novel’s end, what has actually changed for the family, and what has simply been named or acknowledged for the first time? Novel · 2016 Molly Bonamici A literary coming-of-age novel set in Italian-American Boston, whose narrator argues with The Great Gatsby even as she borrows its central image for her own longing. Molly rejects The Great Gatsby on first reading — “Daisy was a pain in the ass, and Gatsby was anything but great” — and then adopts Fitzgerald’s green light as her own image of longing. What does it mean that she argues with a book even as she borrows from it? The novel opens with epigraphs from Shakespeare’s Hamlet and Dante’s Paradiso. How do those two very different texts frame what follows? How does Molly’s relationship with her grandmother, Nonna, differ from her relationship with her mother? What does each relationship supply that the other cannot? Molly fears “the cult of domesticity” and ending up “like my mother in a horrible relationship.” How does the novel treat her resistance to that inherited path — as rebellion, self-preservation, or something else? Discuss the novel as a coming-of-age story set in Italian-American Boston. What does its specific cultural and geographic setting add that a more generic setting would lose? Where does the novel use comedy alongside its more serious family material? What is the effect of that mixture? How does Molly’s voice change, if at all, between the novel’s opening and closing chapters? What does the novel ultimately suggest about the possibility of choosing a different life than the one you were raised inside? Story Collection Assumptions and Other Stories Short fiction exploring interior lives and Catholic imagery, including questions of grace and doctrine. The collection has been compared to Flannery O’Connor, James Joyce, and Edgar Allan Poe. Choose one story and discuss which of those traditions it most resembles, and why. Reviewers have praised the collection’s mixture of “grace and despair.” Choose a story where both are present in the same scene, and discuss how Mulhern balances them. Many of these stories are told from a child’s or adolescent’s point of view looking back. What does that retrospective narration allow the stories to do that a present-tense child’s voice could not? Discuss the role of Catholic imagery and vocabulary across the collection. Is it treated with reverence, irony, both, or something harder to name? Where in the collection does an ordinary object or gesture — food, clothing, a household task — carry more emotional weight than the dialogue around it? How does the collection use humor, and what kind of moments does that humor tend to interrupt or soften? Choose two stories in the collection and compare how each handles a flawed or difficult family member with compassion rather than judgment. What do these stories, taken together, suggest about grace — where it comes from, and who is allowed to receive it? Novella · 2016 A Prayer for Home A spare, lyrical novella praised by The Missouri Review for its complex characters and “fantastic voice,” and a Wishing Shelf Red Ribbon Winner in the UK. The Missouri Review praised the novella’s “well-written, complex characters” and “fantastic voice.” What do you notice about the voice specifically — diction, rhythm, restraint — that creates that effect? As a shorter form than a novel, how does the novella compress its central relationships? What has to be implied rather than shown? The book was praised for feeling like it “literally jumps off the page.” Where does the prose feel most immediate or urgent, and what techniques create that effect? What does the title, A Prayer for Home , suggest about the novella’s central longing? Is that longing satisfied, denied, or left open by the ending? How does the novella’s spare, lyrical style shape your sense of the characters’ inner lives, compared to a more expansive or explanatory style? Discuss the idea of home in the novella — is it a place, a person, a feeling, or some combination?
