From the Reviewers Notices Selected passages from the press, with a brief editorial gloss beside each — attending to matters of style, craft, subject, and the layering of themes. Kirkus Reviews · Starred Give Them Unquiet Dreams · 28 July 2019 “A luminous, beautifully told fairy tale grounded in history and elevated by spirit.” Of the prose itself the reviewer writes that it “is strong, delivering readers a sense of the child in Aiden’s voice and a thorough, descriptive view of the world around him,” and praises “a liberal use of quotes and sayings ranging from Bible verses to Thoreau and Yeats, grounding the various players’ cultural context.” The notice closes on the book’s emotional architecture: “the rich characters who bring the novel to its greatest heights … give the sense that everything and everyone are connected across time, whether or not those ties are immediately perceived.” Editor’s Note on the Review Kirkus identifies Irish Catholic inheritance, the Thoreauvian inward gaze, and a child’s second sight as important elements in the novel. Its description of a “fairy tale grounded in history” suggests how folklore and 1970s Boston sit alongside grief, queer awakening, and the visible dead. The praise for Aiden’s voice also draws attention to a child narrator whose register moves between colloquial and literary language. Read the full review at Kirkus → Kirkus Reviews Molly Bonamici · 16 June 2020 “A gleefully and wonderfully odd protagonist eases readers into a bare-bones plot.” The reviewer reads Molly as a character of philosophical curiosity rather than dysfunction: “Molly’s apathy toward death isn’t as strange as other characters think, more a curiosity than an obsession,” and her religious posture is described as “continually (and interestingly) [questioning] it, like why would God allow horrible things to happen.” Even when the prose “hits the occasional standstill,” the notice grants that Molly’s “distinctiveness is an appealing quality and often amusing,” citing her now-much-quoted aside about maggots and word processors. Editor’s Note on the Review Kirkus has located the book’s real subject: the slow, half-comic theology of a woman who refuses both belief and unbelief and chooses instead to keep asking. The reviewer’s wariness about the “bare-bones plot” is, read another way, a notice of method: the novel is built less by event than by recurrence, returning Molly to the same questions across decades so that the reader feels time pass the way Molly does — through repetition rather than incident. The book belongs to a particular tradition of Catholic-haunted American comedy, and the review’s emphasis on voice is the right emphasis. Read the full review at Kirkus → Readers’ Favorite · Five Stars Molly Bonamici · Reviewed by JJ Phillips “James Mulhern did an excellent job of creating strong, colorful characters that lit up the page. There wasn’t a single clichéd or flat character among the plethora of people that Molly encountered.” Phillips emphasizes the central figure herself — “a strong female character that wasn’t afraid to show her weakness or vulnerabilities” — and the larger thematic claim the novel makes through her: “Molly discovers that life is a giant mystery and no one is prepared for life’s twists and turns.” The review closes simply: “I found her refreshing and very likeable. A job well done.” Editor’s Note on the Review What this review names well is the book’s populated quality. Mulhern is a writer of crowds — faith healers, grandmothers, neighbours, drifters — and the novel’s mood depends on no single one of them being a type. Phillips’s recognition of Molly as vulnerable beneath her composure points to the book’s emotional layering: the supernatural premise (the Angel-of-Death pronouncement) is never allowed to override the realism of an ordinary girl learning that life will not be explained to her in advance. Read the full review at Readers’ Favorite → The Wishing Shelf Book Awards · United Kingdom Give Them Unquiet Dreams · 2020 Finalist Red Ribbon Winner · Highly Recommended by The Wishing Shelf Book Awards . Give Them Unquiet Dreams was named a Finalist in the 2020 Wishing Shelf Book Awards and received the jury’s Red Ribbon — the “highly recommended” distinction reserved by the panel of British readers and book groups who serve as its judges. Editor’s Note on the Award The Wishing Shelf panel is composed of working readers and book clubs rather than trade critics, offering a reader-focused response to the novel. Its recognition notes how the book’s regional setting intersects with broader questions of family, belief, and the dead. View the 2020 Wishing Shelf Finalists → Kirkus Reviews Assumptions and Other Stories · 13 February 2017 “Tales of grace and despair abound … the quieter scenes show the mind of a talented writer at work.” The reviewer traces the early sequence of Molly-and-Nonna stories — the convent-gate robbery, the moral ambiguities — and notes that the collection is “influenced by writers such as Flannery O’Connor, James Joyce, and Edgar Allan Poe.” The praise lands on the muted register: “the quieter scenes show the mind of a talented writer at work.” Editor’s Note on the Review Kirkus places the collection alongside O’Connor and Joyce, noting moral irony, moments of grace, and quiet epiphany. The reviewer’s preference for “the quieter scenes” points toward the collection’s attention to ordinary lives. title: Class, Ethnicity, and the Boston Triple-Decker — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: Class, Ethnicity, and the Boston Triple-Decker
description: A social realist reading of James Mulhern's Irish-Catholic and Italian-American fictional geography — Jamaica Plain, Braintree, Revere — in the tradition of Faulkner's Yoknapatawpha.
text: Class, Ethnicity, and the Boston Triple-Decker — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On Fictional Geography Class, Ethnicity, and the Boston Triple-Decker A social realist reading of the Irish-Catholic and Italian-American neighborhoods — Jamaica Plain, Braintree, Revere — that make up James Mulhern’s coherent fictional map. Abstract This essay reads the Irish-Catholic and Italian-American settings of James Mulhern’s fiction — Jamaica Plain, Braintree, Revere, and the three-decker — as a recurring fictional geography. It draws on comparisons with Faulkner’s Yoknapatawpha and Alice McDermott’s Irish Catholic Long Island while considering how the triple-decker’s stacked, overheard intimacy can shape the confessions and cruelties in these plots. I. A Map Built From Kitchens Regional fiction often develops a sense of place, whether or not an actual map is printed. Faulkner’s Yoknapatawpha County, worked and reworked across more than a dozen novels, is a prominent American example: a single invented Mississippi county with recurring families, feuds, and geography whose layout scholars have assembled from internal textual evidence. 1 Alice McDermott likewise returns to Irish-Catholic parishes of Brooklyn and Long Island in novels like Charming Billy and Someone , revisiting wakes, church basements, and three-family houses. 2 Read across the short stories and Give Them Unquiet Dreams , James Mulhern’s work also returns to a Greater Boston of Jamaica Plain, Braintree, Revere, and the Jamaicaway, populated by Irish-Catholic and Italian-American families and by the recurring form of the three-decker, or triple-decker. Mulhern’s own editors gesture toward this geography without fully mapping it, describing his fiction’s enduring subject as “the streets and kitchens of Irish and Italian Boston” and noting that his Boston functions as “McDermott’s Brooklyn’s cousin: a city of women running households on will and grievance and enormous, unspoken tenderness.” 3 This essay follows that observation by tracing the neighborhoods named across the fiction and considering how their differences — Jamaica Plain’s Irish-Catholic parish culture, Braintree’s lower-middle-class remove from the city, Revere’s Italian immigrant enclave — contribute to the social setting. The triple-decker, in particular, can make intimacy and surveillance plausible pressures in the plots. II. Jamaica Plain: The Irish-Catholic Enclave and Its Casualties Peggy Fleming, the ruined, alcoholic center of “Assumptions,” is explicitly rooted in a single Boston neighborhood: she “grew up in Jamaica Plain, an Irish catholic enclave in Boston,” arriving in America in the nineteen-thirties on the sponsorship of her cousin Mary O’Malley, who had herself “preceded her from County Mayo fifteen years earlier.” 4 The neighborhood is textured with the specific institutions of first-generation Irish-Catholic life — the “socials, weekly gatherings in the basement of Saint Thomas More Church,” the cousin’s husband loading mail at South Station, the cousin herself “cleaning the houses of the ‘filthy rich on the hill’ — Mission Hill she meant.” 4 This is not decorative period detail; it is a precise class map in miniature, placing Peggy’s cousin’s family as domestic labor for the same hill their own parish overlooks, and placing Peggy herself, later, as the family’s trusted nanny — a woman who occupies every rung of unpaid and underpaid female labor available to an Irish immigrant of her generation before her decline into alcoholism and poverty completes the neighborhood’s tragic arc for her. The novella “A Prayer for Home,” set amid the same Boston and Philadelphia interiors, and “A Bath” both return to the Jamaicaway, the “curvy four-lane parkway” that borders Jamaica Pond — the same pond where, the narrator’s mother recalls, “a mother and daughter drowned” before swimming was forbidden in the nineteen-seventies. 5 The detail shows one way the fiction uses Boston geography: an ordinary, verifiable piece of city history (the pond, the ban) can become an ominous frame for the domestic violence the scene is about to reveal, as Billy notices his mother’s bruises change color “like the trees along the water” while they drive past the site of an old drowning on the way to confess a new injury. 5 Jamaica Plain and its pond recur as a site of loss connected with water, echoing water imagery elsewhere in the poetry. III. Braintree: Aspiration, Distance, and the Blessed Mother Where Jamaica Plain is the enclave a family cannot fully leave, Braintree functions in Mulhern’s geography as the destination of a first, modest upward remove — the grandmother in the essay-memoir “Altogether Beautiful” material lives “on Kendall Road in Braintree, Massachusetts,” her devotion to the Blessed Mother made physical through “statuettes and pictures throughout her home,” and her daily geography extended outward toward “Paragon Amusement Park across from the beach” and a nearby square where Peggy Fleming, in her decline, is found “wandering the streets… bruised and beaten-looking.” 6 Braintree is close enough to the old parish network that Peggy remains a next-door presence in the family’s life, but far enough from Jamaica Plain proper that the move itself registers, however faintly, as a class achievement — a family that has left the enclave without fully leaving the people who never could. “A Bath” supplies the geography’s clearest architectural fact: Nana “lived on the second floor of a three-decker,” her building’s stairwell smelling of the Chinese food cooked by the family on the first floor, its walls thin enough that Billy can hear, through Nana’s bathroom door, “splashing and… sighs” but “no conversation” as his mother bathes his grandmother. 5 The three-decker’s stacked intimacy — families audible to each other through floor and wall, doors that “never” lock because, as Nana explains with characteristic bluntness, “that way people could get in if they smelled her dead body” — is the essay’s central architectural claim: this housing form does not merely contain Mulhern’s plots, it generates them. 5 A confession extracted in a bathtub behind a door that does not fully mute sound is a confession that has already, structurally, been half-overheard by the building itself. IV. Revere: The Italian-American Enclave and Its Export Molly Bonamici’s Italian-American geography runs through Revere, the dense immigrant enclave “about five miles to the north” of Boston that she names, with visible neighborhood pride, when a Boston University roommate asks about the Mafia: “I am from a very Italian neighborhood… One of my Nonna’s friends, Mr. Scarfone, has ties to the Mafia. He’s involved in small-time things like gambling, money laundering, and drugs.” 7 The exchange is instructive precisely because of its comic surface: Molly is performing Revere for an outsider, converting the neighborhood’s reputation into a kind of social currency at the exact moment her roommate reveals her own geographic and class naivety, mistaking the African nations Mali and Guinea for cities and assuming Molly’s dorm-room crucifix collection means something it does not. 7 Revere’s Mr. Scarfone reappears later in the same story cycle at a considerably darker register, when Molly, having narrated her own sociopathy in procedural, confessional prose, notes that “obtaining cocaine from Mr. Scarfone, the mobster friend of my grandmother’s, was easy” — the neighborhood’s low-level criminal infrastructure, introduced as comic local color for a roommate’s benefit, converts without any narrative flag into the actual supply chain for a murder. 7 This is the geography essay’s point in miniature: Mulhern’s neighborhoods are never simply backdrop or dialect color. Jamaica Plain generates the specific, class-inflected grief that ruins Peggy Fleming; Braintree generates the aspirational distance from which that ruin is watched with pity but not full intervention; Revere generates both the ethnic pride Molly performs for outsiders and the practical means of the crime she goes on to commit. Each neighborhood is load-bearing. V. A Coherent Geography, Read as One Faulkner’s Yoknapatawpha invites readers to track the Compsons, Sartorises, and Snopeses across books, watching an invented county accrue weight through repetition. McDermott’s Irish Catholic Long Island similarly returns to wakes and three-family houses. Mulhern’s Greater Boston, distributed across stories not necessarily first published as a single mapped world, can be read with similar attention to recurring places: Jamaica Plain’s parish culture, Braintree’s modest remove and Marian piety, Revere’s Italian-American sociability and low-level criminal economy, and the Jamaicaway. The three-decker’s stacked, overheard intimacy offers one context for the family secrets these stories explore. Reading these settings together can reveal how place contributes to the plots’ social and psychological pressures. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. title: The Quiet Cartographer of Irish-American Memory — A Reading of James Mulhern
heading: The Quiet Cartographer of Irish-American Memory
description: A comprehensive reading of the fiction, poetry, and literary achievement of James Mulhern — situating his work within the Irish-American literary tradition alongside Farrell, Kennedy, McDermott, and Trevor.
text: The Quiet Cartographer of Irish-American Memory — A Reading of James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon A Reading · Original to This Site The Quiet Cartographer of Irish-American Memory A reading of James Mulhern's fiction, poetry, and career within the wider tradition of Irish-American storytelling — with Farrell, Kennedy, McDermott, and Trevor as points of reference, not comparison. I. An Introduction: Voices from the Margins There is a particular kind of writer who works at the edges of the American literary establishment—not in exile from it, not in opposition to it, but in a parallel current that runs quieter, deeper, and largely unnoticed by the apparatus of major publishing. These are writers whose books do not arrive heralded by six-figure advances or coast-to-coast publicity tours, whose names do not appear on the shortlists that dominate autumn literary conversation, but whose work, taken whole, is worth a closer look. James Mulhern's fiction sits in that current. His work—spanning novels, short story collections, poetry, and a novelette praised by The Missouri Review for its “well-written, complex characters, themes of the piece, and its fantastic voice”—is one small part of the Irish-American fiction written over the past two decades. Mulhern is a Bostonian by origin, now based in the Philadelphia area, with a career that has threaded through the overlapping worlds of creative writing, literary editing, and education for more than a quarter century. Some background: a BFA with honors and an MFA from Emerson College, a fully funded Creative Writing Fellowship at Oxford University’s Exeter College in 2015, where he earned First Class Distinction. He has served on the editorial staffs of Ploughshares literary magazine and the American Heritage Dictionary (Third Edition), worked at an educational publisher in Boston and a law publishing house in New York City, and taught literature and creative writing at institutions ranging from Emerson College to Broward College, where he spent twelve years as adjunct faculty. His work has appeared in literary journals and anthologies more than 250 times. He donates the proceeds from his curriculum materials to a scholarship fund he established in his father’s name. Alongside this output, Mulhern has had some recognition from readers and small-press reviewers, and less from the literary establishment at large. His 2019 novel Give Them Unquiet Dreams was named a Kirkus Reviews Best Book of 2019 and received a Kirkus Star. He has won the Readers’ Favorite Book Award, been named a Notable Best Indie Book of 2019, earned a Red Ribbon (highly recommended) from The Wishing Shelf Book Awards in the United Kingdom, and seen two novels reach the finals of that same prize. He was a Finalist for the Tuscany Prize in Catholic Fiction in 2013, longlisted for the Fish Short Story Prize in 2015, nominated for a Pushcart Prize in 2017, shortlisted for the Aesthetica Creative Writing Award for poetry in 2020/2021, shortlisted for the InkTears Annual Short Story Contest in 2016, and received two Honorable Mentions for the Short Story America Prize in 2015. It is, at minimum, a steady record of work, built over time without much attention from the literary marketplace. What follows is an attempt to read that body of work within the rich and contested tradition of Irish-American fiction, and to note that the mid-list, the literary margins, and the small-press ecosystem sometimes hold work worth a second look. II. The Irish-American Literary Tradition: A Map of the Territory To understand what Mulhern is doing, one must first understand the literary landscape he inhabits—and complicates. Irish-American fiction is one of the great sub-traditions of American literature, a current that runs from James T. Farrell’s Studs Lonigan trilogy and Edwin O’Connor’s The Last Hurrah through Mary Doyle Curran’s The Parish and the Hill and Mary McCarthy’s Memories of a Catholic Girlhood to Frank McCourt’s Angela’s Ashes , William Kennedy’s Albany cycle, Alice McDermott’s luminous chronicles of Queens and Brooklyn Irish families, Pete Hamill’s journalism-fiction blend, and Colum McCann’s expansive National Book Award–winning Let the Great World Spin . Elizabeth Cullinan’s Yellow Roses and J.P. Donleavy’s The Ginger Man stake out further coordinates on this map. What unites these writers, despite their considerable differences, is a shared thematic territory: Catholic faith and doubt as organizing principles of consciousness; immigrant memory as a living, haunting force rather than a settled historical fact; the family as both battleground and sanctuary; working-class dignity asserted against institutional cruelty; and the tension between assimilation into the American mainstream and fidelity to a heritage that refuses to be left at Ellis Island. Several of these writers—Kennedy most explicitly, McCourt most memorably—have also trafficked in the supernatural or the hallucinatory: ghosts walk through Kennedy’s Albany, ancestral voices murmur through McCourt’s Limerick, and the boundary between the living and the dead proves far more permeable than secular rationalism would allow. It is precisely in this territory—where Catholic ritual meets family dysfunction, where ancestral ghosts materialize in working-class kitchens, where the emigrant’s grief transmutes into a child’s second sight—that James Mulhern has staked his claim. His Boston is not Kennedy’s Albany or McDermott’s Brooklyn, but it shares with those fictional geographies a quality of being simultaneously real and mythic, a place where history lives in the present tense and the dead have as much to say as the living. III. “A Luminous, Beautifully Told Fairy Tale”: Give Them Unquiet Dreams Give Them Unquiet Dreams (2019, Kurti Publishing) is Mulhern’s most acclaimed work, and it represents the fullest expression of his literary sensibility. The novel is a coming-of-age story set in 1970s Boston, centered on fourteen-year-old Aiden Glencar, a boy gifted—or cursed—with “second sight,” the ability to communicate with dead relatives. The central dramatic engine is Aiden’s fight to free his mother from a psychiatric institution, a struggle that pits the fragile resources of childhood against the indifferent machinery of institutional authority. Kirkus Reviews, in awarding the novel its coveted Star designation and naming it a Best Book of 2019, called it “a luminous, beautifully told fairy tale grounded in history and elevated by spirit.” The review praised Mulhern’s prose for “delivering readers a sense of the child in Aiden’s voice and a thorough, descriptive view of the world around him,” noting that “the writing is elevated by a liberal use of quotes and sayings ranging from Bible verses to Thoreau and Yeats, grounding the various players’ cultural context.” But the review reserved its highest praise for the novel’s human architecture: “Ultimately, it’s the rich characters who bring the novel to its greatest heights, as Aiden’s uncertainty, Martin’s protectiveness, their grandmother’s determination, and their mother’s wistfulness and grief make this a story about family and history and give the sense that everything and everyone are connected across time, whether or not those ties are immediately perceived.” That final observation—about connection across time, about ties that may not be immediately perceived—goes to the heart of Mulhern’s project. His fiction insists on a world in which the past is never past, in which the dead maintain an active interest in the living, and in which what might appear, to a clinician, as mental illness is better understood as a form of gifted inheritance. This is not magical realism in the Latin American tradition of García Márquez or Isabel Allende, where the supernatural erupts into an otherwise rational world to dazzling, destabilizing effect. It is something more culturally specific: a supernatural realism rooted in Irish-Catholic folklore and family dynamics, in which ghosts appear not as metaphors but as participants in the ongoing drama of family life. “Second sight is something that has been in your family for years. Your grandmother’s mother possessed it, and she, too, was demonized… There are always people who are blind to the gifts in others.” This passage, from the linked story “Blindfolded,” which shares Aiden’s world, captures the essential move of Mulhern’s supernatural realism. What the institutions would pathologize, the family tradition affirms. What the modern world would medicate, the old world would honor. The grandmother who explains second sight to Aiden is not superstitious or deluded; she is the custodian of an alternative epistemology, one that values intuition, connection, and spiritual perception over the clinical detachment of psychiatric authority. In Mulhern’s hands, the supernatural is not an escape from reality but a deeper engagement with it—a way of insisting that the visible world is not the whole world, and that the connections between generations are not merely genetic but spiritual. The novel’s 1970s Boston setting is rendered with sensory precision and cultural specificity. This is a world of Catholic parishes and public schools, of kitchen-table conversations conducted in the idiom of Irish immigrants one or two generations removed from the crossing. Mulhern captures the textures of working-class Irish-Catholic life with a fidelity that recalls the ethnographic richness of Farrell’s Chicago or Kennedy’s Albany, but filtered through a child’s perception that makes everything shimmer with wonder and dread in equal measure. IV. The Dark Comic Vision: Molly Bonamici and the Short Fiction If Give Them Unquiet Dreams represents the lyrical, elegiac mode of Mulhern’s fiction, Molly Bonamici (2016) reveals his darker, more comedic register. The novel follows Molly, a skeptical teenage girl deemed an “Angel of Death” by a faith healer—a designation that would be terrifying if Molly weren’t so magnificently unimpressed by it. The book tracks her life from 1980s Boston through adulthood as a high school English teacher, a trajectory that allows Mulhern to explore his perennial themes of faith and doubt, family and loss, through a protagonist whose default mode is sardonic detachment. Kirkus Reviews noted that “a gleefully and wonderfully odd protagonist eases readers into a bare-bones plot,” observing that “Molly’s apathy toward death isn’t as strange as other characters think, more a curiosity than an obsession. This is likewise true for her religious views; Molly doesn’t reject religion but continually (and interestingly) questions it.” The review acknowledged that “Mulhern’s narrative hits the occasional standstill, where Molly repeatedly ponders the same issues with Nonna or Gabe”—a fair criticism that points to a tendency in Mulhern’s work toward recursive meditation that can slow narrative momentum. But it concluded that “while she may have a cold exterior, her distinctiveness is an appealing quality and often amusing.” Amusing is, perhaps, an understatement. Consider the moment when Molly, discussing a dead body, tells a store clerk: “Maggots are a good source of protein… Do you sell word processors?” The juxtaposition is pure Mulhern—the macabre and the mundane colliding in a single breath, the horror of death deflated by the practical demands of living. This is comedy in the tradition of Flannery O’Connor, where grotesque physical reality and spiritual aspiration coexist in the same sentence, and where characters are rendered in exaggerated detail yet insist, against all odds, on their dignity and their right to grace, however ambiguous that grace may be. In an interview with Shelf Unbound , Mulhern explained that “Molly is a derivative of Moll, from Daniel Defoe’s Moll Flanders … I was inspired by her character.” But he also revealed the deeper autobiographical source: “The true genesis of Molly is the fact that five important people in my own life died in less than a year.” This confession illuminates the novel’s strange emotional logic: Molly’s detachment from death is not coldness but self-preservation, not apathy but a coping mechanism forged in the crucible of overwhelming loss. The comedy is not a denial of grief but a response to it—a way of surviving what might otherwise be unsurvivable. Readers’ Favorite praised the novel for its “strong, colorful characters,” and this is indeed one of Mulhern’s signature gifts. Whether in his novels or his short fiction, he creates people who feel lived-in, whose voices carry the weight of specific histories and specific neighborhoods. His characters are not types; they are individuals, each with their own idiom, their own wounds, their own strategies for getting through the day. This gift is on full display in his story collections. Assumptions and Other Stories (2016) drew praise from Readers’ Favorite for “that sly, quirky style of Mr. Mulhern’s that slides from the humorous to the macabre at the turn of a page,” with the reviewer going so far as to assert that “Mr. Mulhern’s writing displays all of the storytelling prowess of the contemporary Irish masters.” Blindfolded and Other Stories (2020) extends this achievement across pieces including “Blindfolded,” “Peppermint Candy,” “The Wrong Way,” “A Bath,” “Keep Calm and Carry On,” and “Chrysler”—a range of titles that suggests the tonal variety of the collection, moving from the ominous to the sweetly nostalgic to the darkly ironic. The Weight of Small Mercies is a linked collection of five stories tracing young Aiden’s coming-of-age amid family trauma in working-class Irish-Catholic Boston, and About Aiden: Selected Stories gathers further narratives centered on the character who has become, across Mulhern’s oeuvre, something close to an alter ego—a recurring consciousness through which the author refracts his deepest concerns about family, faith, perception, and survival. V. Close Readings: The Architecture of Epiphany The best way to understand a writer’s achievement is to read closely, to slow down where the prose rewards attention. Mulhern’s fiction operates through what might be called an epiphanic architecture—a structure borrowed, consciously or not, from James Joyce’s Dubliners , in which carefully constructed narratives move toward moments of sudden illumination, often ambiguous, often painful, always resonant. Critics have compared Mulhern’s story “Assumptions” to Joyce’s “Araby”—a “Boston Araby,” in effect—in its portrait of a young consciousness confronting the gap between romantic expectation and disillusioning reality within a specific Catholic urban milieu. But if Joyce is one antecedent, Flannery O’Connor is another. Mulhern shares with O’Connor a fascination with the Catholic grotesque—characters rendered in grotesque physical detail who nevertheless insist on their dignity and their need for grace. And like O’Connor, Mulhern understands that comedy and spiritual seriousness are not opposites but companions, that laughter can be a form of prayer and that the most profound truths sometimes arrive in the most absurd packaging. A third comparison—and perhaps the most illuminating—is with William Trevor, the Irish master of the short story whose quiet tragedies of the marginalized and overlooked represent one of the high points of twentieth-century fiction in English. Like Trevor, Mulhern is drawn to characters whom the world has passed by or pushed aside: the mentally ill mother, the child burdened with unwanted perception, the immigrant grandmother clinging to old-world beliefs in a new-world setting. Like Trevor, he treats these characters with an unflinching tenderness that refuses to sentimentalize their suffering even as it insists on their humanity. Consider the grandmother in the “Blindfolded” stories, who steals a chalice from a church in a desperate attempt to heal her institutionalized daughter: “I’m going to return it, sweetheart. We’re just borrowing the chalice to make your mother well again. I think God will understand.” The passage does a lot in few words. The grandmother’s theft is simultaneously an act of faith and an act of desperation, a belief in the magical power of sacred objects and an acknowledgment that conventional channels—medicine, prayer, institutional authority—have failed. Her reassurance to the child that “God will understand” is both a statement of genuine belief and a rationalization, a moment of spiritual confidence and a confession of helplessness. The sentence trembles between comedy and pathos, between the absurdity of the act and the depth of the love that motivates it — precise, layered, and sympathetic to the resourcefulness of ordinary people in hard circumstances. Or consider this passage about the grandfather’s ghost, quoting Thoreau: “‘Goodness is the only investment that never fails.’ A smart man by the name of Toreau said that.” The misspelling of Thoreau’s name—“Toreau”—does real work as characterization. It tells us that the grandfather is a man of limited formal education who has nevertheless absorbed wisdom from sources far beyond his station; that his engagement with American literature is genuine but approximate, filtered through the oral tradition of immigrant culture rather than the academic precision of the university; and that his authority as a moral guide derives not from scholarly credentials but from lived experience and innate goodness. The ghost does not quote Thoreau to impress; he quotes him because the sentiment is true, and because in Mulhern’s fictional universe, truth can arrive from any quarter—from the living or the dead, from the educated or the unlettered, from the sanctioned or the marginalized. The passage about Irish immigration achieves a similar compression of emotional and historical meaning: “My grandmother and he, though they did not know each other, emigrated from different parts of Ireland in the late 1930s. With hope in their hearts, just a few belongings, I’m sure, and not much money, they journeyed to the promised land of their imaginations.” That final phrase—“the promised land of their imaginations”—is quietly devastating. It acknowledges that America was always partly a fiction to its immigrants, a story they told themselves to justify the rupture of emigration. But it does not dismiss that fiction; it honors it, recognizing that the capacity to imagine a better life is itself a form of courage, and that the gap between the imagined promise and the actual reality is the space in which the immigrant experience—and much of Mulhern’s fiction—unfolds. VI. The Thematic Architecture: Six Pillars Across his novels, stories, and poetry, Mulhern’s work is organized around a set of recurring themes that constitute something close to an obsession—the productive, generative kind of obsession that gives a body of work its coherence and its power. Second Sight and Supernatural Realism. The most distinctive feature of Mulhern’s fiction is its treatment of the supernatural not as genre convention but as cultural inheritance. Irish folklore—particularly the tradition of “second sight,” the ability to perceive the dead or to foresee future events—is woven subtly into his narratives, functioning not as a plot device but as a lens through which characters understand their place in the family and in history. What distinguishes Mulhern’s approach from pure magical realism is its grounding in the specific cultural matrix of Irish-Catholic Boston. The ghosts in his fiction are not symbolic or allegorical; they are family members, with opinions, memories, and agendas of their own. Mental illness, in this framework, is recast as gifted inheritance rather than pathology—a radical reimagining that has profound implications for how we think about neurodivergence, spiritual perception, and the boundaries of the “normal.” Faith and Doubt. Mulhern’s characters do not reject religion; they interrogate it, endlessly and inconclusively. They move between belief and skepticism, sometimes within the space of a single paragraph, finding in Catholic ritual both comfort and confinement, both beauty and absurdity. In the Shelf Unbound interview, Mulhern described this dimension of his work with characteristic directness: “The existential search is within all of us. Why are we here? What is the point of life? What is God?… I was always asking questions, and I still am.” His characters—Aiden, Molly, the various narrators of his stories—are all askers of these questions, and the fiction derives much of its power from its refusal to provide neat answers. Family as Fortress and Prison. The Irish-American family, in Mulhern’s rendering, is a contradictory institution: a source of identity, love, and protection, and also a site of dysfunction, coercion, and inherited trauma. His fictional families are populated by domineering grandmothers, absent fathers, committed mothers, and protective brothers—archetypes, perhaps, but rendered with enough specificity and dark humor to transcend their archetypal origins. The family is the crucible in which Mulhern’s characters are formed, and the cage from which they must, in some measure, escape in order to grow. Coming of Age and Identity. The bildungsroman—the novel of growth and self-discovery—is the form to which Mulhern returns most frequently, and his coming-of-age narratives are distinguished by their willingness to address gay identity in the context of 1970s Catholic Boston, a setting in which such identity was not merely stigmatized but actively pathologized. Mulhern handles this material with a delicacy that avoids both melodrama and didacticism, presenting his young protagonists’ sexual awakening as one strand in a larger tapestry of self-discovery that also includes spiritual questioning, intellectual growth, and the painful acquisition of moral autonomy. The Ordinary as Sacred. One of the most striking features of Mulhern’s prose is its ability to invest small, everyday acts with profound emotional and spiritual significance. Tea. Rescuing a dog. Stealing a chalice. These are the moments around which his narratives crystallize—moments of what might be called transcendence in the ordinary, when the mundane suddenly reveals itself as saturated with meaning. This is a sacramental vision of the world, rooted in the Catholic sensibility that informs all of Mulhern’s work: the belief that grace operates not through spectacular miracles but through the texture of daily life, through gestures of love and stubbornness and improvised faith. Irish-American Diaspora Memory. Running beneath all of Mulhern’s other themes is a deep preoccupation with the dynamics of diaspora—with emigration, inherited trauma, generational curses and redemptions, and the persistence of Old World belief in New World settings. His characters carry Ireland within them like a phantom limb, feeling its presence most acutely in moments of crisis or revelation. The “promised land of their imaginations” that drew their grandparents across the Atlantic remains, for Mulhern’s characters, both a source of strength and a burden—a heritage that enriches their inner lives even as it complicates their relationship with the American present. VII. The Poet’s Voice: Narrative Lyric and the Grammar of Grief Mulhern’s fiction has received the bulk of critical attention, but his poetry constitutes a significant and complementary body of work. His poems have appeared in publications including Impspired , The Galway Review , Academy of the Heart and Mind , and Trouvaille Review , among others, and his poem “Copacetic” was shortlisted for the Aesthetica Creative Writing Award in 2020/2021—a recognition that places his poetry alongside his fiction as work of serious literary ambition. Mulhern’s poetry is best described as narrative-lyric: poems that tell stories, or fragments of stories, in language that aspires to the compression and musicality of lyric verse. His characteristic subjects are fathers, brothers, and emigrant ghosts—the same human landscape that populates his fiction, rendered here in more concentrated form. Key poems include “Copacetic,” “Leaves,” “The Crosswalk,” “Brother,” and “Longing”—titles that suggest the emotional territory: a yearning for balance and peace, a fascination with thresholds and crossings, a deep engagement with sibling bonds and the ache of loss. What the poetry shares with the fiction is a commitment to clarity and emotional directness. Mulhern is not an experimental poet; he does not traffic in opacity or fragmentation for its own sake. His poems seek to communicate—to tell the reader something true about grief, about family, about the strange persistence of love across time and distance. In this, he aligns with the mainstream tradition of narrative poetry, where the poem’s primary obligation is to the human experience it renders rather than to the formal innovations of the avant-garde. Taken together with his fiction, the poetry reveals a writer whose central concern—across all genres and forms—is the mapping of human connection: between the living and the dead, between the Old World and the New, between the self and the family that shaped it. The poetry distills what the fiction elaborates, and the fiction provides the expansive context that the poetry implies. They are complementary enterprises, each illuminating the other. VIII. On Craft: Voice, Character, and the Art of Letting Characters Speak In the Shelf Unbound interview, Mulhern offered a statement of artistic principle that serves as a key to his entire body of work: “If I am writing fiction, the starting point is always a character. The next most important aspect of writing a story is the voice of that character. Many writers have said this before, but it is true: The characters will write the story for you if you let them speak.” This deceptively simple credo—character first, voice second, plot as a consequence of both—explains much about Mulhern’s strengths and, to be fair, some of his limitations. There are real strengths here. The characters in his fiction are vividly realized, each with a distinctive voice, a specific way of seeing the world, a particular set of verbal tics and emotional reflexes. Aiden’s uncertainty, his grandmother’s fierce determination, his mother’s wistful grief, Molly Bonamici’s sardonic detachment—these are not character sketches but fully inhabited consciousnesses, rendered with the kind of patient, accumulative detail that makes fiction feel like life. Mulhern’s prose style—described by critics as “lyrical supernatural realism infused with Irish-Catholic folklore, blending vivid sensory details and authentic Boston-Irish dialogue with poignant family epiphanies”—is the instrument through which these characters come alive, and it is a flexible, responsive instrument, capable of shifting from elegiac lyricism to sharp comedy within a single paragraph. His approach to voice is especially noteworthy. The Boston-Irish dialogue in his fiction has the ring of authenticity—not the self-conscious, overly phonetic rendering that can make literary dialect feel condescending, but a subtler music of syntax and idiom that captures the way a particular community actually speaks. When Mulhern’s characters talk, they sound like themselves, not like a writer’s idea of what Irish-American working-class people should sound like. This is a crucial distinction, and it separates Mulhern’s work from much of the sentimental Irish-American fiction that trades in blarney and begorra stereotypes. The limitation—and it would be dishonest not to acknowledge it—is that a character-first approach can sometimes produce narratives that feel episodic rather than architecturally unified, sequences of vivid scenes connected by association and emotional logic rather than by the kind of tight causal plotting that gives certain novels their irresistible forward momentum. Kirkus Reviews noted this tendency in Molly Bonamici , observing that “Mulhern’s narrative hits the occasional standstill, where Molly repeatedly ponders the same issues.” This is a fair observation, and it applies, to varying degrees, across Mulhern’s oeuvre. His fiction is stronger in the scene than in the arc, more compelling in the moment of revelation than in the machinery that connects one revelation to the next. But this is a limitation shared by many writers whose primary gifts are for voice and character rather than for plot—writers like William Trevor, Alice Munro, and, indeed, James Joyce, whose Dubliners stories are masterpieces of the epiphanic moment rather than models of narrative propulsion. The question is whether the moments are good enough to justify the architecture, and in Mulhern’s best work—the Aiden narratives, the strongest stories in Assumptions and Blindfolded , the most acclaimed passages of Give Them Unquiet Dreams —they emphatically are. Mulhern himself has reflected on the existential dimension of his creative practice: “Any work of art enlarges our consciousness. We become wiser by ‘digging deep’ as we create.” This is not mere platitude. It is a description of a writer’s method—a belief that the act of writing is itself a form of inquiry, a way of discovering what one knows and believes, and that the writer’s primary obligation is not to entertain (though Mulhern’s fiction is frequently entertaining) but to illuminate, to make the reader see more clearly the connections—between people, between generations, between the living and the dead—that constitute the fabric of human experience. IX. The Teacher-Writer: Pedagogy and the Literary Life No account of Mulhern’s literary life would be complete without acknowledging the role of teaching in his creative formation. His career spans more than twenty-six years of classroom instruction—at Emerson College, Broward College, Atlantic Technical College, in high school settings, and teaching Advanced Placement courses. He is the author of How to Analyze Literature (Second Edition), Teaching Literature Creatively , and various AP English analysis guides and curriculum materials. There is a long and honorable tradition of the teacher-writer in American letters—from Flannery O’Connor at Iowa to Raymond Carver at Syracuse, from Tobias Wolff at Stanford to Toni Morrison at Princeton. Teaching, for these writers, was not a distraction from their creative work but a complement to it, a way of staying in daily contact with the craft of writing and the challenge of articulating what makes fiction and poetry work. Mulhern belongs to this tradition, and his educational writing—particularly the curriculum materials whose proceeds he donates entirely to his father’s scholarship fund—suggests a writer for whom the transmission of literary knowledge is not merely a professional obligation but a vocation, a calling as serious as the writing itself. His editorial experience—at Ploughshares , at the American Heritage Dictionary , at publishing houses in Boston and New York—has also shaped his sensibility. A writer who has spent time on the other side of the editorial desk, reading submissions and making judgments about what works and what does not, brings to his own writing a self-critical awareness that is often visible in the precision of Mulhern’s prose, in his attention to the individual sentence, in his unwillingness to settle for the approximately right word when the exactly right word is available. X. The Indie Path: Small Presses and the Question of Literary Value Mulhern’s career raises, in pointed form, one of the most important questions in contemporary American literature: does the path of publication determine the value of the work? The American literary establishment has long operated on the assumption that serious literature is published by major houses, reviewed in major outlets, and validated by major prizes. Writers who publish with small or independent presses—no matter how talented, how prolific, or how well-reviewed—are often consigned to a shadow canon, visible to devoted readers and specialized reviewers but invisible to the broader literary culture. Mulhern’s case challenges this assumption. His work has been published by Kurti Publishing and other small presses, and it has received the kind of critical attention—Kirkus Stars, Best Book designations, award nominations and wins in the United States and the United Kingdom—that suggests genuine literary merit rather than mere commercial viability. His more than 250 publications in literary journals and anthologies (a partial list appears on the Books page ) reflect work that has been accepted, over many years, by editors at a wide range of outlets. What can be said is that Mulhern’s body of work—taken whole and read carefully—is the work of a serious, committed writer. XI. Conclusion: A Place in Contemporary Letters James Mulhern is not a famous writer, nor a best-selling one, nor a prize-winning writer in the sense that the major American literary prizes confer fame and fortune. He is a writer who has spent decades working steadily at his craft, trying to write with intelligence, empathy, dark humor, and a certain spiritual seriousness. His best work— Give Them Unquiet Dreams , the Aiden stories, the strongest pieces in Assumptions and Blindfolded —works in a recognizably Irish-American vein: family as both fortress and prison, the ordinary treated as sacred, the dead persisting among the living. His prose style, a lyrical supernatural realism infused with Irish-Catholic folklore, is distinctive. The themes are old and common ones in serious fiction, handled here with as much care as he could give them. In the Shelf Unbound interview, Mulhern said: “The existential search is within all of us. Why are we here? What is the point of life? What is God?… I was always asking questions, and I still am.” It is this restless, unresolved questioning—conducted not in the abstract but through the lives of specific, vividly realized characters in specific, carefully rendered settings—that gives Mulhern’s work its particular power and its claim on our attention. The literary world is vast, and its attention is finite. But the books themselves are there, for anyone who wants them—Aiden’s second sight and his grandmother’s stolen chalice, Molly’s mordant wit and her refusal to be impressed by death, the emigrant ghosts who quote Thoreau with loving imprecision. This essay draws on reviews published by Kirkus Reviews, Readers’ Favorite, and The Missouri Review; an interview published by Shelf Unbound; and biographical and bibliographic information from the author’s published works and public biographical record. All quoted material is attributed inline to its original source. title: The Comic-Grotesque Tradition — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: The Comic-Grotesque Tradition
description: How James Mulhern's tonal hairpin turns from comedy to violence descend from Flannery O'Connor's Southern Gothic and J. M. Synge's Irish black comedy.
text: The Comic-Grotesque Tradition — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On Genre and Tone The Comic-Grotesque Tradition Mulhern, O’Connor, and Synge — on the tonal hairpin turn from comedy to violence, and what it costs a reader to laugh at the wrong moment. Abstract James Mulhern’s fiction can turn, within a single paragraph and without warning, from broad comedy to violence or grief. This essay considers that tonal turn through comic-grotesque modes associated with Flannery O’Connor’s Southern Gothic and J. M. Synge’s Irish black comedy, arguing through close readings of “Useless Things,” “Myra Bocca,” and “Assumptions” that the technique withholds interpretive safety: the reader is not told when to stop laughing, and that refusal is the essay’s subject. I. A Genre Without a Warning Label The comic grotesque names a specific and uncomfortable reading experience: material that is legibly, even broadly, funny — a pratfall, a malapropism, a scene of farce — abruptly reveals itself to be describing cruelty, death, or degradation, and the text declines to tell the reader which register was the real one. Flannery O’Connor built a career on this refusal. The grandmother in “A Good Man Is Hard to Find” delivers her fussy, faintly ridiculous complaints about Georgia geography and her cat right up until the moment the Misfit’s men walk her family into the woods; O’Connor never rings a bell to announce the shift. 1 J. M. Synge’s The Playboy of the Western World performs the same maneuver from the opposite direction: a young man’s claim to have murdered his father is initially received by an entire Mayo village as delightful, admirable news — comedy built directly on top of a corpse that may or may not exist. 2 Both writers understood that the grotesque is not simply comedy with dark subject matter; it is comedy that refuses to signal, through authorial tone, that darkness has arrived. The reader supplies the horror herself, usually a beat too late, and the guilty half-second of continued laughter is the point. Mulhern’s work draws on elements of this tradition: its comic-grotesque moments recall O’Connor’s American Gothic and, in dialect and communal complicity, Synge’s Irish black comedy. The introduction to The Collected Stories and Poems of James Mulhern (forthcoming) observes that the volume’s Italian-American section looks “to Flannery O’Connor’s sense that grace arrives, when it arrives at all, dressed as violence or humiliation,” and that in these stories “comedy and menace share a kitchen table.” 3 This essay takes that observation as a starting point and asks how, mechanically, the turn is built — what specific sentences do the work of switching registers, and what the reader is left holding once the switch has occurred. II. The Faith Healer’s Parlor: Farce as Camouflage “Useless Things” stages its comic-grotesque turn inside a single scene: Nonna, Mrs. Muldoon, and the narrator Molly visit a Boston storefront faith healer named Lady Jane. The scene is, for most of its length, pure farce — a set piece built from stock comic material: an invented illness (Nonna claims Molly has terminal leukemia to cut the line), a fraudulent mystic with “a fake British accent with a hint of Georgia twang,” and Nonna’s own profane commentary on the proceedings (“How ‘bout you make my breasts perky like yours?”). 4 Molly performs her own farce inside the farce, faking symptoms with real craft: “I managed to create a string of saliva that dropped like the thread of a spider’s web hanging off my chin.” 4 Even the language of Lady Jane’s incantation is played for laughs — Molly and Nonna both hear the word “pussy” buried in the healer’s ostensibly sacred murmuring, a detail so absurd it borders on slapstick. 4 The turn arrives without any change in register at all — which is precisely the technique’s cruelty. Lady Jane, still in the same fraudulent, twangy voice that has supplied every joke in the scene, tells the twelve-year-old Molly: “I hate to tell people things like this. But I see gruesome deaths in your future… You have the unlucky fortune of being someone who will either find dead people or be with them when they die, sometimes in violent situations. I guess you might say, ‘You’re an Angel of Death.’” 4 Lady Jane then “started giggling like a little girl,” still performing the same comic idiom that has organized the whole scene. 4 Mulhern gives the reader no cue — no shift in sentence rhythm, no authorial aside — to distinguish this pronouncement from the healer’s earlier nonsense about perky breasts. Nonna’s response, “Ffangul’!” followed by Molly mouthing “Fuck you” on the way out the door, keeps the scene’s comic surface fully intact even as the family flees a prophecy the story will not let the reader dismiss so easily — the reader who has met this same narrator elsewhere in the volume, poisoning a roommate’s cookies with cocaine, already suspects the fraud has stumbled onto something true. 4 The comedy has not stopped; it has simply become load-bearing for a different kind of weight. III. Myra Bocca and the Con Artist as Comic Engine “Myra Bocca” extends the same technique across a longer arc, using a New Age shop owner’s shameless patter as its comic engine. Myra’s dialogue is constructed almost entirely out of the stock devices of stage comedy — running gags (she cannot get Molly’s name right, calling her “Myrtle” is corrected to “Molly’s” own mispronunciation of Myra), bawdy non sequitur (“keep it in your pocket near your genital chakra. Does wonders for your vagina”), and self-deprecating physical comedy (“Just look at the size of this toosh… but in this town I’m outa luck”). 5 The scene plays, almost to its final page, as a comedy of manners about a lovable con artist too shameless to be truly threatening. Then the story converts Myra’s comic shamelessness into a genuine violation without ever changing key: she steals Molly’s credit card at dinner and charges “a television and some pornographic DVDs” to it. 5 The theft is reported in the same deadpan, comic register that has carried every earlier joke — Molly’s outraged phone call to Gabe (“The bitch stole my card”) and Gabe’s laughing reply (“She’s up to her old tricks”) treat felony fraud as simply Myra’s latest bit, confirmed rather than undercut by Mr. Michaelis’s earlier warning that Myra is “a lying greedy bitch” who “’d sell her sister if she could.” 5 The comic grotesque here works by a kind of narrative bait-and-switch: every piece of foreshadowing (Myra’s shamelessness, her greed, Michaelis’s warning) was delivered as comedy, and comedy is what it turns out to have been telling the truth about. O’Connor’s grotesque often resolves into violence that exposes false grace; here the result is a pettier, more contemporary crime, while the comic surface still supplies accurate information. IV. Peggy Fleming and the Synge Inheritance: Communal Comedy at a Victim’s Expense “Assumptions” opens with a passage that owes more to Synge’s village comedy than to O’Connor’s solitary menace: an entire family’s collective, affectionate cruelty toward a disfigured neighbor, narrated by a child who has absorbed the family’s comic register without yet absorbing its cruelty. Peggy Fleming is introduced as “the ‘homeliest damn woman’” the narrator’s grandfather “had ever seen,” her face described in a baroque simile — broken capillaries “like some dreary river and its tributaries eking over a delta of nasolabial folds to terminate in the red seas of two droopy cheeks” — whose sheer rhetorical extravagance is itself a comic device, the narrator performing an almost show-offy cruelty of description. 6 The family’s card-game commentary on Peggy’s tragic marriage plays exactly as village gossip plays in Synge — delivered for entertainment, punctuated by cigarettes and whiskey and poker chips, with no acknowledgment that the subject is a real woman’s devastated life: “how in God’s name could Jim stand to look at that puss day in and day out?” 6 The turn in “Assumptions” is slower than in the two Nonna stories, because it does not arrive in a single sentence but accumulates until the reader realizes the comic material was, the entire time, describing a woman being destroyed by grief, alcoholism, and poverty in full view of a family that found her entertaining. Peg’s own comic performance — badly singing “When Your Old Wedding Ring Was New” for a drunk grandmother’s amusement — is where the narrator first registers the turn from the inside: “Peg was horrible, of course… but her pain was so real. I knew that she was dreaming… and I think it was then that the first throb of death’s glower entered my consciousness.” 6 The scene shows the comic-grotesque maneuver in slow motion: a scene that might remain simply comic when told from a distance becomes, through the child’s attention, an encounter with mortality. Mulhern leaves the comedy in place and asks the reader to hold both readings simultaneously, an approach that recalls O’Connor and Synge without making the comparison a claim of equivalence. V. What the Refusal to Signal Costs the Reader Across these three texts, the work does not provide the customary genre signal — the tonal throat-clearing that tells a reader when to stop laughing. This formal choice has an ethical dimension. A writer who clearly demarcates comedy from tragedy protects the reader from complicity: laugh here, the text says, and grieve there, and the two responses will never touch. These stories withhold that protection. The reader who laughed at Nonna’s crude joke about Lady Jane’s breasts is the same reader absorbing, two sentences later, a prophecy of violent death delivered to a child; the reader charmed by Myra’s shameless patter is the same reader who must reckon with having been charmed by a thief; the reader amused by a card game’s gossip about an ugly woman’s ugly marriage is the same reader who must recognize, a few pages on, that the joke’s subject was dying of the very grief the joke made light of. The comic grotesque can implicate its audience in the cruelty it depicts. Here, that effect offers one way of reading the stories in relation to work by Synge and O’Connor, rather than placing them on the same plane. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. Flannery O’Connor, “A Good Man Is Hard to Find,” in A Good Man Is Hard to Find and Other Stories (Harcourt, Brace, 1955). ↩ 2. J. M. Synge, The Playboy of the Western World (Maunsel & Co., 1907). ↩ 3. Introduction, The Collected Stories and Poems of James Mulhern (Silver Current Press, forthcoming). ↩ 4. James Mulhern, “Useless Things,” in The Collected Stories and Poems of James Mulhern (Silver Current Press, forthcoming). ↩ 5. James Mulhern, “Myra Bocca,” in The Collected Stories and Poems of James Mulhern (Silver Current Press, forthcoming). ↩ 6. James Mulhern, “Assumptions,” in Assumptions and Other Stories / The Collected Stories and Poems of James Mulhern (Silver Current Press, forthcoming). ↩ Works Quoted Quotations are drawn from “Useless Things,” “Myra Bocca,” and “Assumptions,” all collected in The Collected Stories and Poems of James Mulhern (Silver Current Press, forthcoming); from Flannery O’Connor’s “A Good Man Is Hard to Find” (Harcourt, Brace, 1955); and from J. M. Synge’s The Playboy of the Western World (Maunsel & Co., 1907). title: Communion in the Work of James Mulhern — A Literary Essay
heading: Communion in the Work
description: An updated literary essay on communion in James Mulhern's work: teaching, the pelican emblem, practical care, clerical ministry, folk belief, and poems for the dead.
text: Communion in the Work of James Mulhern — A Literary Essay ← Back to The 2601 Salon A Literary Essay · On Recurring Imagery Communion in the Work Communion in teaching, family care, the pelican emblem, and poems for the dead — with ordained ministry and Irish folk belief kept in view. “This is communion, and teaching will be the pond that I bathe in each morning, every new day.” — “Teaching at Fifty-Six,” The Font: A Literary Journal for Language Teachers Communion, in James Mulhern’s work, is named most directly in “Teaching at Fifty-Six”: “This is communion, and teaching will be the pond that I bathe in each morning, every new day.” The word appears in a classroom rather than at an altar, but the claim is not that the classroom simply replaces the sacrament. It is that sustained attention to another person’s mind can carry a communal and spiritual seriousness that institutional language alone does not exhaust. The pelican scene in the novel Give Them Unquiet Dreams offers a clear emblem for this religious vocabulary. A character tells a child that “A pelican is a symbol of Jesus… a mother pelican will wound herself, striking her breast with her beak to feed the babies.” The medieval pelican-in-her-piety is an established Eucharistic image. Mulhern places that image in a child’s hearing as an ordinary piece of family knowledge, where it becomes one instance in a larger practice of passing religious language through domestic talk. “Assumptions” works at a different scale. On the Feast of the Assumption, under the Marian antiphon Tota Pulchra Es , a family feeds, carries, anoints, covers, and helps Peggy into and out of the water. These actions can suggest sacramental forms, but the story is not arranged as an Order of Mass or a Rosary sequence. Its actual rhythm is irregular and remembered: help is repeated, care passes between people, and no one secures a cure. The point is not to declare a beach trip a liturgy; it is to see how service survives without ceremony. The Weight of Small Mercies makes this distinction especially clear. Women and family members perform much of the continuing pastoral work: intercession, touch, washing, anointing, feeding, rescue, practical care, and protective silence. Yet ordained men are present. They bless, heal, read scripture, and lead acclamation. The correction matters because the book does not erase clerical ministry; it shows that ceremonial acts do not carry the family’s daily burden of care. Nor does any system of healing — clerical, medical, folk, or domestic — yield a final guarantee. The work extends communion across death, but not by making every dead figure a Christian soul in need of release. In Give Them Unquiet Dreams , second sight is hereditary, good dead return to complete relational work, and the hostile force is the Irish folk pooka. Catholic prayer for the dead and folk belief coexist. The novel’s communion across death is therefore relational and local, not a simple purgatorial mechanism. The poems express this practice concisely: “My family members are my prayers. My poems are my prayers. My family members are my poems.” A poem for the dead neither proves redemption nor substitutes for a rite. It continues attention where speech and ordinary repair have ended. Across the corpus, communion names a practice of listening, carrying, feeding, remembering, and refusing to treat a life as finished when its usefulness, health, or ease has failed. One version of “Blindfolded” leaves out material that another version retains. The complete magazine text includes a chalice sequence and an invented miracle in which a healing is likened to “the water that gushed from the rock at Rephidim and Kadesh,” followed by the congregation’s “Thanks be to God.” The shortened version keeps the plot while omitting this liturgical language. That editorial choice is worth noting, because readers may differ on whether the religious material is detachable from the boy’s errand or helps give it a wider resonance. Compression offers a related observation. Length is not necessarily what determines whether devotional material appears; genre may matter more. A comic-horror story of sixteen hundred words, epigraphed from Poe, carries no religious material, while a fourteen-line elegy moves from Communion to adulthood in one gesture: a man who says nothing and crosses himself in the light of a dashboard. In these short forms, sacramental material appears more readily in the elegiac mode and not at all in the comic one, suggesting that the habit may be tied more closely to grief than to doctrine. title: Comparative Studies — James Mulhern
heading: Comparative Studies
description: Four comparative essays on James Mulhern's fiction and poetry alongside James Joyce, Flannery O'Connor, and Raymond Carver.
text: Comparative Studies — James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon Scholarly Essays · Comparative Studies Comparative Studies Four short essays reading James Mulhern’s poetry and fiction alongside Joyce, O’Connor, and Carver. Four short comparative studies, each grounded in direct quotation. Quotations from James Joyce’s “Araby” (1914) are public domain and quoted freely; quotations from Flannery O’Connor’s “A Good Man Is Hard to Find” (1953) and Raymond Carver’s “Cathedral” (1983), both still under copyright, are kept short and limited to widely cited lines, in keeping with scholarly fair use. I. Poetry & Fiction II. Joyce III. O’Connor IV. Carver I. The Same Hand: Poetry and Fiction in the Work of James Mulhern Sources: the poems of Crossings and the short story “Assumptions.” James Mulhern writes in two forms that return to related materials: a grandmother’s kitchen, a grandfather’s silence, a body failing, a small mercy offered instead of an explanation. Reading the poems of Crossings alongside the short story “Assumptions” suggests how related concerns take different shapes in each form. Both bodies of work return to grandmothers as the household’s central moral authority, often speaking in a register that mixes piety with plain talk. In “Assumptions,” the unnamed grandmother explains the Feast of the Assumption to her grandchildren, Beth and the narrator, with the same mixture of certainty and evasion she brings to everything else: “It’s a mystery, Bethie. Just one of those things.” The neighbor Peggy Fleming, called “Lovely Peggy” at the grandmother’s insistence, occupies the story’s comic and tragic centers at once — a woman shaped by alopecia, diabetes, and grief for her late husband, Jim. The poem “Catherine” performs a related maneuver in miniature: a grandmother eased into a warm bath while she remains, in her own mind, swimming decades and an ocean away. The two forms diverge most clearly in their handling of time. “Assumptions” moves forward through a sequence of remembered scenes, accumulating incident until the narrator’s understanding of Peg deepens by accretion. The poems compress this same accretive method into a single stanza or image. “The Crosswalk” collapses an entire relationship with a father into one gesture recalled at a funeral: “Your hands on mine. / Proof that we had closeness for a moment.” Where the story has room to let a decline unfold scene by scene, the poem must locate an equivalent weight in a single image and trust the reader to supply the years around it. What the comparison finally suggests is not that the poems are compressed stories or the story an expanded poem, but that both forms are governed by the same instinct: withhold the statement, trust the object, let the reader arrive at the feeling through what a hand touches or what an old woman remembers about a swim decades gone. II. Epiphany and Its Withholding: James Joyce’s “Araby” and James Mulhern’s “Assumptions” Source for Joyce: “Araby,” Dubliners (1914), public domain. James Joyce’s “Araby” and James Mulhern’s “Assumptions” are separated by more than a century, a nation, and forms of Catholicism practiced differently in Dublin and in an Irish-American household outside Boston. Both use a first-person boy narrator looking back at a formative period, making the comparison useful for considering how religious language may meet disappointment rather than consolation. Joyce’s unnamed narrator turns his infatuation with Mangan’s sister into something close to devotion, imagining that he bears “my chalice safely through a throng of foes.” The bazaar he finally reaches dissolves into overheard trivial flirtation, and the story ends with the narrator seeing himself “as a creature driven and derided by vanity,” his eyes “burned with anguish and anger.” Mulhern’s narrator encounters a quieter disillusionment, structured around an actual religious feast. Told that August 15th commemorates the Virgin Mary’s bodily assumption into heaven, the boy and his sister, Beth, receive an explanation that satisfies nothing: “It’s a mystery, Bethie. Just one of those things.” Unlike Joyce’s narrator, who sees his own vanity against a bazaar’s cheap glamour, Mulhern’s narrator encounters the limits of inherited piety alongside a more ordinary childhood want — and finds, in the neighbor Peggy Fleming, an act of care that complicates rather than resolves the story’s religious framing. III. Grotesque Grace: Flannery O’Connor’s “A Good Man Is Hard to Find” and James Mulhern’s “Assumptions” Source for O’Connor: “A Good Man Is Hard to Find” (1953), still under copyright; quotations kept short. Flannery O’Connor’s “A Good Man Is Hard to Find” and James Mulhern’s “Assumptions” each place tenderness within comic scenes that also attend to physical vulnerability. O’Connor’s grandmother is vain and self-regarding for most of the story; her moment of grace arrives only at gunpoint, when she reaches toward the escaped convict and says, “Why you’re one of my babies. You’re one of my own children!” Mulhern’s story treats comic discomfort in a gentler register. Peggy Fleming is introduced through a childhood catalog of her physical difference — her alopecia, her toothlessness — even as the story reveals her grief for her late husband and her generosity toward the narrator, whom she defends and calls “sweetheart.” Where O’Connor concentrates the grandmother’s grace in a single gesture at gunpoint, Mulhern presents Peg’s care in several small, unglamorous scenes, allowing readers to see a quality initially obscured by comedy. IV. The Hand That Guides: Raymond Carver’s “Cathedral” and James Mulhern’s Poems Source for Carver: “Cathedral,” in the collection Cathedral (1983), still under copyright; quotations limited to the story’s most widely cited closing lines. Raymond Carver’s “Cathedral” and several poems by James Mulhern both use touch where talk proves insufficient. Carver’s narrator spends most of the story walled off by irony toward Robert, his wife’s blind friend; the turning point arrives when language fails and Robert proposes they draw a cathedral together, his hand resting over the narrator’s. “His fingers rode my fingers as my hand went over the paper,” the narrator says, closing the story with its famous last words: “It’s really something.” Mulhern’s poems approach a related concern in scenes far removed from Carver’s living room: a hand placed over another hand when words run out. “The Crosswalk” recalls a father teaching a son to knot a tie, then jumps years ahead to a funeral photograph of that same posture. “Moving Forward” makes the claim explicit: “touch a hand to show we care … All are acts that make us whole again.” Carver lets contact narrow the gap between two people; Mulhern’s poem “Water” leaves that gap unresolved, ending on a reaching hand and water still out of range.
