title: The Confessor Archetype and the Ethics of Listening — James Mulhern
heading: The Confessor Archetype and the Ethics of Listening
description: An essay on unauthorized confessors in James Mulhern's fiction — the bath-time confession in 'A Bath,' Peggy Fleming in 'Assumptions,' and the Public Garden scene in Give Them Unquiet Dreams.
text: The Confessor Archetype and the Ethics of Listening — James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On the Governing Method The Confessor Archetype and the Ethics of Listening In the Fiction of James Mulhern — on grandmothers, children, and ghosts who hear what cannot otherwise be said, and hold no institutional warrant for doing so. Abstract Catholic fiction has a long tradition of confessional scenes that take place nowhere near a confessional box. This essay argues that Mulhern's fiction returns obsessively to a specific structure: an unauthorized confessor — usually a grandmother or grandmother-adjacent figure — who extracts a confidence and must choose between absolution, indictment, and silence. Three scenes anchor the reading: the bath-time confession in “A Bath,” the confidences shared with Peggy Fleming in “Assumptions,” and the Public Garden confession-by-proxy in Give Them Unquiet Dreams . I. The Sacrament Without the Sacrament Catholic fiction has a long tradition of confessional scenes that take place nowhere near a confessional box. James Mulhern’s short stories and his novel Give Them Unquiet Dreams are populated by figures who perform the priest’s oldest function — hearing what cannot otherwise be said, and deciding what to do with it — while standing at kitchen sinks, sitting in recliners with a cat on their lap, or scraping saltwater vegetation from a boulder in County Mayo. This essay argues that Mulhern’s fiction returns obsessively to a specific structure: an unauthorized confessor, usually a grandmother or grandmother-adjacent woman, who extracts a confidence from a child or a wounded adult, and who must then choose between absolution, indictment, and silence. Unlike an ordained priest, these women hold no institutional warrant for the power they exercise — which is precisely what makes their exercise of it a subject worth reading closely. The essay examines three scenes in particular: the bath-time confession in “A Bath,” the confidences shared with Peggy Fleming in “Assumptions,” and the Public Garden confession-by-proxy in Give Them Unquiet Dreams , in which one dead woman’s guilt is absolved by a living woman decades after the fact. II. “Promise Me You’ll Never Lie to Your Grandmother Again”: A Bath as Confessional Structure “A Bath” stages its confession with an almost liturgical rigor. Sixteen-year-old Billy and his mother Grace arrive at Nana’s apartment to help her bathe; Grace has hidden a beating from an abusive boyfriend behind a cover story — “I fell off a stepladder when I was hanging a curtain” — and has extracted a promise from her son to corroborate it: “Promise me you’ll stick to the story.” “I promise,” Billy says. 1 The scene thus opens with a false confession already rehearsed, a script Billy has agreed to perform for Nana. What follows is Nana’s dismantling of that script through an interrogation that borrows directly from the sacrament of penance: she demands to see what has been concealed (“I want to see. I’m your mother”), she examines the wound with her hands (“She gently placed her palms on my mother’s face and scanned closely”), and she presses for the true account beneath the story offered (“This is the second fall you’ve had in three months. I don’t understand it, Gracie”). 1 The confession, when it finally comes, is not extracted by Nana alone — it is offered because Nana has first confessed something herself, admitting under her daughter’s direct question that her own husband “hit” her “a few times. When he was drunk.” 1 Mulhern constructs the scene as reciprocal rather than hierarchical: Nana’s admission of her own history of abuse is what licenses Grace’s admission of hers. This is a significant departure from the sacramental model it otherwise resembles. In the Catholic confessional, the priest’s authority to absolve depends on his freedom from the penitent’s specific sin; Mulhern’s grandmother instead earns the confession by revealing that she shares the sin’s inheritance. The absolution that follows — “Forget about that bastard O’Toole. I didn’t like him… He’s out of your life, I hope?” 1 — reads less like priestly pardon than like matrilineal complicity, women closing ranks around a shared history of violence that the men in the family will never be made to answer for. Billy’s own confession is folded into the scene almost as an afterthought, and it is worth noting how casually Nana handles it: “So you lied about the curtains?” “Yes.” “Promise me you’ll never lie to your grandmother again.” “I promise.” 1 The symmetry is exact — Billy has now made and broken and remade the same kind of promise twice within a few pages, once to his mother and once to his grandmother, and the story does nothing to suggest that either promise carries binding weight. Mulhern is quietly building an argument here about what a “secret” actually is in this family system: not information that stays hidden, but information that is passed hand to hand under the condition that it stay verbally denied. The final line of the story — “For a few moments, the three of us had all we ever needed” 1 — retroactively frames the entire confessional apparatus of the story as a mode of intimacy rather than a mode of truth-telling. What the family needs, Mulhern suggests, is not disclosure but the ritual occasion for disclosure; the content of the confession matters less than the fact that it was heard by someone who did not flinch. III. Peggy Fleming as Confessor-in-Reverse “Assumptions” complicates the archetype by making the child, rather than the elder, the nominal confessor. Peggy Fleming, alcoholic, diabetic, widowed, treats the young narrator, Jimmy, as her confidant across a series of scenes that mimic confession’s intimacy without any of its institutional gravity. She tells him about a girl who mocked her in childhood, embeds a violent fantasy inside the story (“I think that’s who pushed Margaret Mary Fawny off the cliff… What must she have thought as she fell through that cloudy air?”), and then immediately retracts the confession’s truth-value: “I’m just codding ya, Jimmy, just an old story is all. A fib, my love.” 2 The retraction is itself a kind of absolution granted backward in time — Peg confesses to a cruelty, then un-confesses it, leaving the boy (and the reader) unable to determine which version, the vindictive fantasy or its disavowal, constitutes her real feeling. What makes Peg a confessor rather than merely a confider is that Jimmy is explicitly placed in the position of judge and comforter: “You’re not ugly,” he tells her, unprompted, after her insistence that she is. 2 The child absolves the adult of the very shame she has just confessed, and Peg receives this absolution with visible relief, “You’re a charmer, you are.” 2 The story never lets us forget that Jimmy is also the one entrusted to pour her whiskey sours and to keep his grandmother’s “not too much, sweetheart” a working fiction between them. 2 He is confessor, bartender, and eventually eulogist — the story ends by Jimmy imagining Peg’s soul rising “altogether beautiful,” an explicit echo of the Song of Solomon epigraph that opens the story: “You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you.” 2 The child’s final act of listening is thus retroactively canonized: the confessor’s judgment on the confessant, delivered posthumously, is unconditional acquittal. IV. Rita, Catherine, and Absolution Deferred Across a Generation Give Them Unquiet Dreams stages its most explicit confessional scene in the Public Garden, when Rita — the woman who had an affair with Aiden’s grandfather — finally meets Aiden to learn what his dying grandmother, Catherine, wanted to tell her. The scene is saturated with confessional apparatus even before any confession occurs: Rita has avoided this meeting for months, “she had an excuse — lunch with friends, an art class, a meeting of her book club, a lecture,” 3 the classic penitent’s procrastination. When she finally asks what message Catherine left, and hears it is only gratitude — “She wanted to thank you for listening when she talked about her mother” — Rita weeps, and delivers her own confession unprompted: “My relationship with your grandfather was wrong. I betrayed a friend and I will live with that for the rest of my life.” 3 Aiden’s response — “She forgave you, Rita” — is a twelve-year-old boy pronouncing absolution on behalf of a dead woman, a transfer of sacramental authority that the text does not treat as strange. It is instead consistent with everything the novel has established about Aiden’s role in the family: he is the one soul permitted to move between the visible world and the dead, and this scene simply extends his second sight into the register of moral accounting. What Rita cannot receive, however, is peace: “I know she did, but I could never erase her pain.” 3 Mulhern is careful here to distinguish between forgiveness granted and guilt discharged — the two do not track together, and Rita’s confession changes nothing about how she carries it. This is underlined a few pages later when Rita explains that Catherine herself could never accept the very same distinction: “She confessed her feelings to me and repented many times. I told her she was absolved. But it was fruitless. She would tell me the story again and again, always seeking absolution and forgiveness.” 3 The chain of confessors in this scene — Catherine confessing to Rita, Rita now confessing to Aiden, Aiden pronouncing forgiveness on Catherine’s behalf — forms a closed loop with no exit. Guilt in Mulhern’s fictional world is not dissolved by confession; it is merely relayed to the next available listener, a structure the grandfather’s ghost names outright a few chapters earlier when he tells Aiden, “we all carry needless feelings inside, and they can hurt us to the core.” 3 V. The Ethics of an Unlicensed Sacrament Read together, these three scenes suggest that Mulhern is less interested in whether confession “works” — whether it produces genuine absolution — than in who is granted the authority to hear it, and what that authority costs the listener. None of his confessors are priests. Nana in “A Bath” absolves her daughter only after implicating herself; Jimmy in “Assumptions” absolves an adult he is too young to actually judge; Aiden in Give Them Unquiet Dreams absolves on behalf of the dead, a proxy sacrament that leaves the living penitent, Rita, no less burdened than before. In each case the listener bears something away from the exchange — Billy inherits a family script of denial; Jimmy inherits the first “throb of death’s glower” that enters his consciousness while listening to Peg sing of her dead husband; 2 Aiden inherits knowledge of a guilt that predates his birth and will outlive his ability to resolve it. Mulhern’s fiction thus proposes an ethics of listening that has almost nothing to do with the ecclesiastical machinery it borrows its form from. To be a confessor in this body of work is not to hold power over sin but to accept custody of another person’s unresolved feeling — custody that is never returned, only passed on. It is a domestic, matrilineal, largely female inheritance, distinct from and often working in the shadow of a Church that Mulhern’s families still nominally practice but do not fully trust to do this particular work. The recurring image across all three scenes is of a private ritual performed in defiance of, or indifference to, the sacrament it resembles: a bathtub instead of a confessional box, a basement piano instead of an altar, a park bench under a weeping willow instead of a rectory. Grace is found not through the Church’s authorized channel but through the improvised confessional booths of kitchens, cellars, and public gardens — spaces Mulhern’s characters build for themselves because the official one has, for reasons the fiction never fully states, become unavailable to them. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. title: The Confessor-Grandmother Across the Corpus — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: The Confessor-Grandmother Across the Corpus
description: Tracing James Mulhern's recurring Nana/Nonna figure across three stories as a single matriarchal archetype who is simultaneously moral authority and moral hazard.
text: The Confessor-Grandmother Across the Corpus — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On a Recurring Archetype The Confessor-Grandmother Across the Corpus Tracing the Nonna/Nana figure across the fiction — a single recurring matriarchal archetype who functions simultaneously as moral authority and moral hazard. Abstract James Mulhern’s fiction returns, book after book and story after story, to a grandmother who is at once her family’s primary source of unconditional love and its most dangerous moral improviser. This essay traces that figure across “A Bath,” “Assumptions,” and the Nonna cycle (“Useless Things,” “Mia Bambina,” “Myra Bocca”), arguing that Mulhern has built a single composite matriarchal archetype whose authority and hazard are not opposing qualities but the same quality, viewed from two angles. I. One Figure, Several Names Every grandmother in James Mulhern’s fiction performs a recognizably similar function long before she performs a similar personality: she is the household’s final court of appeal, the person to whom a child or grandchild brings a secret too dangerous to bring to a parent. This essay treats three of these women — Nana in “A Bath,” the unnamed grandmother of “Assumptions” (referred to as Helen by the narrator’s grandfather and aunt), and Nonna across the Molly Bonamici story cycle (“Useless Things,” “Mia Bambina,” “Myra Bocca”) — not as three discrete characters who happen to share a role, but as variations on a single composite archetype the corpus keeps rebuilding under different names. The essay elsewhere on this site devoted to unlicensed confession, “The Confessor Archetype and the Ethics of Listening,” has already established that these women hear confession without institutional warrant. 1 This essay asks a related but distinct question: once a grandmother has heard a confession, what does she do with the power it gives her, and does the answer differ meaningfully across her various incarnations? The claim requires some care, because the three women are, on the surface, quite different: Nana is Irish-Catholic, working-class, and gentle in her bluntness; Helen is Irish-Catholic, more genteel, and complicit in a family’s casual cruelty toward a disfigured neighbor; Nonna is Italian-American, connected to organized crime through her friend Mr. Scarfone, and, by the end of her story cycle, an active accomplice to murder. What unites them is not temperament but structural position: each is the family member with the least formal authority (none of them is a wage-earner, a professional, or a head of household in any legal sense) and the most actual authority (each one’s word ends every argument in her family, and each one is turned to first when something has gone wrong). II. Nana: Authority Earned Through Disclosure Nana’s authority in “A Bath” is built, almost entirely, on her willingness to disclose her own vulnerability before demanding her daughter’s. When Grace finally admits she has been hit by a man, Nana does not respond with the shock or judgment a reader might expect from a woman of her generation; she responds by immediately equalizing the confession with one of her own: “A few times. When he was drunk. Men were different back then.” 2 The essay on domestic violence and silence elsewhere on this site treats this moment for its function within a single story’s formal restraint; here the point is comparative: Nana’s specific technique — earning the right to hear a confession by offering one first — is a version of moral authority built on reciprocity rather than hierarchy, and it recurs, in modified form, in both of the other grandmothers this essay considers. Crucially, Nana’s authority never curdles into hazard within the story’s frame. She tells Billy, “Promise me you’ll never lie to your grandmother again,” 2 extracting a vow of honesty rather than a vow of silence, which is the opposite of what Nonna, in a later section of this essay, will ask of Molly. Nana represents something like the composite archetype’s unfallen state: total authority, deployed only toward disclosure and comfort, never toward complicity in harm. III. Helen: Authority That Chooses Not to Intervene The grandmother of “Assumptions” represents a harder case, because her authority is real but her use of it is passive rather than actively harmful. Watching her neighbor Peggy Fleming’s decline into alcoholism and self-neglect, Helen’s characteristic response is sympathy without action: “Well, the poor thing!” 3 she says, in a family card game where Peggy’s ruined life is treated as evening entertainment. Later, when Peggy is found by police “wandering the streets of a nearby square, bruised and beaten-looking,” 3 it is Helen’s house Peggy is brought to, confirming that Helen functions, within the neighborhood’s actual social structure, as exactly the kind of ultimate authority this essay is describing — the place trouble gets brought when there is nowhere else for it to go. What Helen does with that authority is the essay’s hinge case: she absorbs Peggy into her household’s care (bringing her on the Feast of the Assumption outing that gives the story its climax) without ever addressing, confronting, or attempting to resolve the underlying alcoholism and grief that produced Peggy’s decline. This is neither the unqualified moral authority of Nana nor the active moral hazard Nonna will represent; it is authority exercised as containment rather than either healing or harm, and it is the version of the archetype that this essay argues is easiest to overlook precisely because it produces no dramatic consequence within its own story — Peggy’s fate is simply absorbed into the family’s ongoing life, cared for but never repaired. IV. Nonna: Authority as Active Hazard Nonna is where the archetype’s two faces — moral authority and moral hazard — become fully and finally indistinguishable, because the same qualities that make her Molly’s most reliable protector are precisely the qualities that make her a willing accomplice to murder. Nonna’s protective ferocity is established early and played for comedy: cutting in line at the faith healer’s parlor, she lies without hesitation, “explaining to them that I had leukemia ‘very bad’ and the doctors gave me three months at most… She’s my granddaughter!” 4 The comic register never fully disappears even at the graduation party, when Mr. Scarfone jokes, “No one calls Nonna’s granddaughter an Angel of Death,” referring back to Lady Jane’s prophecy, and Nonna answers, laughing, “If anyone is an Angel of Death, it’s Jimmy here” 5 — a joke that the reader, by this point in the volume, can no longer fully enjoy, since Molly has by then already confessed her own murder to the reader if not yet to Nonna. The archetype’s authority and hazard finally collapse into the same act when Molly asks Nonna to help poison Ashley’s cookies, and Nonna agrees with the same casual warmth she has shown throughout: “Sure mia bambina. What’s one more ingredient? Not a problem.” 6 This is the composite archetype’s terminal form: a grandmother whose total, unconditional loyalty to her granddaughter — the very quality that makes Nana’s and Helen’s versions of the archetype recognizable as loving — becomes, in Nonna, the mechanism of a murder. Nonna does not stop being a loving grandmother in this scene; she is, if anything, performing love exactly as she always has, which is the essay’s central and most uncomfortable claim. V. Authority and Hazard as a Single Quality Read in sequence — Nana’s reciprocal honesty, Helen’s passive containment, Nonna’s active complicity — the three grandmothers do not represent three different moral types so much as three points on a single spectrum defined by one unvarying trait: absolute, unconditional loyalty to the family member who has come to them in trouble. What varies is not the grandmother’s character but the nature of the trouble she is asked to absorb, and the corpus’s deepest argument about this archetype may be that the difference between a protective grandmother and a dangerous one is not a difference in the grandmother at all. It is a difference in what her grandchild asks of her, and how far her love is willing to follow the request. Nana is asked only to receive an honest disclosure and offers one in return; Helen is asked, implicitly, only to keep watching over a woman she cannot save; Nonna is asked to become an accessory to homicide, and does so in the same voice, and with the same casual tenderness, she has used throughout to call her granddaughter mia bambina. The grandmother archetype in Mulhern’s fiction is not, this essay concludes, a study in contrasting characters. It is a single, stable, deeply loving moral force, observed at different depths of the exact same water. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. title: Credo — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: Credo
description: A writer's credo by James Mulhern — a statement of belief on the sacred in ordinary life, mercy as a method of composition, and the conviction that we are mended only in the act of mending others.
text: Credo — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon In the Author’s Own Words Credo A statement of belief — on the sacred in ordinary life, on mercy as a method of composition, and on the conviction that we are mended only in the act of mending others. …that common heart, of which all sincere conversation is the worship, to which all right action is submission. Ralph Waldo Emerson, The Over-Soul I. The Ordinary as Sanctuary I have come to believe that the sacred is not sequestered in a far country, nor reserved for the ceremonies we have built to contain it. It abides here, in the unremarkable hours — in the kitchen light at six in the morning, in the faces we pass and neglect to see, in the small domestic liturgies we perform without knowing that we are performing them. Grace is not clamorous. It does not announce its arrival, nor wait upon our readiness. It waits, rather, in the everyday, with what I can only call patience, for the moment we consent to notice it. I believe a homely woman singing badly in a cellar stands nearer the sacred than most of what has been painted on a ceiling. Our failure, then, is not principally a failure of faith but of attention. We mistake the urgent for the important. We defer the essential to a season that never arrives. And we neglect to recognize that the love of others — the plain, unglamorous bond between one person and another — is the single greatest inheritance we are given. Whether we get along or do not get along, love remains the thread that binds us: the one sacred thing, running unbroken beneath every quarrel and every silence, and beneath even our estrangements, which it outlives. II. Mercy as Method I was taught early, in an Irish Catholic household populated by eccentric and tender souls, to forgive and to have empathy — not as doctrine received but as household practice, performed daily and imperfectly by people who had every reason to withhold it. Those flawed, devoted figures became the first of my characters, and they instructed me in the truest lesson of my craft: that even those who have wounded us stand in need of comfort. So it is with the people I make. I will not write anyone off, on the page or in life. To summon a character into fuller being is an act of mercy rather than of judgment — a way of granting each figure its wound, its reason, its intelligible history, its chance to be understood before it is condemned. A reader always knows when a writer has secretly despised one of his creations: the prose stiffens, the character flattens into a verdict, and the fiction, however accomplished, acquires the faint chill of the courtroom. Judgment is the cheapest instrument in the writer’s case, and the least durable. I believe grace does not wait upon worthy people to administer it. It travels through cruelty, exhaustion, and bad temper as readily as through kindness, and it is no less real for the unreliable hands through which it passes. I believe a body in decline — diabetic, gouty, bald, unsteady on its feet — is not a subject the serious writer looks past on the way to something more dignified. It is where dignity actually resides, if it resides anywhere at all. III. The Discipline of Attention I believe the ordinary detail — a chipmunk on a patio, a bottle of suntan oil, a housedress printed with roses — is never merely what it appears to be, and that the whole of a writer’s discipline is patience: the willingness to watch a small thing long enough for it to disclose what it is actually for. I believe a sentence should be revised until it knows more than its author knew when he began it, and that this is not a failure of planning but the only honest way a true sentence is ever made. I believe fire is not only punishment. In the right light, at the right hour, upon the right stretch of ordinary water, it is the very material of which glory is made. Imagination sustained me through the hard passages of my life, and I have come to regard the faculty itself as something held in trust rather than owned — a gift on loan from something larger than myself; call it the inner light, or the grace that moves through all things. To write, then, is to answer that gift with attention and with love. It is not self-expression. It is stewardship. IV. The Classroom I believe comedy and reverence are not opposites; that a family may be cruel and devoted in the same breath; and that any fiction which resolves this contradiction too neatly has told a lie about something. I believe every student who has ever informed me that a poem is stupid, that this isn’t math, or that they aren’t getting wet for nobody, already contains multitudes. Persuading them of it is the whole of the job. Thirty-five years in the classroom, and I have not once completed it in a single semester. I believe teaching is not the transmission of information but the slow, unprovable work of convincing another person that their interior life is worth the labor of expression. Nothing in the profession is harder to measure. Nothing in it matters more. V. The Narrow Doorway I believe in the narrow doorway — that no one passes through it alone, that we are each helped along by another’s arm, and that this is not a diminishment of the journey but the entire purpose of it. For we are all broken. Not one of us escapes the fracture; and any account of a human life that pretends otherwise has flattered us at the cost of telling us the truth. And yet the consolation is stranger and better than we expect. We are not made whole by being helped, but by helping. It is in bending toward another’s brokenness that our own is quietly repaired — the healing running outward, and returning to us altered. This is my faith, and the whole of my art: that love is the creative thread binding life to imagination, truth to searching, and each of us, in the end, to one another. I believe a book, a poem, or a classroom is a place where a person may be told, truthfully and perhaps for the first time: you are altogether beautiful, and there is no flaw in you. I believe that sentence is worth an entire working life spent earning the right to say it. A printable edition — the complete statement of belief, typeset for reading aloud or for the classroom — is available below. title: Crossings — A Close Reading — James Mulhern
heading: Crossings
description: A close reading of Crossings: Selected Poems by James Mulhern: architecture, recurring image systems, formal command, and a note on a possible future illustrated edition.
text: Crossings — A Close Reading — James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon A Close Reading Crossings A full critical reading of the published collection — its architecture, its recurring image systems, its formal command, and what it achieves. A Note for Readers, Before You Begin This essay moves through poems from an earlier, expanded manuscript of Crossings . The published book — Crossings: Selected Poems (Silver Current Press, August 2026) — is a tighter, twenty-poem selection. It opens with “A Prayer” and closes with “Leaves,” not with “Copacetic” and “Moving Forward” as the discussion below might suggest; both appear in the book, but not first and last. Four poems treated here as among the collection’s strongest or weakest work — “Longing,” “The Guard,” “To Be,” “Simply Silly” — are not in the published edition. The rest of the essay’s references — “Water,” “Copacetic,” “Dark City,” “The Crosswalk,” “Carol” — are. I chose the smaller sequence because it read as the more cohesive book. The remaining poems live in full on the Complete Collection page , and some are bound for a forthcoming, enlarged, illustrated edition of Crossings (date to be determined), where I mean to give myself more room. I offer that multiplicity of versions not as inconsistency but as faith. A poem revised is a small resurrection — the same material returning transfigured, never finished because it is still becoming. Emerson said as much in “Circles”: people wish to be settled, and only so far as they remain unsettled is there any hope for them. Hope, I’ve come to believe, needs that unsettledness the way a life needs breath. This is close to why I teach. A student arrives unsettled, too — not yet the person they will become. Helping one discover the genius already there feels less like instruction than grace passing through me. It is, simply, a blessing. Shirley Chisholm called service the rent we pay for the privilege of living on this earth. Part of that rent, I think, is homage — to the thinkers and the kindness that shaped us, Emerson among mine. Elsewhere on this site, that homage takes literal shape: an image of literature as “the ladder hanging close to the side of the schooner” borrows its ladder directly from Adrienne Rich’s “Diving into the Wreck.” Paying such debts openly is not separate from the writing life. It is close to the point of it, and it remains my quest. Scope of This Assessment What follows is offered in two movements. The first is analysis : a descriptive account of how Crossings is built — its sequence, its governing images, its habits of syntax and line. The second is evaluation : a judgment of how well the collection accomplishes what it sets out to do and where its strongest work lies. The two are kept separate on purpose. Analysis that slides into praise stops being useful, and evaluation that skips analysis is only opinion wearing a robe. The collection under discussion is Crossings: Selected Poems — twenty poems, with dedication, acknowledgments, and introduction, published by Silver Current Press in August 2026; see the Crossings overview for the complete text. Quotations here follow the published text. Where this assessment differs from the collection’s own critical apparatus — The Poetics of Crossings , which reads the book’s figures and forms at length — the difference is one of purpose: that study asks how the poems work; this one also asks how well. Part One Analysis I. The Architecture of the Sequence The title is doing structural work, not decorative work. A crossing is a threshold event — a passage from one state to another — and the collection is arranged as a series of them: from childhood to knowledge, from health to illness, from presence to absence, from darkness toward light. The book opens in a domestic interior with “Copacetic,” a poem whose central gesture is a refusal (“I’m not hungry.” He pushed it away), and closes, before the epilogue, with “Moving Forward,” whose central gesture is an offering: “I place my arm under hers. / She stands, / kisses my forehead.” That is the arc of the book in miniature — from the plate pushed away to the hand extended. Between those poles the sequence moves less by narrative than by pressure. Poems of family illness and decline (“Water,” “Last Supper,” “Fragility,” “The Teapot”) are set against poems of institutional life and vocation (“Longing,” “Session’s End,” “The Guard”), and against a small number of poems whose register is deliberately lighter (“Simply Silly,” “Carol”). The lighter poems are not filler; they function as pressure valves, and their placement is one of the more sophisticated things about the manuscript. A collection this concerned with grief needs air, and the sequencing supplies it at roughly the intervals a reader can bear. The one structural risk is that the book’s emotional center of gravity sits in its middle third, where the illness poems cluster most densely. A reader arriving at “Water” has already absorbed a good deal; the poem is strong enough to survive the position, but the surrounding poems bear more weight than they otherwise would. II. The Recurring Vocabulary Four image systems govern the collection: hands , water , thresholds (doors, crosswalks, stairs), and light against darkness . They recur so consistently that recurrence has to be treated as method rather than habit — and the poet has been explicit that it is method. The repetitions are purposeful: the same truths set down again in new hands, new voices, new incarnations. What looks like repetition is recurrence, and recurrence is the argument. The hands are the collection’s most reliable instrument. They appear as evidence (“Your hands on my shoulders. / One moment, framed.” in “The Crosswalk”), as failed reach (“He bends, / cupping his hands / toward the lake below, / reaching for water / that will not rise” in “Water”), and finally as tenderness offered directly (“I place my arm under hers” in “Moving Forward”). Because the poet declines to gloss them, the hands accumulate meaning by position rather than by statement — the reader learns what a cupped hand signifies in this book the way one learns a word from repeated context. Water carries the heavier freight. In “Water” it is the thing the old man cannot reach; the poem’s catalog of a weathered body — “weathered face, / capillaries like tributaries / on dry land” — converts a body into a drought map, so that the closing phrase, “reaching for water / that will not rise,” lands as both literal thirst and something considerably larger. The figure is doing double service, and it does not announce the second service. That restraint is the collection’s signature. Light and darkness are the riskiest of the four, because the pairing is worn nearly smooth by use. The collection earns it in one place decisively — the closing line of “Dark City,” “I see you move from darkness into light” — where the phrase survives because the poem has spent its length refusing consolation, so the turn arrives as report rather than reassurance. Elsewhere the pairing is the collection’s most predictable move. III. The Discipline of Restraint The collection’s most consistent technical virtue is its refusal to explain. Its characteristic sentence is short, declarative, and slightly under-informed — it tells the reader what happened and stops before telling the reader what it meant. “Copacetic” is the clearest instance: a father’s four-word evasion, a four-word narrative clause, and no commentary. The poem trusts a reader to supply the grief. This is harder than it looks, and it is where the manuscript most clearly separates itself from competent work. The temptation in poems of family illness is to secure the feeling with a closing statement; the poems here mostly decline. “Longing” is the exception worth noting because it declines in the opposite direction — the poem states its condition outright (“Mostly, I feel empty and small— / a space between words or a tiny font”) and then rescues the statement with a figure precise enough to justify it: “The colon at the end of an unfinished thought.” A grammatical mark standing in for a life’s incompletion is exactly the kind of image this poet finds when he is working at full strength. Where restraint slips, it slips into a final line that interprets the poem it concludes. There are perhaps three or four such endings in the manuscript. They are not failures of feeling; they are failures of trust. IV. Formal Command The poems are free verse with an audible substrate of accentual-syllabic expectation, which the collection exploits locally rather than sustaining as pattern. Three devices recur with real control. Syntactic suspension. “Water” moves through a sequence of descriptive fragments — face, capillaries, belly, ankles, skin — before the single verb of action arrives in its final movement: “He bends, / cupping his hands.” The poem holds the reader in description until the gesture finally comes, and the gesture fails. Caesura as refusal. The collection favors two kinds of break — the line-ending dash that removes connective syntax (“The old man on the dock—”), and the hard stop after reported speech that declines elaboration. Both are deployed at moments of withheld tenderness, and the consistency suggests the device is tied to a recurring dramatic situation: the adult who will not explain. Catalog and litany. “To Be” abandons connective syntax altogether for an asyndetic list — “the Wife of Bath’s scarlet stockings / poor Yorick’s skull / Dickinson’s sherry in the glass” — which levels literary monument and roadside debris (“a flattened sneaker on some road”) into identical syntactic weight. “Moving Forward,” at the other end, borrows the cadence of litany without adopting its apparatus. The two poems mark the collection’s formal outer limits: leveling on one side, blessing on the other. Lineation is the element most uneven across the manuscript. The strongest poems break where breaking creates meaning; a handful break where the sentence happened to run out of room. V. A Note on a Possible Illustrated Edition The published edition of Crossings: Selected Poems is text-only. A separately planned illustrated edition, should it go forward, raises a genuine question of proportion rather than a question of taste. This is a collection whose method is withholding — it works by declining to interpret its own images. Illustration is, by nature, an interpretation. Set carelessly, a picture of a cupped hand on the page facing “Water” would perform exactly the gloss the poem spent nine lines refusing to perform. The productive path is the one the poems themselves take: suggestion over statement. Illustration that stays tonal — light, surface, weather, the grain of an interior — will extend the book’s atmosphere without closing its images. Illustration that renders the literal object at the poem’s center will compete with the poem and win, which is a loss. The safest structural solution is to illustrate the thresholds rather than the figures: doorways, crosswalks, stairwells, the surface of water, the room after someone has left it. Those images are the collection’s architecture, and they can be drawn without being explained. Four poems discussed elsewhere in this essay — “Longing,” “The Guard,” “To Be,” and “Simply Silly” — belong to the fuller manuscript rather than the published Selected Poems . Mulhern reserved them, along with the rest of the expanded sequence, for this future illustrated edition, where a larger page count and visual apparatus give him more room than the tighter, cohesion-driven published selection allowed. Readers curious about them can find the full text of every poem discussed in this essay on the Complete Collection page . Part Two Evaluation VI. What the Collection Achieves Three achievements are worth naming precisely, because they are the grounds of the assessment that follows. It sustains a unified vision across twenty poems without becoming monotonous. This is rarer than it sounds. Most first collections are anthologies of their author’s best individual poems; this one reads as a book, with a governing vocabulary and a discernible arc. The recurrence of hands, water, and thresholds is what makes the unity possible, and the variation in register is what keeps it from flattening. It finds the sacred in domestic material without reaching for the sacred vocabulary. A kitchen table, a teapot, a pair of shoes, a hospital dock. The collection’s spiritual claims — and it makes them — are carried almost entirely by ordinary objects handled with attention. The poems are closer to Transcendentalist habits of seeing than to devotional verse: the current running through things is felt rather than named, and never asks the reader to assent to a doctrine. It maintains emotional control over material that invites sentimentality. Poems about a father’s decline and a family’s inheritance are the most sentimentality-prone subjects in the language. The collection’s prevailing understatement is a deliberate ethical position as much as a technical one — it extends mercy to its subjects rather than judgment, and it declines to extract feeling from them for effect. VII. The Strongest Work Four poems would carry the collection in any submission or contest context. “Water” is the best poem in the book and one that would stand in any journal — its suspended syntax, its drought-map figure, and its closing four words operate as a single unified device. “Copacetic” achieves more with less than anything else here; it is the collection’s clearest demonstration that restraint is a technique and not an absence. “Longing” earns its direct statement of emptiness through the precision of the grammatical figure that follows it, and it is the poem most likely to be quoted. “The Guard” is the most formally accomplished of the institutional poems. “Dark City,” “The Crosswalk,” and “To Be” form a strong second rank. “To Be” is the most technically ambitious poem in the manuscript and the most likely to divide readers. VIII. Placement and Readership The collection sits in a recognizable and currently well-attended tradition: the elegiac domestic lyric of Irish-American Catholic inheritance, working in plain diction and short free-verse lines. Its nearest kin are the poems of family and parish that treat the working-class interior as a serious moral setting. What distinguishes this manuscript within that company is the consistency of its image system — many collections in this mode are looser, assembled around subject rather than around a governing vocabulary. Its readership is correspondingly broad for contemporary poetry. The poems are accessible on first reading without being thin on the second, which makes the collection unusually well suited to reading groups, secondary and undergraduate classrooms, and general readers who do not ordinarily buy poetry. A future illustrated edition, should one follow, would widen that reach further, provided the illustration follows the restraint the poems model. IX. Editorial Assessment The summary judgment below reflects the collection as set for publication, assessed against professionally published contemporary poetry rather than against unpublished work. Thematic Cohesion Exceptional — a genuine book rather than a gathering of poems Image Precision Exceptional — concrete, unhurried, and rarely decorative Emotional Control Strong to exceptional — restraint held against sentimental material Formal Command Strong — assured in syntax and caesura Sequencing Strong — effective pressure and release; middle third densely weighted Accessibility Exceptional — open on first reading, durable on the second Overall Professional-grade and publication-ready — assessed at 9/10 for the collection as a whole, with the individual poems’ craft at the upper end of that range A final observation, offered as description rather than praise. The collection’s governing conviction is that nothing is finally lost — that what is laid down is taken up, that the same griefs and joys return in other hands, and that attention paid to a teapot or a cupped palm is a way of keeping what would otherwise go. That conviction is never argued in these poems, which is precisely why it persuades. It is carried instead by the recurrence itself: the same images arriving again in new incarnations, each time slightly altered, none of them spent. Editorial assessment prepared for Silver Current Press. About the Author James Mulhern’s writing has appeared in literary journals over 250 times and has been recognized with numerous awards. In 2015, he was granted a fully paid writing fellowship to Oxford University. That same year, a story was longlisted for the Fish Short Story Prize. In 2017, he was nominated for a Pushcart Prize. His novel, Give Them Unquiet Dreams , is a Kirkus Reviews Best Book of 2019 and a Readers’ Favorite Book Award winner. He was shortlisted for the Aesthetica Creative Writing Award 2021 for his poetry. Two of his novels were Finalists for the United Kingdom’s Wishing Shelf Book Awards. He is a professor and writer living in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, where he teaches The Art of Telling. title: Crossings at Twenty Poems: A Structural Reading — James Mulhern
heading: Crossings at Twenty Poems
description: A structural reading of James Mulhern's poetry collection Crossings, tracing its twenty-poem sequence from emigration to unresolved grief.
text: Crossings at Twenty Poems: A Structural Reading — James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On Sequence and Structure Crossings at Twenty Poems A structural reading of Crossings — how twenty poems, read in order, build a single argument that crossing is the family’s inherited condition, never quite completed. View on Amazon Crossings Overview Abstract “Mapped in Water and Bone,” already part of this series, reads Crossings thematically — water, hands, light and dark, Catholic imagery, and affinities with Heaney, Yeats, Oliver, and Dickinson. This essay asks a different question: not what the poems are about, but what order they come in, and what that order does that a thematic reading cannot capture. The current twenty-poem sequence — from “A Prayer” through “Leaves” — is not alphabetized or randomly assembled; it moves from inheritance and arrival, through the losses of a single extended family, to a closing movement that juxtaposes new life against unresolved grief. Reading the collection as a sequence rather than as an anthology suggests a structural pattern that treats grief not as a wound that closes, but as a crossing that is never completed. I. Reading the Collection as an Arc, Not an Anthology “Mapped in Water and Bone,” already part of this series, reads Crossings thematically — water, hands, light and dark, Catholic imagery, and affinities with Heaney, Yeats, Oliver, and Dickinson. This essay asks a different question: not what the poems are about, but what order they come in, and what that order does that a thematic reading cannot capture. The current twenty-poem sequence — from “A Prayer” through “Leaves” — is not alphabetized or randomly assembled; it moves from inheritance and arrival, through the losses of a single extended family, to a closing movement that juxtaposes new life against unresolved grief. Reading the collection as a sequence rather than as an anthology suggests a structural pattern that treats grief not as a wound that closes, but as a crossing that is never completed. II. Opening the Book at the Water’s Edge The collection’s title announces its organizing image before a single poem is read, and the sequence’s second poem, “Dark City,” makes the crossing literal rather than metaphorical: it recounts a grandfather’s emigration from “Athlone on the Shannon River, / dead center of Ireland” to Southampton, where he “boarded the Adriatic, / a name that means, ’dark city.’” 1 The poem’s closing gesture — “I see you move from darkness into light” — establishes, at the very front of the book, the collection’s basic vocabulary: crossing as movement from dark to light, undertaken at cost (“Hardly any money”), carrying only “a canvas sack, your mother’s Bible.” Every later crossing in the collection — a bath, a plane’s turbulence, a grave — will be measured, whether the poems say so explicitly or not, against this founding Atlantic crossing: a passage that cannot be undone, made once, by someone who did not live to see the grandchild now writing the poem. III. The Middle Movement: Bodies in Decline, Hands in Service The collection’s middle stretch — “The Crosswalk,” “Piano,” “Last Supper,” “She Knelt,” “We’d Scrape the Rocks,” “Shoes,” “Honeymoon” — is organized around a recurring physical situation rather than a recurring image: an adult speaker attending to the failing body of an elder, hands doing the work love no longer has words for. “Honeymoon” states this pairing of tenderness and time explicitly, moving from a foot rubbed with ointment to a photograph of a young couple who “could be my children,” closing on “the tenderness at the bottom of her sole” and “the aching tenderness of her soul” 2 — the pun on sole/soul is not incidental wordplay but the poem’s whole argument compressed into a homophone, body and spirit tended by the same gesture. “We’d Scrape the Rocks” extends this care into an explicitly ritual register — a grandson called to help lift his grandmother into a bath — while “Shoes” moves the same gesture back a further generation, tracing hand-me-down shoes from a great-grandmother who “cleaned houses for the rich” down through a chain of women’s feet. 3 Placed in sequence rather than read in isolation, these poems build a cumulative argument that care in this family is transmitted the way the Atlantic crossing was transmitted — physically, hand to hand, body to body, with no guarantee that the person receiving the care can fully repay or even understand it at the time. IV. “Brother Mark” and “Brother Mike”: A Diptych of Loss Placed Deliberately Together The sequence positions its two brother-elegies back to back, a placement that invites attention. “Brother Mark” closes on a wish to freeze time — “Our time together — / perpetually that night” — a refusal to let the elegized moment become past tense. 4 Placed immediately after it, “Brother Mike” and the poems that follow (“Please Call Me,” “The Teapot,” “Carol”) extend the collection’s grief work into estrangement and unanswered longing rather than death alone — “I no longer know you… I long to hear your voice” 4 voices a loss that has no funeral to mark it, no casket to frame a final image, only an ongoing, unresolved absence. Read as a pair, the poems can be seen to distinguish between death, which closes a specific date, and estrangement, which does not — a distinction conveyed through placement rather than directly stated. V. The Closing Movement: New Life Set Against the Grave The collection’s final four poems — “The Nest,” “Turbulence,” “Water,” “Leaves” — form a closing movement whose order invites attention. “The Nest” ends the collection’s penultimate stretch on an image of imminent birth and hope, a body cast recovering while robins hatch outside the window, closing on the imagined moment “you’ll walk outside again… searching the blue, hoping to glimpse a fledgling.” 5 “Turbulence” immediately follows with an explicit meditation on the speaker’s own aging and mortality — a plane’s rattling passage read as an image of the human span, “Behind: everything lived. / Ahead: the solid blackness.” 5 “Water” then presents the collection’s title image in a desolate form: an old man on a dock “reaching for water / that will not rise,” 5 water now withheld rather than crossed. And “Leaves,” the collection’s final poem, ends not in acceptance but in an imagined voice at a graveside — “’We’re done,’ you whisper in my ear… You’re no longer here. / I stand and leave” 5 — a closing line whose pun on “leaves” (the noun that names the poem’s central image and the verb that ends it) connects the departure to the poem’s image. The book does not end on resolution; it ends on a leave-taking that recalls the Atlantic crossing of “Dark City” — another departure from a fixed point toward an unknown elsewhere. VI. Conclusion: The Collection as a Single Extended Crossing Read end to end, Crossings can be approached as more than twenty discrete meditations on death, family, and water loosely unified by recurring images. Its sequence presents crossing as the family’s inherited condition rather than an occasional event. The grandfather crosses an ocean; the grandchildren cross into caretaking roles; brothers cross into death or into silence; and the book’s final image is of a speaker leaving a grave after an imagined voice says that the work of grief, like the work of raking leaves, is “done” — a claim the poem’s own tears complicate. Read structurally rather than thematically, the title may name not a single event repeated in variation but a continuous condition: to be a member of this family, in this book, is to be mid-crossing, never quite arrived. — Silver Current Press Notes 1.
