title: The Grammar of Interruption: Dialogue Mechanics and Withheld Speech in the Fiction of James Mulhern — James Mulhern
heading: The Grammar of Interruption
description: A technical stylistics essay on dialogue mechanics in James Mulhern's fiction — tag omission, action-beat attribution, and interruption.
text: The Grammar of Interruption: Dialogue Mechanics and Withheld Speech in the Fiction of James Mulhern — James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On Dialogue Mechanics The Grammar of Interruption In the Fiction of James Mulhern — how missing tags, action beats, and the em dash render interruption and withheld speech without a word of narratorial comment. Abstract Discussions of Mulhern’s dialogue often focus on what his characters say — the dialect, the dark humor, the confessions extracted at kitchen tables. This essay instead considers how the dialogue is assembled: where tags fall, how often they are omitted, how interruption is rendered typographically, and what happens syntactically when one character cuts off another. It identifies recurring technical choices — limited explanatory dialogue tags, action beats in place of “he said”/“she said,” and em dashes for interruption — and considers how they can let scenes carry emotion without extensive narratorial commentary. I. A Craft Element Hiding in Plain Sight Discussions of Mulhern’s dialogue often focus on what his characters say — the dialect, the dark humor, the confessions extracted at kitchen tables. This essay instead looks at how the dialogue is assembled: where tags fall, how often they are omitted, how interruption is rendered typographically, and what happens syntactically when one character cuts off another. It identifies recurring choices — limited explanatory dialogue tags, action beats in place of “he said”/“she said,” and em dashes for interruption — and considers how they can let scenes carry emotion without extensive narratorial commentary. II. The Vanishing Tag: “A Bath” as a Case Study “A Bath” is instructive because it sustains long stretches of two-person dialogue with almost no attribution at all, relying entirely on alternating turns and the reader’s ability to track voice by content. Consider the exchange in which Billy asks his mother about his father: > “Why don’t you ever talk about my father?” > She lit a cigarette and opened the window a crack. I smelled wet leaves before the smoke overpowered the space. “It’s complicated.” > “How complicated could it be?” 1 Only one line in this sequence receives any attribution at all, and even that attribution (“She lit a cigarette”) is an action beat, not a tag — there is no “she said” anywhere in the passage. The technique intensifies as the scene turns toward its confession: “Did he ever hit you?” my mother said. / “Who?” / “Dad.” / “Why would you ask such a thing?” 1 — four consecutive lines of dialogue carry exactly one attribution between them, and that single “my mother said” exists only because the speaker had briefly changed from the preceding exchange between Billy and Nana; once the two-person volley resumes, tags disappear entirely for the rest of the confession: “Well, did he?” / “A few times. When he was drunk. Men were different back then.” / “Not so different.” 1 The absence of tags here is not a labor-saving shortcut; it produces a specific reading experience of overhearing rather than being told — the prose refuses to insert an authorial presence between the reader and the confession, mimicking Billy’s own position as a silent witness whose only participation is listening. III. The Action Beat as Silent Attribution Where Mulhern marks a turn, he often uses a physical action performed by the speaker in the same sentence or immediately before the dialogue rather than a speech verb. In “Myra Bocca,” a scene of introduction and provocation uses this method: “She turned around and saw that I was reading a sign… Both Gabe and Myra laughed. She nodded at the sign, then said, ’Yes, Molly. I’m Italian just like you.’” 2 Even here, where “said” appears, it follows physical actions (turning, nodding) that help identify the turn. The same story renders a rapid comic exchange through beats: “’Whadaya say?’ She smiled. ’Sure. Why not?’ Gabe answered.” 2 The tag “Gabe answered” arrives after context has identified the turn. This beat-first pattern recurs in the examples considered here, placing speech alongside gesture, glance, and posture. IV. Interruption as Syntactic Violence: The Em Dash and the Cut-Off Clause When Mulhern’s characters genuinely interrupt one another — rather than simply alternating turns — he reaches for a specific and recognizable device: the em dash breaking a clause mid-word or mid-thought, frequently nested inside a single speaker’s own self-interruption rather than between two speakers. Brian’s extended monologue about Myra in “Myra Bocca” is built almost entirely from this device: “Those stepchildren — great people by the way — wanted nothing more than to settle the trust as it was designed”; “This after he treated her like a queen their whole marriage. Not only did he take care of her, but he took care of all her kids — bought them cars, gave them money, paid for their schooling”; “There’s two other things I want to tell you about what she did, though… These things will let you know just how bad she is. She fired an older woman salesclerk… And the most heinous thing — is that the right word?” 2 The final example is the technique at its most self-conscious: the speaker interrupts his own accusatory momentum to interrogate his own diction, a hesitation rendered entirely through the dash rather than through any narratorial comment on his uncertainty. The effect across the monologue is of a man whose outrage keeps overtaking his syntax, each dash marking a place where indignation outpaces the sentence’s original plan. V. Withheld Speech: What the Grammar Omits The essay’s title names interruption and withholding as a single phenomenon because Mulhern frequently uses the identical toolkit — action beat, missing tag, clipped line — to mark not an interruption but a refusal to answer. In “A Bath,” Nana’s evasions about her late husband’s violence are rendered with exactly the same spareness as the story’s ordinary small talk, so that the reader must notice the withholding by its brevity rather than by any signal of reluctance: “’Did he ever hit you?’ my mother said. / ’Who?’ / ’Dad.’ / ’Why would you ask such a thing?’” 1 Nana’s “Who?” is not confusion; it is a stalling tactic disguised as a one-word answer, and the prose refuses to gloss it as such — no “she said, evading the question” — leaving the reader to infer evasion purely from the mismatch between a simple question and a needlessly obtuse response. The technique recurs in “Myra Bocca” when Molly deflects a direct personal question with a bare declarative rather than an explanation: “’Why aren’t you married?’ ’Because I don’t want to be,’ I said. ’Men are a pain in the ass.’” 2 The clipped answer forecloses further inquiry by its very brevity; Mulhern lets the shortness of the line itself perform the work of a door closing, without narration describing Molly’s tone or intent. VI. Conclusion: A Prosody of Speech Tag omission, action-beat attribution, dash-driven self-interruption, and clipped withholding all reduce explanatory mediation between the reader and spoken exchange. Where a more conventional prose stylist might use “she said hesitantly” or “he interrupted, flustered,” these examples rely on syntax — the presence or absence of a tag, the placement of a dash, the length of a line — to carry emotional information that adverbs and narratorial commentary might otherwise supply. The result can make dialogue feel overheard rather than fully explained, with the mechanics of a sentence helping readers infer who has been cut off, who has evaded, or who has momentarily lost control of their syntax. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. James Mulhern, “A Bath,” in All We Ever Needed (Silver Current Press, 2026). ↩ 2. James Mulhern, “Myra Bocca,” in All We Ever Needed (Silver Current Press, 2026). ↩ Works Quoted Quotations are drawn from “A Bath” and “Myra Bocca,” both collected in All We Ever Needed (Silver Current Press, 2026). title: The Greatest Short Stories — A Reading List for Student Writers | James Mulhern
heading: The Greatest Short Stories
description: Twelve short stories every student writer should read closely, with notes on what each one teaches about voice, structure, subtext, and craft, from Hemingway and Jackson to Baldwin and O'Brien.
text: The Greatest Short Stories — A Reading List for Student Writers | James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon A Reading List · For Student Writers & Instructors The Greatest Short Stories Twelve stories that belong on every writer’s shelf — not because a syllabus says so, but because each one solves a different problem of craft so completely that it becomes the model other writers measure themselves against. A great short story is an argument made in miniature: every sentence has to earn its place because there is nowhere to hide. The twelve stories below span a century and a half and a wide range of temperaments — terse and voluble, gothic and plain, comic and devastating — but each one rewards a second and third reading the way only the best short fiction can. Read them as a writer reads: not just for what happens, but for how the sentences were built to make it happen. After each title, a short note names the single craft lesson most worth stealing. Voice & Economy What to Leave Out Three stories built almost entirely from what is withheld, understated, or said sideways. 01 1927 Hills Like White Elephants Ernest Hemingway A man and a woman sit at a train-station bar in Spain, drinking Anis del Toro and talking around the one subject that actually matters between them. Hemingway never names the operation the man keeps urging her to have; he never has to. The hills in the distance, the two lines of rails, the beaded curtain — every object in the story is doing the emotional work the dialogue refuses to do. What Students Can Learn Subtext is not vagueness. Hemingway’s “iceberg theory” — that the true weight of a story sits below the surface — only works because the surface dialogue is precise, concrete, and entirely in character. Cut the narrator’s commentary and trust the reader to feel what the characters won’t say. Read the story (public domain, Project Gutenberg) 02 1948 The Lottery Shirley Jackson A small New England village gathers in the square on a warm June morning for its annual lottery — a homely, orderly civic ritual, described in the same flat, cheerful tone you’d use for a bake sale, right up until the moment the reader understands exactly what has been won. Jackson’s genius is pacing: she tells you everything and hides nothing, and the horror arrives anyway, entirely on schedule. What Students Can Learn Tone can carry more menace than any adjective. By refusing to editorialize or foreshadow with dread, Jackson lets the gap between her narrator’s placid voice and the reader’s dawning understanding do all the horror. Withholding judgment is itself a technique. Read the story (free at The New Yorker) 03 1953 A Good Man Is Hard to Find Flannery O’Connor A grandmother’s petty vanity steers her family’s car straight into the path of an escaped convict called the Misfit, and what begins as a broadly comic road-trip story pivots, in a handful of pages, into a theological confrontation about grace, cruelty, and the instant before death. O’Connor called this swerve “the moment of grace” — the instant a story stops being clever and starts being true. What Students Can Learn Comedy and violence can share a sentence. O’Connor’s tonal whiplash works because she never breaks character to signal the shift — the grandmother stays exactly, infuriatingly herself all the way to the end, and it is that consistency, not a change in style, that makes the final scene land. Still under copyright — find it in The Complete Stories or your library’s collection. Interior Life The Architecture of Epiphany Three stories that live almost entirely inside a single consciousness, and earn the moment it finally breaks open. 04 1914 The Dead James Joyce, from Dubliners Gabriel Conroy makes small talk at his aunts’ annual holiday party, delivers a competent after-dinner speech, and takes his wife home — and then, in the story’s final pages, learns something about her past that dissolves his entire sense of himself. The famous closing paragraph, with snow falling “upon all the living and the dead,” is the single most imitated cadence in the English short story. What Students Can Learn An epiphany has to be earned by accumulation, not announced. Joyce spends the first three-quarters of the story on ordinary social detail so that Gabriel’s late, quiet devastation feels inevitable rather than engineered. Build the room fully before you let the roof come off it. Read the story (public domain, Project Gutenberg) 05 1892 The Yellow Wallpaper Charlotte Perkins Gilman A woman confined by her physician husband to a country nursery for a “rest cure” begins keeping a secret journal, and as her isolation deepens, so does her fixation on the sprawling, sickly pattern of the wallpaper covering her room. The prose degrades in lockstep with her mind — sentences shorten, logic frays, the wallpaper starts to move — until narrator and reader are equally uncertain what is real. What Students Can Learn First-person narration can be an instrument of diagnosis. Gilman never states that her narrator is unraveling; the syntax itself performs the unraveling. This is the clearest classroom model for how sentence rhythm can mirror psychological state rather than merely describing it. Read the story (public domain, Project Gutenberg) 06 1930 A Rose for Emily William Faulkner The women and men of a small Mississippi town narrate the strange, cloistered life and death of Emily Grierson collectively, as “we,” circling back and forth through decades before the story’s final image forces every earlier detail into a new, appalling light. Faulkner scrambles the timeline on purpose — the horror depends on not knowing what you already half-know. What Students Can Learn A collective narrator changes what a story can get away with. The town’s communal “we” lets Faulkner report gossip and rumor as fact, and it is exactly that unreliable, secondhand telling — plus a nonlinear structure that plants the ending in plain sight — that makes the final line unforgettable rather than merely shocking. Still under copyright — find it in Collected Stories of William Faulkner or your library’s collection. Structure & Subtext How a Story Turns Three stories built around a single hinge — a reversal, a confession, a revelation — and the machinery that makes the turn feel inevitable. 07 1983 Cathedral Raymond Carver A resentful, half-drunk narrator begrudgingly hosts his wife’s blind friend for the evening, and after the wife falls asleep, the two men end up on the couch in front of a television documentary about medieval cathedrals — which the blind man, of course, cannot see. What follows, as the narrator tries to draw a cathedral with his eyes closed so his guest can “see” it through his hand, is one of the most understated conversions in American fiction. What Students Can Learn Minimalism is a structural choice, not an absence of feeling. Carver strips adverbs, backstory, and interior commentary to almost nothing, which means the story’s single, hard-won moment of connection has to carry the entire emotional weight — and does, because nothing around it is competing for the reader’s attention. Still under copyright — find it in Cathedral or your library’s collection. 08 1843 The Tell-Tale Heart Edgar Allan Poe A nameless narrator insists, from the first line, that he is perfectly sane — and then spends the rest of the story proving, with mounting, feverish precision, exactly the opposite, as the imagined beating of a dead man’s heart grows louder beneath the floorboards. Poe compresses an entire psychological collapse into a few thousand breathless words. What Students Can Learn An unreliable narrator’s protests are the real story. The narrator’s insistence on his own sanity is the confession; readers learn to distrust a first-person voice not by what it hides, but by how hard it works to convince them of something. Read the story (public domain, Project Gutenberg) 09 1905 The Gift of the Magi O. Henry A young couple, poor but devoted, each secretly sell their one prized possession to buy the other a Christmas gift worthy of it — and each gift, once unwrapped, is rendered useless by the very sacrifice that paid for it. O. Henry’s famous twist ending has been imitated so often it can seem quaint, but the story’s real achievement is how tightly the irony is engineered from the first paragraph. What Students Can Learn A twist only satisfies if it is inevitable in hindsight. Every detail in the setup — Della’s hair, Jim’s watch, their shared poverty — is load-bearing. Study this one for plotting: nothing in a tightly built short story is there merely for color. Read the story (public domain, Project Gutenberg) Voice & Witness The Contemporary Story Three stories that widen the form — through music, through a mother’s litany, through the blurred line between memory and invention. 10 1957 Sonny’s Blues James Baldwin A Harlem schoolteacher learns his younger brother has been arrested for heroin, and the story that follows — told entirely in the older brother’s guarded, self-justifying voice — moves toward a jazz club where Sonny, at the piano, finally says everything he could never say in words. The closing set piece, where music becomes the only adequate language for suffering, is one of the great endings in American fiction. What Students Can Learn A narrator’s limitations can be the subject of the story. Baldwin lets the older brother’s fear and respectability color every judgment he makes about Sonny, so readers have to read past the narrator to understand what he still can’t admit. Point of view is characterization. Still under copyright — find it in Going to Meet the Man or your library’s collection. 11 1978 Girl Jamaica Kincaid In a single unbroken paragraph — almost entirely one long, cascading sentence — a mother instructs her daughter in everything from washing clothes to walking like a lady to, unmistakably, not becoming “the slut you are so bent on becoming.” The daughter gets in only two brief interruptions. Kincaid compresses an entire coming-of-age, and an entire inherited anxiety about womanhood, into two pages. What Students Can Learn Form can be the argument. The relentless, comma-spliced sentence structure enacts the mother’s control before the reader consciously registers it. When a story’s subject is pressure or inheritance, consider making the sentence itself feel that pressure. Still under copyright — find it in At the Bottom of the River or your library’s collection. 12 1990 The Things They Carried Tim O’Brien A platoon in Vietnam is defined, almost taxonomically, by the objects each soldier carries — rations and rifles alongside letters, photographs, and superstitions — until the inventory becomes a devastating account of grief, guilt, and the impossible weight of memory itself. O’Brien’s narrator repeatedly reminds readers that “story-truth” can be truer than “happening-truth,” turning the story into an argument about fiction itself. What Students Can Learn A concrete list, deployed with discipline, can carry abstraction better than any direct statement of theme. O’Brien also models metafiction for beginners: a narrator can question his own reliability without collapsing the story’s emotional truth. Still under copyright — find it in The Things They Carried or your library’s collection. A Note for Instructors Pairing this list with a lesson Every story above is a natural pairing for the exercises in The Art of Telling a Story and the Silver Current Writing Workshop Handbook , both free to download on the Guides page . For close-reading practice built from public-domain passages, see the Student Workbook for Literary Analysis as well. title: The Unspoken Elegy: Objective Correlative and the Grief-Work of Crossings — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: The Unspoken Elegy
description: How Crossings converts a father's folded robe, a photograph on a table, and a shattered print of The Last Supper into instruments of grief that never once name the word.
text: The Unspoken Elegy: Objective Correlative and the Grief-Work of Crossings — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On the Poetry of Crossings The Unspoken Elegy Objective correlative and the grief-work of Crossings — how a folded robe, a photograph on a table, and a shattered print of The Last Supper carry loss that the poems never once name outright. Abstract Crossings rarely uses the vocabulary of grief — the words loss , grief , and mourning are almost entirely absent from the collection. In their place stand objects: a bathrobe folded on a table, a photograph propped beside a casket, a shattered print of The Last Supper on a living-room floor, a yellow teapot recovered years after it was promised, a pair of Doctor Scholls eased onto an old woman's crooked toes. This essay considers whether Mulhern's poems work in a mode close to T. S. Eliot's objective correlative — grief rendered through a physical thing rather than declared as a feeling — across nine poems: “Copacetic,” “The Crosswalk,” “Brother Mark,” “Dark City,” “Brother Mike,” “The Teapot,” “Shoes,” “Fragility,” and “Last Supper,” with “Water” offering a compact example of that approach. I. The Word Grief Never Appears Search Crossings for its own vocabulary of mourning and the search comes back nearly empty. The collection concerns itself largely with death — a father's decline in a hospital room, a great-uncle's emigration and death, a father-in-law's collapse on an ordinary morning — yet words such as grief , loss , devastated , and heartbroken do not appear in the poems this essay examines. What appears instead is a robe, folded; a photograph, framed; a print, shattered on a floor. That absence may be a significant part of the collection's method, helping spare, often flat statements carry emotion without naming it directly. The method has a name in criticism — T. S. Eliot's objective correlative, the idea that emotion in art must be conveyed through a specific object or chain of events rather than asserted directly. 1 But invoking Eliot risks making the technique sound cooler and more theoretical than it feels on the page. In Crossings , the object is never merely a symbol selected to represent grief from the outside. It is a piece of evidence the poem has actually witnessed — something the speaker touched, folded, or found broken — and the poem's authority comes from the specificity of that witnessing, not from any commentary laid over it. II. The Robe on the Table: “Copacetic” “Copacetic” opens the collection with a word borrowed from the speaker's father, a Marine who picked it up in Korea: “‘Everything copacetic?’ he says.” 2 The poem's real subject is a hospital deathwatch, but it never says so in those terms. It reports instead: the father refuses Jell-O from a spoon, sleeps through most of a visit, grows agitated one night with “something about a trip,” and near the end stands at a window wearing “the robe my sister said / brought out the blue in his eyes.” 2 When the speaker repeats the father's own question back to him — “Everything copacetic?” — the father's answer breaks the pattern of the euphemism that has organized the whole poem: “It was tough,” he says, the one moment in the poem where the family's inherited vocabulary of composure fails and something plainer gets through. 2 The poem could have ended there, on that admission. Instead it ends four lines later, on the object: “By dawn, he'd gone. / His robe, folded, / on the table by the door.” 2 Nothing in those lines states that the father has died; “he'd gone” carries the fact, while the folded robe suggests what remains unsaid. A robe folded and left by a door is, mechanically, a small, ordinary act of tidying. Read after the poem's accumulated detail, it can become the last domestic gesture available to a man who can no longer perform any other kind of care, and a sign of a body no longer in the room to wear it. The word grief would explain the ending; the folded robe leaves readers to infer it. III. The Photograph on the Table: “The Crosswalk” “The Crosswalk” performs the identical maneuver with a different artifact and a sharper structural irony. The poem's occasion is a stepfather or father-figure whom another sibling claims credit for a memory that belongs, in fact, to the speaker — “I heard you say, / ‘Remember when Danny and I built the shed?’ / But it wasn't my brother who cut wood / and hammered nails with you.” 3 Rather than adjudicate the dispute, the speaker retreats to a memory no one else can claim: “your help knotting my tie. / We looked in the mirror. / My face reflected in yours.” 3 The poem's final image collapses past and present into a single photograph: “Someone crossed the room / and took a picture. // It was on the table by your casket. // Your hands on my shoulders. // One moment, framed.” 3 The line break that isolates “Your hands on my shoulders” as its own single-line stanza lets a physical, tactile detail stand alone without gloss. “One moment, framed” closes the poem on a possible double sense: framed as photographed, and framed as fixed permanently, the only tense left available to a relationship that has ended. IV. Fire, Threshold, and the Refusal to Leave: “Brother Mark” and “Dark City” “Brother Mark” and “Dark City” extend the same restraint to a different kind of artifact: not an object left behind, but a threshold the speaker cannot bring himself to cross. In “Brother Mark,” two brothers build a fire under a bridge on the way to a dance, singing, drinking, warmed by flame and by each other's presence — “Your arm on my shoulder, / your face orange from flames.” 4 The poem's closing wish inverts the usual elegiac gesture of moving a lost person forward into memory; instead it asks to stay fixed at the threshold itself: “I wish we'd stayed, / never stepped into the snowy light. / Our time together— / perpetually that night.” 4 The poem never states that the brother has died. The wish to remain inside one unrepeatable night, rather than move into whatever came after it, does that work instead. “Dark City” performs a structurally similar refusal at greater historical distance, built around a single childhood memory of a great-uncle — “I was two, you were sixty” — and a name, discovered only in research: the ship Adriatic , on which the man emigrated from Athlone, whose name the poem translates directly, “a name that means, ‘dark city.’” 5 The poem's closing gesture returns the speaker, now “close to your age,” to the abandoned homestead in Ireland, where he presses his palm against the same wall the great-uncle once touched: “I press my palm against the homestead wall, / as you touched my head so many years ago. / I see you move from darkness into light.” 5 The title's darkness resolves not into a statement about death or the afterlife but into a physical gesture — a hand on stone, echoing a hand on a child's head decades before — that lets the poem end on contact rather than conclusion. V. The Cross Traced in Dashboard Light: “Brother Mike” “Brother Mike” locates its artifact not in an object but in a gesture repeated twice, twenty years apart. As children, the brothers kneel “after Communion / in a church that smelled / of stone, incense, and shellac,” the speaker watching his brother's “quiet strength” and wishing “you'd talked more.” 6 Years later, the brother picks the speaker up from an airport, listens to his worry over a sick friend, and instead of offering the advice the speaker expects, “simply looked at me / and crossed yourself / in the dashboard light.” 6 The poem's closing stanza names its own method with unusual directness for this collection, and is worth reading as something close to a statement of the whole book's technique: “Communion— / the road we share, / as when you traced the cross / and turned to me / with a soft and caring glance.” 6 What the brother cannot say in words — comfort, reassurance, love — is transmitted instead through a single physical sign, the sign of the cross, made small and private in a car's dashboard light rather than large and public in a church. The poem does not need to state that the gesture communicates more than speech would. The word “Communion,” doing double duty as sacrament and as ordinary human connection, has already said it. VI. Inherited Objects: “The Teapot” and “Shoes” Two further poems extend the collection’s artifact-logic from the singular emblem of loss to the inherited object that survives across generations. “The Teapot” begins with a small domestic puzzle — the speaker’s mother asking for a yellow, gold-trimmed porcelain teapot that was “promised” to him “long ago,” a promise he cannot locate in memory any more than he can locate the object itself: “I searched cabinets, closets, every shelf— / never found that gold-trimmed porcelain.” 6a The poem then reconstructs, almost incidentally, an entire lost Christmas — siblings gathered, a Streisand album, “Nanna’s Irish prayer— / ‘thy gifts’—received” — before the teapot resurfaces, years later, “in an upstairs room.” 6a The poem’s closing line performs a small but exact pun: “Memories—‘these thy gifts.’” 6a A grace said over food becomes, by the poem’s end, a grace said over memory itself — the teapot is never explained as a symbol of the dead relatives it recalls; it is simply found, and the finding does the remembering for the poem. “Shoes” performs a more explicit three-generation transfer through a single article of clothing. The poem opens with the unglamorous intimacy of caregiving — the speaker fitting an aging mother’s feet into her “favorite pair of Doctor Scholls” — and the mother’s embarrassment at her own “crooked” toes, which she traces back to her own mother’s poverty: “My mother cleaned houses for the rich… We had to wear the shoes she brought home. / They were often small. / That’s why they look this way.” 6b The speaker’s imagination then reaches back a further generation, to a great-grandmother he never met, picturing her “hugging a bag of discarded shoes / as she walked down the street, / shoulders curled in the wind,” her own shoes “worn and broken, / like the skin on her red, cracked hands.” 6b The poem’s final image resolves the chain of scarcity into something closer to grace than grievance: the great-grandmother, imagined giving away shoes she can barely spare, would be “teary / but smiling, / relieved she had something / to give.” 6b Three generations of women are compressed into a single object passed hand to hand, and the poem never states its theme of inherited poverty and inherited generosity outright; the shoes, small and ill-fitting across three lifetimes, state it instead. VII. The Restraint That Predates the Poet: “Fragility” “Fragility” makes the collection’s aesthetic principle into an explicit intergenerational argument, contrasting a modern meeting room where “a question asked / hurts someone’s feelings” against the speaker’s grandmother, who “lived / in a dirt-floor house, / walked a mile to a well, / slept in a bed with two siblings / and a few fire-warmed bricks.” 6c The poem’s central claim is stark: the grandmother “Never once said, / ‘My feelings are hurt,’ / wouldn’t understand / the word / fragility.” 6c This is the collection’s restraint traced back to its likely biographical source — not a literary technique adopted for its effects, but a family inheritance of stoicism that the poems themselves are, in some sense, continuing to practice. The grandmother’s daily walk to the well, made “most mornings” after kneeling to say her rosary, ends not in complaint but in blessing: she “gingerly avoided stones / that stabbed her feet, / stones that bruised— / Still, she whispered / blessings / into the early light.” 6c Read alongside “Copacetic,” “The Crosswalk,” and the other poems this essay has examined, “Fragility” suggests that the collection’s refusal to name grief directly is not merely a craft choice imposed on inherently emotional material from the outside. It is continuous with a family ethic in which suffering is carried physically — in a pail, across broken planks, into blistered feet — and answered with a whispered blessing rather than a stated complaint. The poems of Crossings do what the grandmother did: they walk the mile, and they do not say the walking hurt. VIII. The Shattered Print: “Last Supper” “Last Supper” brings the collection's method to its most literal object: a devotional print of da Vinci's painting, knocked from a wall at the moment a father dies. The poem opens on an unrelated domestic accident — a dog's whimpering, a bleeding arm pressed with a pillowcase — before the telephone call arrives: “‘My father's dead. / Can you shine my shoes?’” 7 The request is almost comically practical, and the poem does not soften or explain it; the incongruity between the news and the errand is left to do its own work. The central image arrives without ceremony: “In the living room, / the cheap print of The Last Supper / lay on the floor / its frame splintered.” 7 The word cheap matters as much as the image itself — this is not a museum reproduction treated with reverence but a mass-produced devotional object of the kind found in countless working-class Catholic homes, and its ordinariness is precisely what allows it to carry sacred weight without the poem overreaching for one. The print's fall is never explicitly connected to the father's death; the two events simply occupy the same room, in the same broken hour, and the poem lets the reader make the connection the way the family, in shock, would have made it themselves — wordlessly, and only half-consciously. The poem's final image returns to the print directly: “At home, he knelt / beside the shattered print. / His shoulders drooped, / his back shook.” 7 The verb of grief — shaking — is present at last, but it arrives attached to a body kneeling before a broken object, not as an abstract noun standing alone. Even at its most direct, the poem still needs the artifact to hold the feeling steady. IX. “Water” as the Collection's Ars Poetica If “Brother Mike” states the method's logic in miniature, the four-stanza poem “Water” states its physics. An old man stands on a dock, his body itself rendered as landscape — “capillaries like tributaries / on dry land,” “skin rippled like water” — before the poem's closing gesture: “He bends, / cupping his hands / toward the lake below, / reaching for water / that will not rise.” 8 The image is not explicitly elegiac; no one in the poem has died. But its logic describes exactly what every artifact in this essay is doing: reaching toward something real, close, and specific, in the full knowledge that the reaching itself is the only act available, and that no amount of wanting will make the water rise into the waiting hands. Grief, in Crossings , does not get spoken. It gets reached for, in the shape of a robe, a photograph, a threshold, a dashboard cross, a recovered teapot, a pair of worn shoes, a whispered blessing, a shattered print — each object a cupped hand held out toward a water that has already receded, doing what language alone, in these poems, is never trusted to do. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. T. S. Eliot, “Hamlet and His Problems,” The Sacred Wood: Essays on Poetry and Criticism (1920), the essay in which the term “objective correlative” originates. ↩ 2. James Mulhern, “Copacetic,” in Crossings (Silver Current Press). ↩ 3. James Mulhern, “The Crosswalk,” in Crossings (Silver Current Press). ↩ 4. James Mulhern, “Brother Mark,” in Crossings (Silver Current Press). ↩ 5. James Mulhern, “Dark City,” in Crossings (Silver Current Press). ↩ 6. James Mulhern, “Brother Mike,” in Crossings (Silver Current Press). ↩ 6a. James Mulhern, “The Teapot,” in Crossings (Silver Current Press). ↩ 6b. James Mulhern, “Shoes,” in Crossings (Silver Current Press). ↩ 6c. James Mulhern, “Fragility,” in Crossings (Silver Current Press). ↩ 7. James Mulhern, “Last Supper,” in Crossings (Silver Current Press). ↩ 8. S. Eliot's The Sacred Wood (1920). Explore the Books Read Sample Writing Join the Reader's Circle Get The Quiet Craft , a free booklet of unreleased writing notes — plus occasional word of new work. Get the Free Booklet 300+ Journal Appearances Oxford Writing Fellow 2017 Pushcart Nominee ★ Kirkus Starred Review A Welcome For readers, writers, and students of the craft James Mulhern is a Philadelphia-based novelist, poet, essayist, and professor emeritus of English whose novels, short stories, poetry, and nonfiction have appeared in international literary journals and anthologies more than three hundred times. His novel Give Them Unquiet Dreams received a Kirkus starred review and was named one of the Best Books of 2019. He was awarded a fully paid Creative Writing Fellowship to the University of Oxford, nominated for a Pushcart Prize , shortlisted for the Aesthetica Creative Writing Award , longlisted for the Fish Short Story Prize , and named a Finalist for the Tuscany Prize in Catholic Fiction. His novels have earned favorable critiques from Kirkus Reviews , awards from Readers' Favorite Book Awards , and Red Ribbon recognition from the United Kingdom's Wishing Shelf Book Awards . He is the founder of Silver Current Press , a Philadelphia imprint devoted to literary fiction, poetry, and the art of the well-made book. After three decades in the classroom, he now writes and publishes full time. I fell in love with the characters and grieved when the book ended, wanting it to go on and on." Debra O. — Amazon ★★★★★ Give Them Unquiet Dreams "What an amazing book — I didn't want it to end. The characters are quirky and unforgettable while the adventures are both zany and thought-provoking. Mulhern's good-humored treatment of Irish and Italian cultures disarms and charms while surprising the reader." Kathleen Scherpa — Amazon ★★★★★ Assumptions and Other Stories "Excellent. Very visual. Mulhern at his best." The Galway Review (Editorial Note) "Triggers" — Poem "Mulhern's book gets to the heart of storytelling and those moments that render us speechless. The poignancy of the brothers' relationship and the themes of loss, grief and wonder are telltale signs of a born writer." Ann Bauer — Amazon ★★★★★ Give Them Unquiet Dreams In the Tradition Of What Reviewers Have Noted A few comparisons reviewers and editors have drawn — offered here as their words, not as a claim of kinship on the author's part. Flannery O'Connor, James Joyce & Edgar Allan Poe "Influenced by writers such as Flannery O'Connor, James Joyce, and Edgar Allan Poe, Mulhern renders slices of Boston and South Florida life with comedy, horror, and moments of grace." — Editorial description, Barnes & Noble The Irish Masters "All of the storytelling prowess of the contemporary Irish masters" — Readers' Favorite . The Gothic Tradition Give Them Unquiet Dreams works in the long American tradition of haunted houses and haunted families — paranormal seasoning grounded in psychological realism. Daniel Defoe The title character of Molly Bonamici takes her name and her resilient spirit from Defoe's Moll Flanders — a strong female protagonist who, in Mulhern's words, "respects the integrity of her own mind." Thoreau & Yeats Kirkus noted that Mulhern's prose is "elevated by a liberal use of quotes and sayings ranging from Bible verses to Thoreau and Yeats." title: Pastiche and Undertow — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: Pastiche and Undertow
description: An essay on allusion and structure in Molly Bonamici, revised with new findings on Molly's Margaret-Mary name, Bonamici's meaning, domestic iconography, and altered doubles.
text: Pastiche and Undertow — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On the Novel Pastiche and Undertow How Molly Bonamici works with Dante, Defoe, Poe, Shakespeare, Fitzgerald, Dickinson, and Kate Chopin — with new attention to naming, domestic iconography, and altered doubles. “Open your mind to what I shall disclose, and hold it fast within you; / he who hears, but does not hold what he has heard, learns nothing.” — Dante Alighieri, quoted as the epigraph to Molly Bonamici Molly Bonamici announces a literary inheritance before its first chapter begins. The epigraphs pair Hamlet with Dante’s Paradiso , and the novel returns to both questions: what exceeds an orderly philosophy, and what a reader is willing to hold. The Dantean material is real and recurrent — the policeman called Virgil, the final cab driver Bea, short for Beatrice, and a last movement toward sea, light, and home — but it works as a framework inside a realist, comic, often violent life rather than as a one-to-one reproduction of the Comedy . Molly’s journey can accordingly be read through descent, difficult reckoning, and a final opening toward possibility. Her language of dark woods and a steep ascent makes the Dantean echo available; the novel’s ending returns it to lived time, grief, bodily memory, and an unornamented walk out of the water. The value of the pattern is not that it makes Molly’s crimes harmless or assures a tidy conversion. It establishes an imaginative measure against which the narrator’s coldness, skepticism, and eventual receptivity can be read. The new work on names changes the first page of that reading. “Molly” is a nickname joining Margaret and Mary , so the protagonist carries Mrs. Muldoon’s Margaret Mary Alacoque association from the outset. The final scene takes place on the feast of Saint Margaret Mary. What seemed at first a familiar diminutive turns out to be an inherited devotional identity, disclosed only after the novel has made a subject of names, nicknames, and the authority to give them. “Bonamici” means “good friends” in Italian. The name’s irony belongs to a novel in which loyalty, information, family obligation, and violence remain inseparable. It is more productive to keep the irony at that scale than to make it a single allusion-key: the name measures the distance between a promise of fellowship and the damaged relations through which Molly moves. Defoe, Poe, Fitzgerald, Dickinson, Chopin, and Shakespeare remain part of the novel’s visible conversation. The Defoe parallel places a female rogue inside a confessional first-person tradition; Fitzgerald’s green light is explicitly revised as Molly’s demand for authenticity; Dickinson supplies both Nonna’s instruction to tell truth “slant” and the final vocabulary of possibility. The closing swim closely reworks The Awakening , retaining its sensory pressure and solitary movement into water while reversing its terminal direction: Molly rises and walks back to shore. The new concordance also makes the novel’s quieter preparation easier to see. A gecko watches the work’s one sustained theological dispute; a cardinal arrives as Gabe asks for a sign; and a Bleeding Heart vine droops and revives with Molly’s changing state before the Sacred Heart is named. These are not arguments by themselves. They give the final chapter a prepared visual vocabulary of animal witness, sign, wound, and renewal. The women who recur around Molly should not be treated as hidden instances of one unchanged grandmother. The books work through altered doubles: similar household roles, phrases, gestures, and moral mixtures recur, but each reappears under new pressure. The resemblance between Nonna and Nana is therefore a form of composition, not a license to collapse two novels into a single continuous biography. A full census of the novel’s proper names settles a question the doubled name raises. Mulhern does not run a moral code through his naming: sacred names are not reserved for the devout, nor secular ones for the cruel. He loads a small set of hinge-names, usually against their bearers, and leaves the walk-ons semantically ordinary. Agnella carries the Italian and Latin sense of lamb , chosen by a woman it does not describe. Felicity is the Latin virtue-name for happiness, set on a life short of it. Gabriel, the messenger, belongs to a former priest. Hulga arrives straight out of Flannery O’Connor, and Dr. Diver out of Fitzgerald. The restraint is the point: names carry meaning here only where the novel wants pressure applied. The same restraint governs the narrator’s voice. Molly does not become scriptural at sacred moments, and it is worth saying so plainly, because a religious reading would prefer that she did. Her domestic prose alternates between sensuous catalogue and flat inventory; violence contracts into terse Anglo-Saxon; death expands into clinical, Latinate observation; the funeral Mass turns formal and hypotactic because she is examining its claim rather than assenting to it. Even the sea, the novel’s most charged element, is rendered comparatively plainly, with a single personification in place of biblical parallelism. What actually raises her diction is interpretation itself — the moment she consciously reads an event, whether through a rite, a literary memory, or water. Belief, in this novel, is a late act of reading rather than a settled register. Read together, the Dantean frame, the doubled name, the Italian surname, and the novel’s overt literary debts make a layered pastiche rather than a puzzle with one answer. The book uses inherited texts to make judgment harder, not easier. Its final possibility is earned neither by innocence nor by a doctrinal resolution, but by a narrator learning that the language she has dismissed may still describe something she can receive. title: Molly Bonamici: A Comprehensive Study — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: Molly Bonamici
description: A close reading of the novel Molly Bonamici — its structure, its Angel of Death premise, its Defoe inheritance, and the coping-through-comedy that grew out of a year of overwhelming loss.
text: Molly Bonamici: A Comprehensive Study — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon A Close Reading · On the Novel Molly Bonamici A full-length study of the Kirkus-reviewed novel — its Angel of Death premise, its Defoe inheritance, its deadpan comedy, and the year of overwhelming loss that produced it. Abstract Molly Bonamici (Silver Current Press, 2016) tracks its title character from a sixteen-year-old witness to domestic violence in 1980s Italian-American Boston through adulthood as a high school English teacher, narrated throughout in a flat, deadpan register that a faith healer, early in the novel, diagnoses as supernatural: Molly, she declares, is an “Angel of Death.” This essay reads the novel whole — its structural strategy of displaced affect, its debt to Daniel Defoe's Moll Flanders , its comic method that draws on a mode associated with Flannery O’Connor, and the biographical fact, confirmed by the author, that the novel's detachment was forged in a single year in which five people close to him died. Read against that fact, Molly's comedy can be read as a way the novel handles loss rather than as coldness alone. Contents I. The Angel of Death Premise II. The Toad and the Kitchen: Affect Displaced, Not Absent III. Aunt Bianca's Diagnosis and Molly's Deflection IV. The Ghost of Moll Flanders V. Comedy as Survival: The Maggots and the Word Processor VI. The Adult Narrator Who Never Softened VII. Reception and the Question of Structure VIII. Conclusion: What the Comedy Was For I. The Angel of Death Premise Molly Bonamici announces its central conceit early and directly: a local faith healer, encountering the teenage Molly, declares her an “Angel of Death” — a designation the novel treats with the same flat, unalarmed register it applies to everything else, and one that would be genuinely unsettling if Molly herself were not so thoroughly unmoved by it. 1 Kirkus Reviews, assessing the novel, put the effect precisely: “a gleefully and wonderfully odd protagonist eases readers into a bare-bones plot,” adding that “Molly's apathy toward death isn't as strange as other characters think, more a curiosity than an obsession” and that the same is true of “her religious views; Molly doesn't reject religion but continually (and interestingly) questions it.” 2 The premise does real structural work beyond its shock value: it gives the novel license to have death follow Molly through the whole of her adolescence and adulthood — the smashed toad, a neighbor's decomposed body, eventually the poisoning recounted in the related story “Mia Bambina” — without needing to explain each occurrence as coincidence, curse, or plot contrivance. Once the reader has accepted the Angel of Death framing, death's recurrence around Molly reads as thematic coherence rather than authorial convenience. II. The Toad and the Kitchen: Affect Displaced, Not Absent The novel's opening establishes its central technical method in the space of a single page. Sixteen-year-old Molly, having just witnessed her father choke her mother in the kitchen, retreats to the backyard and turns her attention to a sick toad: “I searched the backyard for several minutes until I found a large rock. I walked over to where the toad sat, lifted the lid of the trashcan until he fell onto the cement pad, where he continued to croak and shake. To put him out of his misery, I smashed the rock against him a few times and watched his guts smear across the concrete. Then I sat on the bottom step for at least twenty minutes.” 3 A companion essay on this site identifies exactly what the prose withholds here: no shock, no interpretive frame, no causal link drawn between the violence indoors and the violence Molly commits on the animal — the narration juxtaposes the two acts with equal flatness, displacing affect from the domestic trauma onto an ostensibly unrelated action and leaving the reader to do the connecting work. 4 The very next paragraph confirms the register will not shift: Molly mixes herself a drink — “I added some vodka from my stash hidden in the closet, and took a few sips” 3 — reported in the identical declarative calm used to describe the toad's death moments before. III. Aunt Bianca's Diagnosis and Molly's Deflection The novel is careful to name Molly's flatness through another character rather than through Molly's own self-awareness — a structural choice that keeps the diagnosis external and contestable rather than settling the question from inside Molly's own head. Watching Molly's unmoved reaction to a chaotic kitchen accident, Aunt Bianca says: “The girl doesn't seem human sometimes. It's like she doesn't feel things… Always so cool, so cold… It's not normal. I tell you it ain't right.” 5 Molly's response is characteristic of the novel's whole comic strategy: rather than refute the accusation, she escalates it into a deadpan joke — “I come from another galaxy. I am an alien… My people are planning an invasion” — delivered, the narration specifies, “completely straight-faced.” 5 The joke performs the very detachment Bianca has just diagnosed, which is the point: Molly does not defend herself against the charge of inhumanity by demonstrating warmth, she defends herself by being even stranger, leaving the reader (and Bianca) with no ground to stand on except the observation that something in Molly does not operate the way grief is supposed to operate. IV. The Ghost of Moll Flanders Mulhern has stated directly, in an interview with Shelf Unbound , that “Molly is a derivative of Moll, from Daniel Defoe's Moll Flanders … I was inspired by her character,” 6 and the allusion rewards attention precisely because the novel never announces it internally. A companion essay on this site traces the structural inheritance: both Mollys are women whose survival depends on hard-won self-sufficiency acquired through deprivation, both narrate their own lives retrospectively without excessive self-pity, and both ask the reader to weigh their moral standing against a society that had already failed them before either committed her own transgressions. 7 The surname “Bonamici” — Italian for “good friends” — supplies the novel's central irony: a name promising warmth and fellowship, worn by a character whose defining trait, per Bianca's own diagnosis, is precisely the opposite. 8 V. Comedy as Survival: The Maggots and the Word Processor The novel's comic register appears clearly in a moment a companion essay singles out as characteristic of the whole book: discussing a dead body with a store clerk, Molly asks, without transition, “Maggots are a good source of protein… Do you sell word processors?” 9 The juxtaposition — the macabre and the mundane colliding inside a single breath, the horror of death deflated by the practical demands of shopping — draws on a comic mode associated with Flannery O'Connor, where grotesque physical reality and ordinary aspiration coexist in the same sentence and characters retain, against all odds, their dignity and their claim to some form of grace, however ambiguous. 10 The difference in tone is worth noting: where O'Connor's grotesque comedy typically arrives freighted with impending violence, Molly's version arrives as simple non sequitur, a mind moving without transition between the fact of death and the errand of the afternoon, which is itself the joke and the diagnosis at once. VI. The Adult Narrator Who Never Softened The novel is narrated from adulthood looking back, and it takes unusual care to specify exactly how much distance separates the narrating adult from the remembered teenager — not, as a reader might expect, in order to show growth away from the child's coldness, but to confirm its persistence. Molly's opening chapter is dated with documentary precision — “I was sixteen, a senior in high school; the year was 1980” 11 — and later, discussing public fascination with a neighbor's death, the adult narrator writes: “I found it a strange paradox then, as I still do now, that most of us don't want to think about death, our own mortality… Yet, when we hear about someone else's death…” 12 A companion essay identifies the construction “then, as I still do now” as the novel's most important single clause: it collapses the distance between the sixteen-year-old and the narrating adult that the book has otherwise carefully maintained, confirming that the detachment Bianca diagnosed was never a phase to be outgrown but a durable, permanent feature of the consciousness narrating the entire novel. 13 This is a significant interpretive choice: a reader who assumed Molly's coldness was trauma-response, likely to soften with age and hindsight, is told directly that it did not soften, which removes the comfortable redemptive reading and leaves the harder, more interesting one — that this is simply who Molly is, and the novel is not interested in curing her of it. VII. Reception and the Question of Structure Kirkus Reviews' assessment of the novel is notable for pairing real praise with a specific structural criticism: “while she may have a cold exterior, her distinctiveness is an appealing quality and often amusing,” but “Mulhern's narrative hits the occasional standstill, where Molly repeatedly ponders the same issues with Nonna or Gabe” 14 — a fair observation, and one that a full-length comparative study on this site extends into a broader claim about Mulhern's fiction generally: that the work is stronger in the scene than in the arc, more interested in moments of revelation than in the machinery that connects one revelation to the next. Similar limitations can be found in some scene-centered fiction by William Trevor, Alice Munro, and James Joyce. 15 The criticism is worth taking seriously rather than dismissing as an unfriendly review, because it identifies what the novel trades away in exchange for its deadpan method: a narrator committed to withholding interpretation will tend to produce scenes that circle the same unresolved question rather than scenes that resolve it and move the plot decisively forward. VIII. Conclusion: What the Comedy Was For The novel's emotional logic is illuminated by a fact Mulhern has disclosed about its origin: in the same Shelf Unbound interview that confirms the Defoe allusion, he revealed that “the true genesis of Molly is the fact that five important people in my own life died in less than a year.” 16 Read against that disclosure, the toad, the vodka, the maggots-and-word-processor non sequitur, and the adult narrator's unsoftened detachment can be read as a coping mechanism rather than as coldness for its own sake. The comedy does not deny grief; it functions as a defense against it and does not provide the false comfort of a character who eventually learns to feel the "right" amount. Molly Bonamici does not become warmer by the novel's end. She remains strange and funny, offering one account of surviving overwhelming loss. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. title: The Habit of Return: Repeated Motifs in the Work of James Mulhern
heading: The Habit of Return
description: An essay on recurring motifs in the fiction and poetry of James Mulhern — the threshold, the hand, water, the slant of light, and the domestic object — with close readings of craft, purpose, theme, and technical skill.
text: The Habit of Return: Repeated Motifs in the Work of James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On Recurrence as Method The Habit of Return Repeated Motifs in the Fiction and Poetry of James Mulhern Abstract This essay treats the recurring images in Mulhern’s work — the threshold, the hand, water, the slant of interior light, and the household object — not as a signature but as a compositional system. It argues that recurrence in this body of work is a deliberate method with a definable technique, a consistent thematic claim, and an identifiable purpose: to hold what would otherwise be lost. Close readings are drawn from Crossings and from the Aiden Glencar fiction. A companion essay, Thin Places , treats the psychological and Romantic genealogy of the same disposition; this one stays with the images themselves and with the craft that puts them to work. I. The Author’s Own Account It is unusual for a writer to name his own method in his front matter. Mulhern does exactly that. The introduction to Crossings opens with a proposition about memory and then, without transition, states the organising principle of the book: Memory is an act of attention. We choose what to preserve, which words to carry forward, which silences to honor. In this collection of poetry, I return to thresholds— doorways where my father asked, “Everything copacetic?” Near a fire under a bridge, when my brother hugged my shoulder, in a hallway where my grandfather touched my head, by the hospital bed where a face I knew would soon be gone. 1 Three claims are packed into that passage, and the whole of the poetics follows from them. The first is that memory is selective and therefore moral: to remember is to choose, and choosing is an act for which one is answerable. The second is that the chosen units are not scenes or stories but positions — doorway, bridge, hallway, bedside. The third is the verb: I return . Not I remember , which would make the poems retrospective, but I return , which makes them present-tense and repeatable. The threshold is not where something once happened. It is where the poet goes. The introduction closes with a chiasmus that should be read as a statement of purpose rather than as a flourish: My family members are my prayers. My poems are my prayers. My family members are my poems. 2 The figure works by substitution: if family equals prayer, and poem equals prayer, then family equals poem. What the syllogism licenses is a particular understanding of what these poems are for . A prayer is not a description of an absent person; it is an address to one. The poems are therefore not elegies in the ordinary sense — not reports on loss — but attempts to keep an address open. This distinction will matter when we come to the technique, because it explains why so many of these poems decline to conclude. II. Recurrence Distinguished from Repetition A motif that returns without gaining anything is repetition, and it is a fault. A motif that returns altered, in a new position, carrying what it acquired the last time, is recurrence, and it is a structure. The distinction is not merely terminological in Mulhern’s case, because the same image is frequently made to change function between appearances. Consider the doorway. In “Copacetic” it is occupied by a living man: “My father stands in the doorway. / ‘Everything copacetic?’ he says.” 3 In the dedication to the same volume the doorway has become the place where the father is remembered standing: “Dad—You stood in doorways asking / if everything was copacetic.” 4 By the end of “Copacetic” the threshold has migrated into euphemism — the dying man “wants to leave— / something about a trip” 3 — and in the dedication it has become metaphysical: the family consists of “those who remain / and those who have passed / into the other room.” 4 Four appearances; four different jobs. The doorway is by turns a literal architectural feature, a habit of character, a euphemism for dying, and a cosmology. Nothing is restated. Each instance depends on the reader having met the image before, and each adds a meaning the previous one could not carry. That dependency is what makes the collection a book rather than a gathering. III. The Threshold The threshold is the governing motif, and it is unusually literal. Mulhern rarely reaches for the abstract liminal; he reaches for architecture. The reader is given doorways, hallways, crosswalks, windows, and the edges of rooms, and the emotional event is almost always positioned at one rather than inside one. “Dark City” is the clearest instance, and it is worth quoting at length because the poem is built on a single spatial contrast: My only memory of you— in the dark hallway of your Boston house, just off the sunny kitchen. I was two, you were sixty. Tall and thin, wispy silver hair, light-blue eyes lit by a slant of kitchen sun. 5 The grandfather is placed in the dark hallway; the light is in the kitchen behind him and reaches him only as a slant. The poem does not say that the man is between life and death, or that memory is partial, or that the child cannot follow him. It puts him in a corridor between a lit room and an unlit one and lets the architecture make the claim. When he leaves, he leaves along the corridor — “then walked down the shellacked hallway” — and the next line is his death. The hallway does the work that a paraphrase would ruin. “The Crosswalk” relocates the same structure outdoors. The poem opens with the speaker stopped at a threshold he is not crossing, watching a father and son cross it: “Today, I saw a father and son / step onto the crosswalk. / I braked and watched them pass—.” 6 The speaker is stationary and enclosed; the pair he envies are in motion and in the open. The poem’s subject — a son’s unmet wish to have been carried — is stated by the geometry before it is stated in words. The window performs a quieter version of the same function. In “Shoes,” after the grandmother has explained why her toes are crooked, the poem gives her a window rather than a reflection: “She looked out the window and sighed.” 7 The speaker then supplies what she may be seeing — her own mother carrying home a bag of cast-off shoes. The window is the hinge between two generations; it is also, characteristically, a way of not asking her. IV. The Hand If the threshold is the governing motif, the hand is the most reliable instrument. It recurs in three distinct offices, and the sequence in which they appear amounts to an argument. The hand as evidence In “The Crosswalk,” the speaker has been cataloguing his father’s failures of affection — the lifting that never happened, the misattributed memory of building a shed. Against that he sets one image: “I had other memories— / your hands over mine, / knotting my tie.” 6 The hands are offered as counter-evidence in a case the speaker is arguing with himself. Note the preposition. Not on mine but over mine: the father’s hands enclose the son’s and guide them, which is instruction and tenderness at once, and which requires no gloss. The hand as failed reach “Water” ends with a gesture that cannot complete itself. After a long catalogue of a ruined body, the poem arrives at “On the dock, / hands cupped,” 8 the cupped hand being the oldest vessel there is and, here, an empty one. The reach is toward water the man cannot get to. The hand as instruction The final movement of the book converts the image into an imperative. “Moving Forward” closes on the plainest statement of ethics in the collection: to “touch a hand to show we care, / massage a pained foot, / or simply listen to someone’s despair.” 9 The hand that was evidence in one poem and futility in another becomes, at the end, a thing the reader is asked to use. The sequence can be read as deliberate: the hand is first something done to the speaker, then something the speaker cannot do, then something anyone may do. A motif moves from passivity through helplessness to agency without a line of commentary marking the transit. V. Water Water is the motif most often noticed in this work and the one most at risk of being over-read, since it is also the most conventional. What distinguishes Mulhern’s use of it is that he almost never lets it be symbolic on its own terms; he makes it do descriptive labour first, and permits the resonance to arrive as a by-product. The opening of “Water” is a catalogue of a body rendered as terrain: The old man— flaccid face, blue-water eyes, rough-sloped nose, broken capillaries like tributaries on arid land. His belly— a white boulder strewn with seaweed hair. 8 The governing conceit is drought. Eyes hold water; capillaries are “tributaries” on land that is “arid”; the belly is a “boulder” with “seaweed” on it, which is to say a rock left behind by a tide that has gone out. The body is a landscape from which the water has withdrawn. Only after this is established does the poem reach the dock and the empty cupped hands. The symbolic charge of the ending is entirely produced by the accuracy of the description that precedes it; nothing has to be asserted. Elsewhere water is domestic and unremarked. A woman “put dishes in the sink and ran water”; 10 a man caring for a dying dog “made sure she had water.” 9 These are not symbols so much as chores, and their unremarkableness is the point: in this body of work the sacramental and the menial use the same tap. That equivalence is a settled conviction rather than an effect, and it is treated at greater length in the companion essay Water, and What It Carries . VI. Light, and the Slant of Kitchen Sun Light and darkness form the most conventional pairing in the work, and Mulhern’s handling of it is uneven — a candid assessment must say so. Where it succeeds, it succeeds because the light is given a source and an angle rather than a meaning. “A slant of kitchen sun” is the exemplary instance. 5 The phrase is doing three things at once: it locates the light (kitchen), it gives it a geometry (slant), and it declines to interpret it. That the grandfather’s pale eyes are “lit” by it is simply what happens when a man stands at the edge of a lit room. Any reader who wishes to hear Dickinson’s “certain Slant of light” behind the line is free to, and the poem neither invites nor forbids it. Compare the shadow in “Copacetic”: “I sat by him until shadows crossed his face.” 3 The verb is crossed — the book’s title-word, arriving as a description of late-afternoon light in a hospital room. The pun is available but unpressed. This is the collection’s characteristic tact: the resonance is placed within reach and then left alone. Where the pairing is less successful, it is because light has been asked to signify without being seen — to stand for hope or transcendence as a general proposition. The difference between the strong and the weak instances is consistently the presence or absence of a physical source. VII. The Domestic Object as Reliquary Mulhern’s fourth recurring system is the household object charged with more feeling than it can comfortably hold. A yellow teapot, a pair of Dr. Scholl’s, a spoonful of red Jell-O, a cheap framed print. “The Teapot” begins as a search: “‘Do you have the yellow teapot?’ my mother asked. / ‘Beth told me I promised it to you long ago.’” 11 The object is missing, and the search for it releases the Christmas table — the pies, the mahogany, Streisand, “Nanna’s Irish prayer— / ‘thy gifts’—received.” 11 The teapot is a reliquary in the strict sense: an ordinary container whose value is entirely a function of what it has been near. “Shoes” performs the same operation on footwear, and adds a generational turn. The grandmother explains her crooked toes: “‘My mother cleaned houses for the rich,’ she said. / ‘We had to wear the shoes she brought home. / They were often small.’” 7 A deformity is revealed as a class inheritance, delivered without complaint and closed with a laugh. The poem’s tact is that it never says poverty ; it says the toes, I mean . The most compressed instance is in “Last Supper,” where the news of a death and a domestic emergency arrive in the same breath: “‘My father’s dead. / Can you shine my shoes?’” 12 Two sentences, no connective, no comment. Grief and errand are set side by side because that is how they arrive. A few lines later the print of The Last Supper is found face-down with “its frame splintered” 12 — a devotional image broken by an accident nobody intended, which is as close as the poem comes to saying anything about faith. VIII. The Unasked Question and the Withheld Gloss A fifth motif is verbal rather than visual: the question that stands in for an unaskable one. “Everything copacetic?” is the book’s recurring formula, and the introduction identifies its subjects as “men who couldn’t cry, women who worked until their feet hurt, / children who waited for words that never came.” 1 The dedication offers an interpretive turn on the father’s formula: “It wasn’t always, but your asking / made it so.” 4 The inadequate question is not excused; it is reclassified. The asking, not the answer, was the love. This is a recurring ethical concern in the work — the reading of insufficient speech as sufficient feeling — and it keeps the family poems from becoming grievances. Formally, the corollary is the withheld gloss. “Copacetic” is the pattern case: “Don’t want it.” “You’ve got to eat, Dad.” “I’m not hungry.” He pushed it away. 3 Three lines of speech, one clause of action, no interpretation. The refusal of food by a dying man is among the most heavily freighted moments available to a writer, and the poem spends four words on it. What follows is equally spare: “Mostly, he slept. / Sometimes he asked the time. / I left at nine.” The flat report of the hour is the poem’s most affecting line precisely because it declines to be affecting. IX. The Motifs in the Fiction The system is not confined to the poems. The Aiden Glencar story “Arise and Go Now” opens by putting its narrator at a door and moving him, immediately, through a house toward light: I arrived at Rita’s house about noon. Her blue eyes widened when she opened the door. … We walked through the hallway and kitchen to a brick patio covered by a pergola. … Sunlight glimmered through the red cedar lattice above us, dappling her face. 13 Door, hallway, kitchen, dappled light on a face: the same sequence as “Dark City,” in prose, at a different tempo, with the valence reversed — here the passage leads outward into sun rather than inward into a dark corridor. The recurrence across genres suggests that these images may function as a compositional system rather than as the local furniture of a single book. The fiction also supplies the juxtaposition the poems favour. Rita, having opened the door in a nightdress patterned with honey-bees, holds a paperback whose cover shows “[a] girl in a red dress… in front of a grave” with “[t]he ground… on fire,” and dismisses it in a word: “Junk.” 13 A lurid image of the afterlife is introduced and waved away inside two sentences, in a scene otherwise made of sunlight and grass. The author’s own note on his prose describes this habit precisely: “a willingness to slow down” and “a habit of placing the ordinary and the unspeakable in the same paragraph.” 14 X. Technique: How the Motifs Function Motifs do not function because they are repeated. They function because of what the sentences around them are doing. Four techniques recur. 1. Syntactic suspension “Water” withholds a finite verb through its entire opening: “The old man— / flaccid face, / blue-water eyes, / rough-sloped nose…” is a noun and a series of appositives with nothing to predicate them. The reader is held in grammatical incompletion for the length of the description, which is a formal analogue of a life suspended. The poem’s structure and its subject are the same thing. 2. The dash as removed connective Mulhern’s dash almost always marks an omission he does not intend to supply: “My only memory of you—”; “The old man—”; “I braked and watched them pass—”; “I had other memories—.” In each case the dash stands where an explanatory clause would go. The punctuation is load-bearing: it is the visible sign of the withheld gloss. 3. Understatement as measurement After discovering that his father has credited a shared memory to another son, the speaker of “The Crosswalk” reports: “I was bothered just a bit.” 6 The line is not modest; it is calibrated. The gap between the size of the wound and the size of the phrase is where the feeling is kept, and a reader who has been paying attention supplies the difference. 4. The catalogue, levelled Where the poems widen their scope they do so by list, and the lists deliberately refuse hierarchy. “To Be” places “the Wife of Bath’s scarlet stockings” and “poor Yorick’s skull” in the same syntactic rank as “a flattened sneaker on some highway” and “a lost sock under a sagging couch.” 15 Monument and litter are given identical grammatical weight. The device is the formal expression of the collection’s central conviction — that nothing is too small to be kept — and it is the same conviction that produces the teapot and the shoes. XI. Purpose: Prayer, Mercy, and the Unfinished Why return at all? The introduction has already answered: the poems are prayers, and a prayer is an address rather than a report. But there is a second answer available in the shape of the work. Almost none of these poems resolve. “Copacetic” ends with a nurse’s phone call and a man who “wants to leave— / something about a trip”; the trip of the opening stanza has returned, transformed, and the poem stops there. “The Crosswalk” does not forgive the father and does not indict him. “Moving Forward” euthanises the dog and moves directly to a stranger’s formula — “Sorry for your loss” — and a man leaning on a steering wheel. The refusal of closure is consistent enough to be structural. This is where recurrence and purpose meet. If a poem concluded, the image inside it would be finished with, and the address would close. By leaving the poems open and letting the images travel between them, the writer keeps the material in circulation. The doorway is available to the next poem because no poem has used it up. What looks like a habit of return is, functionally, a refusal to let anything be over. The ethical name for this in Mulhern’s work is mercy. The father who could only ask “Everything copacetic?” is not corrected; he is re-read. The grandmother’s crooked toes are not made into an indictment of the households her mother cleaned. The dog is not spared the diapers or the needle, and the mother who suggests otherwise is answered but not condemned. Judgment would require conclusions, and conclusions are precisely what these poems decline to reach. XII. Conclusion: What Recurrence Argues Taken together, the motifs make a claim that no single poem states. The threshold says that the important moments happen at edges, between one condition and another. The hand says that what passes between people passes through touch rather than speech. Water says that the body is a landscape and that landscapes dry. The household object says that value is conferred by proximity to love. The unasked question says that insufficient words may still be sufficient feeling. Each of these is arguable on its own. Together, and repeated across two genres and several decades, they form a sustained proposal that ordinary life is the whole of the material, and that attention is an instrument for approaching it. The poems do not ask the reader to believe anything in particular. They invite the reader to look at a doorway, a pair of shoes, or a spoon of red Jell-O, and to notice how memory is kept in such objects. That is what the recurrence appears to be for. It is less a stylistic signature than a method for keeping things in view. — Silver Current Press Notes 1.
