title: Mulhern's Transcendentalism — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: Mulhern’s Transcendentalism
description: Emerson, Thoreau, Whitman, and the Oversoul — how James Mulhern's own Artistic Creed reveals a Transcendentalist philosophy structuring his Irish-Catholic and Italian-American fiction.
text: Mulhern's Transcendentalism — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On Intellectual Inheritance Mulhern’s Transcendentalism Emerson, Thoreau, Whitman, and the Oversoul — how a nineteenth-century American philosophy structures a contemporary Irish-Catholic and Italian-American fictional world. Abstract James Mulhern has named his own governing philosophy directly, in an “Artistic Creed” that declares, “I write as a Transcendentalist — in sensibility and in spirit,” crediting Emerson’s Oversoul, Thoreau’s attention to the near and small, and Whitman’s democratic self as direct influences. This essay treats that creed as a citable primary source and traces its structuring presence through the fiction’s doctrine of recurrence, its classroom scenes of Transcendentalist pedagogy, and the tension between a Catholic sacramental worldview and an Emersonian one that the fiction never fully resolves. I. A Creed Stated, Not Inferred Criticism ordinarily has to infer a writer’s philosophical commitments from pattern and implication. In “An Artistic Creed,” printed as a companion piece to the “Note from the Author” in The Collected Stories and Poems of James Mulhern (forthcoming), Mulhern identifies his intellectual lineage directly: “I write as a Transcendentalist — in sensibility and in spirit. I came to this not as a doctrine to be argued but as a way of seeing I could not put down. Emerson taught me to trust the inner light and to call the great current of things the Oversoul. Thoreau taught me to look long and closely at the near and the small until they open. Whitman taught me that a single life, honestly told, contains multitudes and belongs to everyone. I am in their debt, and I do not pretend otherwise.” 1 The document offers a useful primary source for considering terms that recur in the work: the Oversoul, the inner light, recurrence, and the single life that “belongs to everyone.” The creed continues into territory that would be heretical in a strictly doctrinal Catholic framework and states it as considered belief rather than accident: “I believe the sacred is not far off but here — in a kitchen, a sickroom, a stretch of shoreline, the face of someone loved and lost. I believe the soul is not sealed within us but joined, through the Oversoul, to every other soul that has been or will be.” 1 A companion “Note from the Author” extends the theology of recurrence explicitly: “What looks like repetition is recurrence, and recurrence is how the spirit comes to know itself… This is resurrection — the same old truths rising again and again… And it is the Oversoul’s work as much as mine.” 2 Where an essay elsewhere on this site, “The Habit of Return,” treats recurrence primarily as a craft technique, this essay argues that recurrence is, for Mulhern, first a metaphysical claim and only secondarily a compositional method — the method exists because the belief demands it. II. Emerson and Thoreau in the Classroom: “Drenched to the Bone” Mulhern’s fiction does not merely allude to Transcendentalism from a distance; it stages the tradition’s actual texts being taught, misheard, and half-understood inside an American public-school classroom, which is itself a Transcendentalist gesture — Emerson and Thoreau surviving their own domestication into curriculum. In “Drenched to the Bone,” the narrator, a Florida high-school English teacher named Jack, reads Thoreau’s “Civil Disobedience” aloud to a restless class and paraphrases its central claim: “Thoreau is talking about an individual’s conscience as being the most important aspect of who we are. You remember Emerson? ‘Nothing is at last sacred but the integrity of your own mind’ and his other quote, ‘What have I to do with the sacredness of traditions, if I live wholly from within?’” 3 The direct citation of Emerson’s “Self-Reliance” inside a scene of failing pedagogy is a deliberate irony: the students immediately misunderstand or mishear nearly everything, one asking, “Isn’t he the guy that invented electricity?” (confusing Emerson with Edison), while another calls Marx’s “opium of the people” the “oxycodone of the masses.” 3 Yet the scene does not simply mock the students’ ignorance; it dramatizes Transcendentalism working precisely as Emerson intended, on minds untrained to recognize the philosophy by name. Two students, Amelia and Brandi, arrive independently at a lay version of civil disobedience once black roofing dust begins falling from a vent during the lesson: “This school is like a prison,” Amelia says, and moments later, following a real disruption, “This is a type of injustice. We should break a law or something… We should stage some kinda civil obedience… Make a big statement,” a malaprop (disobedience for obedience) that the story allows to stand uncorrected, itself a small Emersonian joke about trusting one’s own garbled formulation of an idea over its received, correct phrasing. 3 The scene’s final adversary to Transcendentalist individualism is Mary Grace, a devout evangelical student who denounces Thoreau directly: “You can read all you want but it won’t make you a better person. You need to act in the world, not retire from it like Thoreau. Helping others is what God wants us to do,” 3 a critique that lands with real force precisely because the story does not resolve it in either direction — Mary Grace’s subsequent violent breakdown neither vindicates nor refutes her theological objection to Emersonian self-reliance, leaving the tension exactly where Mulhern’s creed leaves it: faith and Transcendentalist self-trust “held in the same hand, neither one permitted to win outright.” 4 III. Whitman’s Multitudes: The Single Life That Belongs to Everyone The creed’s Whitman debt — “a single life, honestly told, contains multitudes and belongs to everyone” 1 — supplies the philosophical justification for a device that might otherwise seem simply comprehensive: Mulhern’s insistence, across the introduction to his collected volume, that his work constitutes “one people, gathered and remade” rather than a set of discrete, unrelated character studies. 2 The editors’ introduction makes the Whitmanian claim about the volume’s design explicit, describing water as the master symbol precisely because it “is what carries you away from where you were and what returns you, altered, to the place you started,” language that transposes Whitman’s democratic, boundary-dissolving self into Mulhern’s own hydraulic register. 5 One textual instance of this Whitmanian claim may be Nonna’s vernacular theology in “A Bath,” where a working-class Irish grandmother, without any exposure to Emerson or Whitman that the text records, describes individual suffering as shared rather than sealed off. Confessing that her own husband hit her, she tells her daughter Grace, “You’re not that horrible word, Gracie. You’re opinionated and strong. I wish I could have been more like you when I was a young woman. I followed the mold. Too afraid to do what I really wanted… To be a competitive swimmer. But we were poor, and poor women had little chance of pursuing such a dream.” 6 Nana’s recognition that her daughter’s strength may fulfill a thwarted part of her own life — not a separate person to be judged but a “multitude” she contains — echoes the joined-soul claim the Artistic Creed states directly, in an idiom of whiskey and stepladders rather than philosophy. IV. The Unresolved Seam: Oversoul Against Sacrament One important critical question this material raises is whether an Emersonian Oversoul, which dissolves the individual soul into “every other soul that has been or will be,” 1 is philosophically compatible with the Catholic sacramental theology — confession, communion, the Assumption of Mary — that structures the same body of work, and which other essays on this site have treated as the fiction’s primary theological register. Mulhern’s own language suggests he sees no contradiction, treating the two systems as mutually reinforcing rather than competing: “In art, as in faith, what is laid down is taken up — and it becomes life eternal,” 2 a sentence that borrows the vocabulary of the Mass (offertory, elevation) to describe an Emersonian process of recurrence. But the seam is visible in the fiction, not just smoothed over in the creed. Emerson’s Transcendentalism is famously a philosophy of the sovereign individual conscience, distrustful of inherited institution and “the sacredness of traditions” 3 ; Catholicism, especially the Catholicism of Mulhern’s Irish and Italian grandmothers, is a religion of inherited institution nearly by definition, its authority residing precisely in tradition’s unbroken transmission. The unauthorized-confessor structure examined elsewhere on this site — grandmothers hearing confession with no priestly warrant — can be read as one response to this seam: an institutional sacrament (confession) performed by an individual, uncredentialed conscience (Nana, Peggy, Aiden), which is to say a Catholic form filled with Transcendentalist content. Mulhern’s Boston and Philadelphia interiors can be read as sites of negotiation between two American religious inheritances that rarely speak to each other directly — the immigrant Church of his grandmothers and the native Protestant dissent of Concord — conducted largely without the characters naming the negotiation as such. The Artistic Creed is a useful document for considering that negotiation alongside the fiction. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. title: Musings: Notebook to Essay — Notes on Teaching, Writing & Reading by James Mulhern
heading: Musings: Notebook to Essay
description: Short reflections from James Mulhern on teaching, writing, literature, and the writing life — the notebook fragments that grow into the full scholarly essays on this site.
text: Musings: Notebook to Essay — Notes on Teaching, Writing & Reading by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon A Commonplace Book Musings: Notebook to Essay A working journal — poems, borrowed lines that won't leave a writer alone, fragments from a notebook. Some stay fragments. Others, given time, grow into the full essays on the Criticism & Craft page. This is where that growing happens. New entries appear here as they are written — a poem of mine, a sentence from another writer that has not yet stopped speaking, a passage from a student's essay, a thought from yesterday's notebook. A commonplace book, the old writers called it. 13 August 2026 Writing I Like Whitman and Dickinson: two foreparents, two temperaments I keep these two on the same shelf, though they never met and would likely have unsettled each other if they had. Walt Whitman and Emily Dickinson are commonly named the first great American poets, and I think the label holds — not because they wrote alike, but because each, independently and almost simultaneously, broke with English precedent and invented a native way of hearing. Whitman did it by knocking down the wall between the poet and the world. Here he is at the opening of Song of Myself , already refusing the modesty English verse expected of him: I celebrate myself, and sing myself, And what I assume you shall assume, For every atom belonging to me as good belongs to you. I loafe and invite my soul, I lean and loafe at my ease observing a spear of summer grass. — Walt Whitman, Song of Myself , 1 Dickinson broke the same wall from the opposite direction — not by enlarging the self until it held everyone, but by narrowing the aperture until a single perception could not be paraphrased away. Where Whitman's line runs long, cumulative, and breathing, hers stops, doubts itself, and starts again on a dash: I'm Nobody! Who are you? Are you — Nobody — too? Then there's a pair of us! Don't tell! they'd advertise — you know! How dreary — to be — Somebody! How public — like a Frog — To tell one's name — the livelong June — To an admiring Bog! — Emily Dickinson, 288 Set side by side, the two techniques could hardly be more opposed. Whitman writes in long, unrhymed, incantatory lines built on anaphora and cataloguing — the famous lists of occupations, landscapes, and bodies that pour down the page until the poem feels less like a description of America than an act of ingesting it. His grammar is additive: and, and, and , one clause opening onto the next, because his premise requires that nothing be left out. Dickinson writes in the clipped meter of the hymnal — common meter and ballad meter, the very forms she heard every Sunday in an Amherst pew — but she interrupts that inherited music with slant rhyme, eccentric capitalization, and the dash that has generated a century of scholarly argument. Her grammar is subtractive: she tells the truth, as she says elsewhere, by telling it slant, withholding as much as she reveals. Whitman annexes the world line by line. Dickinson interrogates a single instant until it yields more than it wants to. Both are among my favorite poets, and I hold them there for almost opposite reasons. I love Dickinson for her intellectuality and her enigmatic lines — the sense that every poem is a locked room with the key visible but just out of reach, and that rereading her is less a pleasure than an ongoing negotiation. I love Whitman for the opposite reason: his expansive self-presentation, his celebratory tone, the way he seems constitutionally incapable of closing a door once he has opened it. I find something quietly ironic in loving them equally, since to love both is to love a contradiction. And yet the contradiction resolves itself, I think, at a deeper level, because both poets are, at bottom, iconoclasts of versification — perseverant and entirely certain of their own craft, unwilling to write the poems their century expected of them. They simply arrived at that certainty from opposite directions. Whitman abolished the line to make room for everyone. Dickinson fractured the line to make room for the one true thing she meant. Both are, underneath the technique, evoking the same American spirit — independence, self-reliance, the conviction that the poem answers to no authority but the poet's own perception. In today's psychological terms, I would call Dickinson an introvert and Whitman an extrovert, and I do not think the anachronism does either poet a disservice. Whitman's is a poetics of merger — he wants to absorb the crowd and be absorbed by it, to feel the "kelson of the creation" running through every body he catalogues. Dickinson's is a poetics of withdrawal — her speaker is most herself alone, at the window, cataloguing not the world but the mind's report of it. And this is where the two of them stop being merely a matched pair of nineteenth-century originals and start speaking, I think, for two permanent strands of American ideology: the pull toward community and the pull toward being left alone. Whitman is the poet of the "barbaric yawp," the crowded ferry, the "I" that dilates until it contains multitudes. Dickinson is the poet of the shut door, the letter never sent, the self that insists on its right to remain illegible. America has always wanted both things at once — the town meeting and the cabin in the woods — and it is fitting that our two foreparents of poetry embody the choice so completely that neither one alone would do. I have a more private reason for returning to Dickinson, one that has nothing to do with prosody. I lived for five years a few blocks from her homestead in Amherst, Massachusetts, now a museum, and I passed it often enough that the house stopped being a historical marker and became, in my imagination, simply inhabited. I would look up at her bedroom window and imagine her at it, looking back down at me. Sometimes I glanced into her garden and wished, in the frankly impossible way one wishes for such things, that I could travel back and know her — sit with her, even briefly, in that garden. But I suspect, as the biographical criticism consistently suggests, that any approach of mine would have sent her hurrying back inside, her black dress billowing behind her like dark contrails, the wake of a speeding jet. That, too, seems fitting. The poet who wrote "I'm Nobody" and meant it would hardly have made an exception for an admirer two centuries early or two centuries late. I did not always make that walk alone. Often my companion past the homestead was Kathy Scherpa , one of the kindest people I have ever known, and I find now that I cherish those unhurried walks even more than the poetry itself — which is a high bar, since I love the poetry a great deal. We would pass the same fence, the same hedge, the same second-floor window, and talk of nothing urgent, which is to say we talked of everything that mattered. I did not know then to call those afternoons some of the best moments of my life. I know it now, plainly, and I suspect Dickinson — who prized nothing so highly as an afternoon rescued from the ordinary and made luminous by attention — would have approved of the accounting, even if she would not have approved of the company. Whitman, I suspect, would have done the opposite: seen me on the path, called out, and insisted I stay for supper. That, in the end, is the whole difference between them, and the whole reason American poetry needed both. ❖ ❖ ❖ 10 August 2026 From My Notebook The same doorway, more than once I have written the same doorway more times than I can count. In “Copacetic” it is the doorway of my father’s hospital room, and he is at the window in the blue bathrobe my sister gave him. In Give Them Unquiet Dreams it is a doorway on Winthrop Street in Braintree, and my grandmother is standing in it with the rosary in one hand and a lit cigarette in the other. In the Aiden stories I am still writing, it is a doorway I have not yet described but that will arrive when it wants to. For years I thought I was repeating myself — and worried about it, in the way writers are told to worry about it. I have begun, at sixty-three, to think of this less as repetition than as return. There may be a difference. You repeat what you have exhausted. You return to what you have not yet learned to see. The grandmother in the doorway is the same grandmother, and she has always been the same grandmother. I am not putting her there each time. She is there, and I am learning to look. I take it as a small consolation that this is not a new theory. Emerson might have called the doorway a “porch.” Chekhov might simply have gone on writing. ❖ ❖ ❖ 28 July 2026 A Borrowed Line From Marilynne Robinson I read this passage from Gilead once a year, sometimes twice. It is the letter of an old minister to his young son, and I know few sentences in modern American fiction that carry as much weight so lightly: “I’ll pray, and then I’ll sleep.” — Marilynne Robinson, Gilead Five words. The last sentence of the book. What it does is refuse the summing-up that every other closing sentence in the American canon has been reaching for since Fitzgerald’s green light. Robinson trusts the reader to have understood everything. She simply names the two things her narrator is still willing to do: pray, and sleep. In that order. I sometimes tell students that if they can end a story with two verbs and no explanation, they are already doing something most published writers never manage. Robinson can. Chekhov could. You get there by learning to trust the reader more than you trust your own summary. ❖ ❖ ❖ 14 June 2026 From My Notebook What I mean by mercy People ask me, when I say I write from mercy rather than judgment, what mercy has to do with fiction. Fair question. Mercy sounds like something you extend to the deserving. In a story you have made up yourself, no one is deserving because no one is real. You could summarize a character in a sentence and be done with them. Judgment is the easier thing. But this is what I mean. When I sit down with a character who has done something I do not admire — the father who is drinking, the mother who is failing her children, the boy who has stolen and then lied about it — I try not to have already decided what they are. I try to sit at the kitchen table with them and let them explain themselves in the way they would explain themselves to a friend at four in the morning. Not to me. To a friend. My job, if I do it well, is to have overheard what they said and set it down as accurately as I can. Mercy in fiction is not forgiveness. It is the willingness to let a character say what they would actually say, in the words they would actually use, without the writer standing behind them with a red pencil marking them as guilty. This is not, for the record, moral relativism. It is the opposite. It is the belief that every person, in real life, is too complicated to be reduced — and that the writer’s job is to honor that in the invented person too. If the story is good, the reader will do the judging themselves, and their judgment will be more accurate than mine could have been. I get out of the way. I learned this, or began to learn it, from Chekhov. I try to teach it every semester. I fail at it, in my own work, all the time. This fragment grew into the essay All We Ever Needed: The Architecture of Mercy , a full study of the short story collection built on this idea. ❖ ❖ ❖ 11 May 2026 From My Notebook Teaching as the pond I bathe in A passage I keep returning to — from an essay of mine called "Teaching at Fifty-Six." Written near the end of three decades of teaching inner-city kids, and never far from my desk. It occurs to me that teaching is my salvation. There are wonderful moments, when things move so fluidly, and the pitch of our discussion seems just right — students are smiling, engaged, sharing feelings, excited. A palpable energy moves through all of us — a realness, an in-the-momentness that charges the air and electrifies our conversations. Connections are made. Questions are answered. We learn who we are. If we are fortunate, we intuit an answer to the question Why? Sometimes we discover what is really true. — From "Teaching at Fifty-Six" People like to imagine that rare and delectable places lurk in some remote part of the universe or some distant epoch from the past, but right now, in my classroom, surrounded by students, I dwell in that delectable place, a most memorable season of any day. I feel intensely awake, most alive — renewed. This is communion , I think, and teaching will be the pond that I bathe in each morning, every new day. ❖ ❖ ❖ 7 May 2026 A Borrowed Line From William Trevor I keep coming back to this passage from Trevor's "The News from Ireland." It is the kind of sentence that teaches you, every time you read it, what the short story is for: "There is, in his clerical opinion, no part of the world more forsaken by God, no part where charity is more thinly given, kindness more rarely shown." — William Trevor, "The News from Ireland" What strikes me is the construction. Trevor begins with a tucked-in clause — in his clerical opinion — that identifies the speaker without naming him, and then keeps the sentence moving forward in two parallel halves whose rhythm mimics the very judgment they describe. The sentence becomes the clergyman's mind on the page. We are taught to admire writers for what they say. We should also admire them for how they hold the reader in a single breath. ❖ ❖ ❖ 18 April 2026 Writing I Like A stanza by Emily Dickinson I taught Dickinson for years. I am still teaching her, even now, by reading her in the morning before I write. This is the stanza I came back to this week: Tell all the truth but tell it slant — Success in Circuit lies Too bright for our infirm Delight The Truth's superb surprise — Emily Dickinson The instruction is to a poet, but I have come to think it is also an instruction to a novelist. The slant truth is the one the reader can bear; the head-on truth is the one the reader resists. Fiction's whole technology — point of view, scene, dialogue, metaphor, the careful arrangement of what is shown and what is withheld — is in service of telling it slant. Dickinson knew at thirty what most of us are still working out at sixty. ❖ ❖ ❖ More entries will appear here as they are written. title: Naming as Fate: Onomastics and Allusive Christening in the Fiction of James Mulhern — James Mulhern
heading: Naming as Fate
description: An onomastics essay on character naming in James Mulhern's fiction — Molly Bonamici, Myra Bocca, and Peggy Fleming as allusive instruments of meaning.
text: Naming as Fate: Onomastics and Allusive Christening in the Fiction of James Mulhern — James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On Character Names Naming as Fate In the Fiction of James Mulhern — Molly Bonamici, Myra Bocca, and Peggy Fleming as deliberate citations, each name a promise the narrative keeps. Abstract Mulhern’s own introduction to All We Ever Needed states a governing principle explicitly: “I take language to be a sacred inheritance and the act of naming to be a kind of devotion.” 1 Read alongside the character names in the corpus, the statement offers a useful way to consider how he approaches them. Molly Bonamici, Aiden Glencar, Myra Bocca, and Peggy Fleming are more than neutral labels attached to already-formed characters; some invite external references — a novel, a historical death, a homophonic pun, an Olympic champion — that the character’s arc may confirm, ironize, or literalize. This essay considers Mulhern’s names as an allusive practice, one that can serve as a compressed form of foreshadowing for readers who hear the names as citations rather than sounds. I. Names as Instructions for Reading Mulhern’s own introduction to All We Ever Needed states a governing principle explicitly: “I take language to be a sacred inheritance and the act of naming to be a kind of devotion.” 1 Read alongside the character names in the corpus, the statement offers a useful way to consider how he approaches them. Molly Bonamici, Aiden Glencar, Myra Bocca, and Peggy Fleming are more than neutral labels attached to already-formed characters; some invite external references — a novel, a historical death, a homophonic pun, an Olympic champion — that the character’s arc may confirm, ironize, or literalize. This essay considers Mulhern’s names as an allusive practice, one that can serve as a compressed form of foreshadowing for readers who hear the names as citations rather than sounds. II. Molly Bonamici and the Ghost of Moll Flanders Mulhern has stated directly that “Molly” derives from “Moll,” the heroine of Daniel Defoe’s Moll Flanders (1722), whose character shaped his own protagonist. The allusion rewards attention precisely because it is understated rather than announced within the text itself — nothing in Molly Bonamici explicitly cites Defoe, yet the two Mollys share a structural situation that the name quietly insists the reader notice: both are women whose survival depends on a hard-won self-sufficiency acquired through deprivation, who narrate their own lives retrospectively and without excessive self-pity, and whose moral standing the reader is repeatedly asked to weigh against a society that has already failed them before they commit their own transgressions. Moll Flanders spends a criminal life justifying herself in a plain, unsentimental first-person voice remarkably close to adult Molly’s own retrospective narration of the toad-killing and the eventual poisoning in “Mia Bambina” — a killer who narrates her own crime with the same declarative calm she applies to pouring orange juice. The surname “Bonamici” — “good friends” in Italian — supplies the counter-current: a name that promises fellowship and warmth precisely for a character whose defining trait, per Aunt Bianca’s diagnosis, is that she “doesn’t feel things” and treats even murder as an act of family loyalty. The name is thus doubly ironic — Moll Flanders without Defoe’s explicit criminality announced up front, wrapped in a surname that means “good friends” and is worn by a woman capable of killing for family. III. Myra Bocca and the Death That Repeats The Molly Bonamici material may also echo Fitzgerald through a name that operates by sound rather than by explicit citation: “Myra Bocca” is a near-homophonic echo of Myrtle Wilson, the woman killed by a car in The Great Gatsby , struck down on a road after running toward a vehicle she mistakes for her lover’s. The echo is suggestive. Myra’s introduction to Molly is marked by automotive death from the outset of her arc — the reader meets a woman whose fate, once the name is heard in that way, may seem foreshadowed — and the story later has Myra die after being struck, her body found beside the road, the black stone she gave Molly “for grieving” thrown by Molly herself toward the wreck in the story’s final gesture. 2 The possible echo lets a reader hear an element of the plot in advance, though the text does not announce the allusion directly. “Bocca” — Italian for “mouth” — adds another possible resonance: Myra is characterized largely through speech, a compulsive talker who “dominated the conversation” and cannot stop supplying unsolicited detail about her own life, 2 so that her surname may point toward a central trait. IV. Peggy Fleming and the Cruelty of a Beautiful Name “Assumptions” names its central figure after Peggy Fleming, the American figure skater who won Olympic gold in 1968 — a fact the story itself makes explicit rather than leaving implicit, with the narrator noting that he “always thought it a cruel irony that she had the same name as the graceful and beautiful skater.” 3 This is Mulhern’s most direct authorial signal that names in his fiction are meant to be read allusively, since the story pauses its own action to gloss the joke rather than trusting the reader to catch it unassisted — a rare moment of the technique surfacing into visibility. The cruelty the narrator identifies is precise: Peg Fleming, “hairless as well, suffering from a mysterious childhood disease,” toothless, alcoholic, carries a name synonymous with grace, athleticism, and youthful beauty, and the gap between name and body is the story’s first characterization of her before a word of her biography is given. 3 But the irony cuts a second way that the narrator does not name explicitly: the historical Peggy Fleming’s public identity was built on disciplined, controlled, beautiful movement under pressure, and Mulhern’s Peg, for all her physical wreckage, possesses an analogous discipline of voice — she can still sing, drunk and toothless, with enough residual control that the narrator remembers “the swelling sadness in her voice” decades later. 3 The name does not simply mock; it identifies the one faculty — performed grace under difficult conditions — that survives intact beneath the physical ruin the story otherwise dwells on. V. Aiden Glencar and the Absence of a Key Not every name in the corpus yields to this method, and the exception is instructive. Aiden Glencar, the second-sighted narrator of Give Them Unquiet Dreams , carries no documented etymological or allusive rationale — no interview or paratext explains the choice, unlike Molly, Myra, or Peggy. What can be said is that “Glencar” is an actual Irish place-name (a glen and waterfall in County Sligo, in the heart of Yeats’s own home territory), which — whether or not Mulhern intended the specific echo — locates Aiden’s surname inside the same folkloric geography that supplies his family’s banshees, pookas, and inherited second sight. Where Molly, Myra, and Peggy are named after other characters or other people, Aiden is named, if the geographic reading holds, after a place: a boy whose defining trait is an inherited connection to a landscape and a family history he has never physically visited, carrying that landscape’s name as his own surname before he ever crosses the ocean to Achill Island. The absence of a confirmed source is itself worth noting critically: it marks a boundary between the corpus’s demonstrably allusive names and its merely evocative ones, and a responsible reading should not manufacture certainty the record does not support. VI. Conclusion: The Character Arrives Already Written Read together, these names suggest that, for Mulhern, christening a character can establish elements the story will later complicate or literalize rather than mechanically determine. Molly Bonamici combines a possible echo of Defoe’s survivor with a surname meaning “good friends” in a plot about loyalty curdled into murder. Myra Bocca may draw on Fitzgerald’s roadside death and a mouth-word surname in a story that ends with her death on a road after a great deal of talk. Peggy Fleming sets an Olympic champion’s grace beside a body that has lost much but retains the capacity to sing, drunk, in a basement, for an audience of one child. Mulhern’s claim that “the act of naming” is “a kind of devotion” offers a helpful frame for these choices: rather than names chosen solely for euphony, they can function as small citations that shape a reader’s expectations. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. title: The Philosophy of Writing — James Mulhern's Working Notes on Craft
heading: The Philosophyof Writing
description: James Mulhern's reflections on attention, revision, mercy, and communion in the work of writing.
text: The Philosophy of Writing — James Mulhern's Working Notes on Craft ← Back to The 2601 Salon Working Notes on Craft The Philosophy of Writing Notes on attention, revision, mercy, and communion in the everyday work of writing. …that common heart, of which all sincere conversation is the worship, to which all right action is submission. Ralph Waldo Emerson, The Over-Soul Movement I The Ordinary as Sanctuary I have come to believe that the sacred is not sequestered in a far country, nor reserved for the ceremonies we have built to contain it. It abides here, in the unremarkable hours — in the kitchen light at six in the morning, in the faces we pass and neglect to see, in the small domestic liturgies we perform without knowing that we are performing them. Grace is not clamorous. It does not announce its arrival, nor wait upon our readiness. It waits, rather, in the everyday, with what I can only call patience, for the moment we consent to notice it. I sometimes find the sacred closer in a homely woman singing badly in a cellar than in what has been painted on a ceiling. For me, failure is often less a failure of faith than of attention. We mistake the urgent for the important and defer the essential to a season that never arrives. I try to remember that the love of others — the plain, unglamorous bond between one person and another — remains present beneath many quarrels and silences, even estrangements. Movement II Mercy as Method II was raised in a Boston Irish Catholic family where forgiveness, humility, and concern for others were understood less as principles to be announced than as obligations to be lived. No one was perfect; we were taught, largely through example, to forgive and forget. In the secluded Study Room my father designated as my own—a space I had not asked for but that, in retrospect, became my chapel—I often read and annotated the Bible. There I absorbed the underlying lesson of Philippians 2:3–4: to regard others with humility and to look beyond one’s own concerns toward the needs of others. Long before I could have expressed it, I began to feel that God’s grace and the presence of the Holy Spirit inhabited other people and the ordinary events of life; that the sacred abides in all things, both profane and hallowed. I do not want to look past a body in decline — diabetic, gouty, bald, unsteady on its feet — on the way to something more dignified. A character’s diabetes, asthma, gout, baldness, and drinking need not be obstacles to holiness in a story; examined closely, they may be part of the ground from which it grows. Sentimentality, as I understand it, can begin when a writer flinches from the actual body in front of them. Compassion asks the writer to keep looking. Movement III The Discipline of Attention I did not arrive at a philosophy of writing by sitting down to invent one. It arrived the way most working philosophies do — backwards, out of a classroom, after years of watching what actually moved a roomful of unconvinced teenagers, and after years of noticing which of my own sentences held up under a second and third reading and which ones were only trying to impress me. I do not think a sentence earns its seriousness by being about a serious subject. I think it earns seriousness by paying close, undistracted attention to something most writing would consider beneath its notice: a chipmunk crossing a patio, a scent of roses arriving mid-sentence, a bottle of suntan oil, a housedress with a pattern of tiny roses on it. My habit, which I did not choose so much as discover I already had, is to place the ordinary and the unspeakable in the same paragraph — a teacup poured, a lie confessed; a hand laid on a bald scalp, a body quietly dying under it. I often find that an ordinary detail is more than it first appears to be, and that patience is one part of a writer’s discipline: the willingness to watch a small thing long enough for further meanings to emerge. I hope that if I watch closely and long enough, it may suggest what it is for. I believe fire is not only punishment. In the right light, at the right hour, upon the right stretch of ordinary water, it is the very material of which glory is made. “Watch the shabby detail long enough to see what else it may contain.” Movement IV Revision as Listening This is, I recognize, a philosophy built on faith in revision as much as on any single technique. I do not think the religious architecture in a story like “Assumptions” arrived because I sat down and planned a Marian allegory. I think it arrived because I kept returning to the same image — a woman anointed with oil on a beach, a housedress, a sea catching fire in the late light — until the language underneath the language declared itself. Revision, for me, is less a matter of correcting mistakes than of listening harder to a draft that may know more than I did when I wrote it. I try to revise a sentence until it has discovered more than I knew when I began it; for me, that is not necessarily a failure of planning, but part of the work. Movement V Writing as Communion I have said before that teaching is communion — that a roomful of unconvinced teenagers and one exhausted teacher, meeting honestly for fifty minutes, amounts to a kind of sacrament administered without a priest. I have come to believe the same is true of writing itself, and I only ever discovered it backwards, sentence by sentence, the way a person discovers most things they already half-believed. A sentence, when it is working, is not a message sent from a writer who already knows something to a reader who does not. It is closer to a shared table. I sit down not entirely certain what I mean, and the sentence, if I am patient enough with it, tells me — the way a good conversation tells both people something neither of them arrived already knowing. That is the first communion: between the writer and the page, two parties neither of whom fully controls what gets said. The second is between the writer and the subject — and here I mean subject in the oldest sense, the person or memory or ordinary object being written about. I cannot write about a grandmother anointing a bald scalp with tanning oil, or a mother’s calloused heel, or a housedress with roses on it, without in some sense sitting with that person again, at that table, in that weather. Writing does not preserve the dead so much as it reopens a chair for them. My family members are my prayers. I wrote that once and meant it more literally than the sentence lets on. To write about a person with enough attention to get their gestures right — the exact word they used, the exact slant of light in the kitchen when they said it — is to hold them in mind the way a prayer holds its subject in mind: not to fix them, not to improve them, only to keep them present a little longer than memory alone would manage. The third communion is the one I have the least control over: the one between the finished page and a reader I will likely never meet. A poem written out of one family’s grief may become, in a stranger’s late-night reading, a poem about their own. I do not take this as a failure of specificity, but as one reason to write something down rather than feel it privately. Movement VI Comedy and Reverence, in the Same Breath Finally — and this is less a technique than a debt I owe my own upbringing — I do not believe moral seriousness and comedy are opposites, or that reverence and mockery cannot occupy the same sentence. My characters are cruel and devoted in the same breath because the people I grew up among were cruel and devoted in the same breath, and I have never trusted fiction that resolves that contradiction too neatly. I do not see comedy and reverence as opposites. A family may be cruel and devoted in the same breath, and fiction that resolves this contradiction too neatly can miss something important. Ten Working Reminders I look for the sacred in unremarkable hours rather than only in formal ceremony. I sometimes find the sacred closer in a homely woman singing badly in a cellar than in what has been painted on a ceiling. I try to treat attention as important as belief. I try to summon a character into fuller being before judging them. I do not want to look past a body in decline on the way to something more dignified. An ordinary detail may hold more than it first appears to hold. I revise until a sentence has found more than I knew when I began it. I sometimes see fire as more than punishment, depending on its setting and light. I think of writing as a table shared by the page, the subject, and a reader I may never meet. I try to leave room for comedy and reverence to coexist. I try to hold imagination in trust rather than claim to own it. For me, writing is more than self-expression; it is also a form of stewardship. Drawn from “A Working Philosophy,” “Credo,” and “Writing as Communion” — James Mulhern's own reflections on craft collected on this site. title: A Working Philosophy — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: A Working Philosophy
description: James Mulhern's working philosophy of writing and teaching — on attention, revision, moral seriousness, and finding the sacred in ordinary lives.
text: A Working Philosophy — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon On Craft · In the Author’s Own Words A Working Philosophy Notes on attention, revision, and the hope that a sentence, closely enough watched, may suggest what it is for. I did not arrive at a philosophy of writing by sitting down to invent one. It arrived the way most working philosophies do — backwards, out of a classroom, after years of watching what actually moved a roomful of unconvinced teenagers, and after years of noticing which of my own sentences held up under a second and third reading and which ones were only trying to impress me. I tell my students, in whatever ways I can, that they contain multitudes, that nothing is at last sacred but the integrity of their own minds, and that the real business of life is to live in the present and find eternity in a moment. I borrow this, gladly and openly, from Whitman, Thoreau, Emerson, and Dickinson — patron saints, as I think of them, of American literature. I ask my students to explore the circumference of their own lives, to celebrate themselves, to write toward a sacred self they have not yet been given permission to notice. Most of them think I am out of my mind. A fair number of them tell me so. I have come to think the skepticism is not an obstacle to the method — it is the method working correctly. Nobody discovers they contain multitudes by being told so gently. The same conviction runs underneath the fiction. I do not think a sentence earns its seriousness by being about a serious subject. I think it earns seriousness by paying close, undistracted attention to something most writing would consider beneath its notice: a chipmunk crossing a patio, a scent of roses arriving mid-sentence, a bottle of suntan oil, a housedress with a pattern of tiny roses on it. My habit, which I did not choose so much as discover I already had, is to place the ordinary and the unspeakable in the same paragraph — a teacup poured, a lie confessed; a hand laid on a bald scalp, a body quietly dying under it. I trust that if I watch the ordinary detail closely enough and long enough, it will tell me what it is actually for. It is very rarely only what it appears to be. This is, I recognize, a philosophy built on faith in revision as much as on any single technique. I do not think the religious architecture in a story like “Assumptions” arrived because I sat down and planned a Marian allegory. I think it arrived because I kept returning to the same image — a woman anointed with oil on a beach, a housedress, a sea catching fire in the late light — until the language underneath the language declared itself. Revision, for me, is less a matter of correcting mistakes than of listening harder to a draft that already knows more than I did when I wrote it. I am also, I’ll admit, incapable of writing about a body in decline without cataloging it in full. The instinct comes from the same place as the classroom instinct: I do not believe dignity should be conditional on being presentable. A character’s diabetes, asthma, gout, baldness, and drinking are not obstacles to her holiness in a story; they are, examined closely enough, the very ground it grows out of. I would rather write toward that ground than around it. Sentimentality, as I understand it, is what happens when a writer flinches from the actual body in front of them. Compassion is what happens when the writer keeps looking. Finally — and this is less a technique than a debt I owe my own upbringing — I do not believe moral seriousness and comedy are opposites, or that reverence and mockery cannot occupy the same sentence. My characters are cruel and devoted in the same breath because the people I grew up among were cruel and devoted in the same breath, and I have never trusted fiction that resolves that contradiction too neatly. A working philosophy, in the end, is only a writer’s honest report of what they have found true often enough to build a habit out of. Mine, distilled: watch the shabby detail long enough to see what else it may contain. title: Mapped in Water and Bone — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: Mapped in Water and Bone
description: An essay on themes, tropes, religious imagery, and poetic lineage across the poetry of James Mulhern — water, touch, light, and a personal liturgy of recurring images, read alongside Pound, Heaney, Yeats, Oliver, Kenyon, and Dickinson.
text: Mapped in Water and Bone — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On the Poetry Mapped in Water and Bone Themes, tropes, and religious imagery across the poetry of James Mulhern — and the poetic lineage, from Pound to Heaney to Dickinson, that shapes how he handles them. “On the dock—hands cupped bending. / Water he cannot reach.” — “Water,” Crossings Across the poems gathered in Crossings , a small set of images recurs: water that cannot be reached, hands that speak where words fail, light crossing into darkness or darkness into light, and the sacraments and feast days of Irish Catholicism used as a vocabulary for grief. Read as a body of work, the poems can be seen as variations on an inherited grammar of family, faith, and loss. Read alongside poets Mulhern has cited or studied, they also show affinities with a particular lineage rather than emerging only from temperament. I. Water as Inheritance and Deprivation Water appears throughout the collection not as comfort but as a measure of distance. The poem “Water” renders a dying man almost entirely through withheld liquid: “blue-water eyes,” “broken capillaries / like tributaries on arid land,” ending on “hands cupped bending. / Water he cannot reach.” “Catherine” complicates the image by tying it to labor and memory at once: a grandmother’s recollection of swimming “through dark water to reach a boulder crashed by foam” to gather sea lettuce, “scrape the rocks and then make stew,” even as her present body is lowered into a warm domestic bath. “Scrape the Rocks” returns to the same Clew Bay boulder and the same grandmother, now lowered into “Clew Bay in an old white tub” — the girl who once swam for sea lettuce and the old woman bathed by her family are the same body, forty years apart, held in the same water. “Triggers” grounds the element in unglamorous work, a grandmother who “hugged a wooden pail, stepped onto earth, / and trekked to the water” without complaint. In each case, water is inherited alongside hardship; it is rarely simply given, and the collection never lets the reader forget what it cost to fetch it. II. Hands as the Site of Unspoken Love Where speech in these poems tends toward reticence, touch is permitted to say what dialogue will not. “The Crosswalk” fixes an entire father-son relationship in a single recalled gesture, a tie knotted, hands positioned, and then, years later, a funeral photograph: “Your hands on mine. / Proof that we had closeness for a moment.” “Moving Forward” universalizes the gesture into an ethic: “touch a hand to show we care, / massage a pained foot, / … / All are acts that make us whole again.” “Honeymoon” and “Shoes” extend the same vocabulary to the feet — ointment worked into a heel, a grandmother’s toes eased into shoes too small, the crooked toes of a woman named Helen who carried “shoes passed house to house” her whole life. The hand, across the collection, is trusted the way statement is not. III. Thresholds of Light and Dark A third recurring trope marks passage itself — the literal and figurative crossing that gives the collection its title. “Dark City” stages a grandfather’s emigration from Ireland as a threshold scene, moving from a two-year-old’s single memory of the man in a “dark hallway” to an adult speaker standing at his abandoned homestead, pressing “my palm against the homestead wall, / as you touched my head so many years ago” — the touched head becoming the touching hand, recurrence rendered as physical rhyme rather than statement, before the poem resolves: “I see you move from darkness into the light and beyond.” “Brother Mike” compresses the same crossing into a wordless gesture of faith glimpsed “in dashboard light.” “The Guard” locates a related light inside a church’s stained glass, “red, gold, and green illuminations,” presiding over a scene of doubt rather than certainty. Light in these poems does not resolve; it marks the place where a crossing is underway — a preoccupation the poems share with Yeats, whose own thresholds, lakes, and birds mark the same pull between this world and what Mulhern’s fiction calls simply “the other room.” IV. A Personal Liturgy The collection draws its structural vocabulary from Irish Catholic practice — crossing oneself, communion, feast days, prayer — but rarely uses that vocabulary to deliver doctrine. “Brother Mike” ends on an act of private communion offered instead of advice; “Leaves” pairs a recited prayer at a graveside with the plain admission “We’re done,” repeated later as memory rather than instruction, its last lines rejoining the father’s breath to the speaker’s own: “Yours joins with mine. / I cannot see you gone.” This is not confined to Crossings ; the same handful of formulae recur across Mulhern’s five books with enough consistency to function as an actual liturgy rather than a metaphorical one — the Feast of the Assumption, the seawater cure at Nantasket, a wet silvery scalp and a crown the boy will not touch, a mourning dove rising and descending over water, “Up you go. On the count of three,” a halo-shaped pool of blood, the borrowed Thoreau line “Goodness is the only investment that never fails,” and the flat verdict “a useless thing” — a small set of formulae returned to on a cycle, the way a missal returns to the same propers every August 15th. Mulhern has said as much himself, in the poems, in one line that functions as a statement of genre rather than a figure of speech: “My family members are my poems. / My poems are my prayers.” V. The Poetic Lineage The poems draw on a recognizable lineage. An Imagist preference for concrete objects recalls Pound’s image and Williams’s conviction that there are “no ideas but in things.” The folded robe, the gold-trimmed teapot, and the burlap bag of shoes carry emotions the poems do not state outright; “Water,” with its old man “reaching for water / that will not rise,” works in a similarly image-centered mode. The Irish memory-poems about ancestral labor share an interest with Seamus Heaney’s work in a working forebear’s hands and tools as ways of understanding oneself. Yeats’s poems offer another reference point for thresholds, lakes, and birds pulling between two worlds. Mary Oliver’s devotional attention to the natural world helps illuminate the robins’ nest of “The Nest” and the trilling birds of “She Knelt.” The plainspoken American domestic elegy of Jane Kenyon and Ted Kooser — quiet, unshowy, set in kitchens and sickrooms and cars, alert to ordinary objects — is a register the collection often approaches. And Emily Dickinson’s dash, deferred turn, and refusal to over-explain offer one context for Mulhern’s phrase “the permission to end on a hyphen,” a permission the poems sometimes take up directly. These influences meet a plainspoken, working-class Boston-Irish diction (“copacetic,” “malarkey,” “mad as a box of frogs”); attention to a shined shoe, a cut heel dressed with ointment, or a cross traced on a forehead in dashboard light; and a tendency toward understatement, often allowing a final image to carry emotion. The recurring belief that the dead are “in the other room” also shifts these elegies toward ongoing presence as well as loss. VI. The Elegy That Refuses to Close A recurring move in the collection is the elegy that reaches the edge of final loss and then, in its last lines, reopens the door — not through doctrine, but through a recovered image, a retained voice, or a present-tense return. “Leaves” states “You’re no longer here. / I stand and leave,” and yet the whisper “We’re done” has just been heard. “Copacetic” withholds its grief until the closing image of the robe “folded, / on the table by the door.” “Carol” lets its subject become “just part of the current / carrying you safely home.” Rather than argue their way to comfort, these poems leave the loss open to continued memory and presence. VII. Poetry Against Prose: A Note on Craft Set beside Mulhern’s short fiction, particularly “Assumptions,” the poems show what changes when related materials are compressed into verse. A story can let a relationship unfold across scenes and years — a dog rehomed, a beach pilgrimage, a decline witnessed in stages. A poem may locate a comparable weight in a single stanza or image, leaving the reader to supply the surrounding years. The relationship can run in both directions: “Copacetic” — the father in the doorway, the untouched Jell-O, the folded robe — anticipates elements later developed in “The Wrong Way” and in the father’s death in Give Them Unquiet Dreams . “Scrape the Rocks” relates closely to bath scenes in “A Bath” and “Blindfolded.” “Shoes” and “She Knelt” provide parts of an immigrant backstory that recurs across the books. “Moving Forward” includes the blind mother whose “fingers trace my face,” a gesture that also recurs in the fiction. The poems often isolate recurring images — an object, memory, or threshold — that the fiction later places in scenes and relationships. Taken together, these recurring materials — reached-for water, speaking hands, thresholds of light, a personal liturgy, a chosen lineage, and an elegy that will not fully close — describe a single imaginative territory that the poems return to from different angles, poem after poem, the way memory itself returns to the same handful of scenes without ever quite exhausting them. A fuller treatment of this method, and of the poems’ place in Mulhern’s wider body of work, appears in the critical study The Writing Style of James Mulhern (Silver Current Press). title: Profanity as Intimacy — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: Profanity as Intimacy
description: How vulgarity marks trust rather than breach in James Mulhern's fiction, and what it costs when the same words are aimed by a stranger instead of a grandmother.
text: Profanity as Intimacy — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On Register and Voice Profanity as Intimacy How vulgarity marks trust rather than breach in James Mulhern’s fiction — and what it costs when the same words are aimed by a stranger instead of a grandmother. Abstract In the stories considered here, profanity is less a marker of anger, class, or crudeness than a sign of familiarity. It tends to appear between people who trust one another and to recede in the presence of people who do not yet share that trust. This essay traces the pattern across the Nonna cycle and “A Bath,” suggesting that cursing can function as a register associated with affection. I. Vulgarity as a Password, Not a Symptom A common assumption in both popular and critical reading is that profanity in fiction signals a breakdown — of composure, of civility, of relationship. In these stories, however, profanity often appears among people who know one another well, while its absence can signal distance or caution. This essay follows that pattern as a recurring feature of voice rather than assuming that every instance carries the same meaning. One useful statement of this pattern comes from Nonna herself, correcting Molly’s directness with a borrowed line of poetry rather than objecting to profanity as such: “She had spoken with me a few weeks back about perceptions and how important it was for me to develop good interpersonal skills. She said that my directness was admirable, but others might perceive it as rudeness.” 1 Nonna does not seem to object to bluntness itself — she is, after all, frequently profane — but cautions against using that register with people who do not know Molly well. The distinction guiding this essay is therefore tentative: profanity among family can be affectionate, while profanity aimed at strangers can create a social risk that Nonna coaches her granddaughter to manage. II. Nonna’s Profanity as a Love Language Nonna’s cursing is inseparable from her tenderness throughout the story cycle, frequently occurring in the very same sentence as an endearment, so that the two registers reinforce rather than contradict each other. Describing her relationship with Mr. Scarfone, she tells Molly, without embarrassment or hesitation, “Oh, he’s just a good fuck,” and when Molly reacts with shock, Nonna “whacked me playfully with the bag of fruit and Italian bread she had brought,” a gesture of physical affection delivered in the same breath as the vulgarity. 2 The scene repeats, nearly verbatim, later in the volume, which is itself significant: Mulhern does not treat this joke as a single comic beat but as a stable feature of how Nonna and Molly relate to each other, worth restating because it is characteristic rather than exceptional. 2 The pattern holds even at Nonna’s most protective and most frightened. Fleeing Lady Jane’s parlor after the “Angel of Death” prophecy, Nonna’s parting words are pure profanity — “Ffangul’!” — and Molly, absorbing her grandmother’s register in the moment of greatest anxiety, silently mouths “Fuck you” back at the healer. 3 The grandmother and granddaughter share a private linguistic register in this scene precisely because they are frightened together; the profanity is the sound their intimacy makes under pressure, not a breakdown of the relationship but a demonstration of how completely aligned the two of them are in that moment. III. Nana’s Restraint as the System’s Negative Space “A Bath” supplies the essay’s most important control case, because Nana is markedly less profane than Nonna, and the essay argues this is not a difference in the two grandmothers’ capacity for intimacy but a difference in what kind of intimacy each scene requires. Nana’s one moment of registered vulgarity arrives exactly where the story’s emotional stakes are highest, when she learns her daughter has been hit: she does not curse at the man who did it, or curse in anger at all; instead, her profanity is reserved for the earlier, lesser offense of her son’s absence and his wife’s falseness — “Darlene’s a phony through and through. Even her body is fake. I know those breasts aren’t real” 4 — leaving her response to the actual disclosure of violence to occur in a register of plain tenderness rather than profanity: “You’re not that horrible word, Gracie. You’re opinionated and strong.” 4 This distinction matters to the essay’s argument: in these stories, profanity often accompanies casual, comic, everyday intimacy (Nonna’s register with Molly, Nana’s register describing her daughter-in-law) but may be withheld at moments of grave disclosure, in favor of plainer diction. Billy’s single profanity in the story — “You fucked him, didn’t you?”, asked of his mother about the father he has never known — earns him an immediate slap, the story’s clearest instance of profanity producing rupture rather than intimacy. 4 Rather than proving a rule, the episode complicates the pattern: Billy directs a familiar register at his mother’s trauma as an accusation, not as solidarity, and the exchange has not developed the shared comic context found in Nonna and Molly’s conversations about Mr. Scarfone or Lady Jane. IV. A Register Reserved for Love Taken together, the two grandmothers suggest a recurring pattern: profanity in these stories is not simply a marker of class, education, or moral looseness, and it is more than comic relief, though it can produce comedy. It often accompanies relationships able to absorb it, and it may be withheld or challenged when a character reaches for it before trust is established or when a subject is too raw for its casualness. Nonna curses often and warmly; Nana curses more rarely; Billy curses once, in an ill-timed question, and is slapped for it. Across these cases, vulgarity can help a reader notice shifts in intimacy and distance without fixing the meaning of every exchange in advance. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. title: Queer Kinship and Chosen Family — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: Queer Kinship and Chosen Family
description: Gabe, Wilton Manors, and the household James Mulhern builds outside the Irish-Catholic and Italian-American bloodline, read as chosen family.
text: Queer Kinship and Chosen Family — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On Chosen Family Queer Kinship and Chosen Family Gabe, Wilton Manors, and the households James Mulhern builds outside the Irish-Catholic and Italian-American bloodline. Abstract Alongside its Irish-Catholic and Italian-American blood families, James Mulhern’s fiction presents another model of domestic loyalty in the household Molly Bonamici shares with her gay best friend Gabe in Wilton Manors, Florida. This essay considers that household — and the bigotry it survives, including from within its own adopted community — as an example of how chosen family can perform many of the functions of blood family, including its cruelties. I. A Second Household, Built on Choice Every essay on this site devoted to Mulhern’s grandmothers, aunts, and mothers has, by necessity, been an essay about family defined by blood and by the accidents of birth into a specific Irish-Catholic or Italian-American household. The “Myra Bocca” sequence of the Molly Bonamici story cycle introduces a household built on the opposite principle: cohabitation and loyalty chosen in adulthood, between a straight woman and her gay best friend, sharing domestic life — dinners, wine, a media room, weekend plans, the small liturgies of an ordinary home — in Wilton Manors, a real and well-known LGBTQ enclave in South Florida. 1 This essay argues that Molly and Gabe’s household deserves to be read as seriously as any of the blood families examined elsewhere on this site, and that the bigotry it survives — some of it startlingly casual, some of it startlingly close to home — is essential to understanding what chosen family costs as well as what it offers. The household’s ordinary tenderness is established quickly and without fanfare: “What I enjoyed most about living with Gabe was dinnertime and afterwards when we would sit together in the media area of the living room to enjoy news or a movie.” 1 The scene gives ordinary domestic attention to chosen family, much as other stories do to Nana’s bathtub or Nonna’s kitchen table. It suggests that chosen family can involve the same daily work of care as blood family. II. Loyalty Tested by Slurs, From Both Directions The household’s first real test comes not from outside the LGBTQ community but from within it, when Myra Bocca — herself introduced as warm, funny, and eager for friendship — reveals a startling capacity for casual homophobia in the same breath she claims tolerance. Describing her own stepson, she says: “The boy was one of those vindictive fag types. Jimmy was… is his name. God, I wish he were dead,” before immediately backpedaling: “Oh, I got nothin’ against gays, Gabe. I wouldn’t be living here if I…” 2 The scene is structured so that the reader watches the exact mechanism by which bigotry disguises itself even to the person expressing it: Myra’s casual slur and her immediate claim of innocence occupy the same paragraph, with no space between them for the reader to be fooled by the second sentence. Mulhern places this scene in Wilton Manors specifically — a place chosen by its residents, including Myra, precisely because it is supposed to be safe — which sharpens rather than softens the betrayal. Molly’s earlier defense of Gabe, before this later scene, has already established that she experiences slurs directed at him as a direct assault on her own household: when a stranger refers to her as a “fag hag,” the narration records that the term “irked me,” 1 a small but telling detail, since Molly is otherwise the corpus’s most defiantly thick-skinned narrator, unmoved by insults that would wound other characters. That a slur aimed sideways at her chosen family unsettles her where direct insults to herself do not is the essay’s clearest evidence that Molly experiences her bond with Gabe as genuinely familial rather than merely convenient. III. Espresso Boys: A Second Chosen Community Mulhern extends the chosen-family argument outward from the household to the neighborhood itself in the extended Espresso Boys café scene, which functions as a kind of secular parish for Wilton Manors’ gay community — a recurring gathering place with its own regulars, its own gossip network, and its own elder statesman in Alexander Michaelis, the Greek café owner who warns Molly away from Myra: “She’s a lying greedy bitch. She’d sell her sister if she could.” 3 Michaelis’s warning is delivered with the exact cadence of a worried relative protecting a newcomer from a con artist already known to the family — which, functionally, is precisely his role. Molly notes that the café’s regulars display an unmistakable hierarchy of belonging: “women, I soon learned, were sometimes met with hostility in establishments that catered to gay men,” while a beautiful man like Gabe is treated as an insider from his first visit. 1 The scene does not flatten Wilton Manors into an idealized queer utopia; it gives the neighborhood the same mix of genuine welcome and internal exclusion that characterizes every other community in Mulhern’s fiction, chosen or inherited. The corpus’s most pointed detail about this chosen community’s internal contradictions may be the throwaway fact, delivered by Michaelis, that Myra’s own sister Catherine “lives up in Massachusetts… The sister hates Myra. They haven’t talked in years” 3 — meaning that Myra, who has built an entire new life and a New Age business on performing warmth and instant intimacy with strangers, has failed at the one relationship, blood kinship with her own sister, that chosen family is supposed to be able to repair or replace. Myra herself has fled a broken blood family into a constructed community and constructed profession, and the story is quietly unsparing about how imperfectly that flight succeeds. IV. What Chosen Family Proves Placed beside the grandmother-centered blood families studied elsewhere on this site, Molly and Gabe’s household suggests that the fiction does not present chosen family as simply superior to or a substitute for blood family, but as capable of both failure and care. Gabe offers Molly steady loyalty through her aunt’s death, her professional life, and her skepticism about romance, even as Molly needles him about his vanity or his optimism about Myra. Myra Bocca, despite belonging to the same chosen community as Gabe and Molly, is capable of betrayal and casual bigotry, as blood-family members elsewhere in the stories can be. Wilton Manors therefore offers one way to see that loyalty has to be practiced in both directions, whether a family is assigned at birth or built by adults choosing each other. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. title: The Reader as Confessor: Second-Person Address in the Poetry of James Mulhern — James Mulhern
heading: The Reader as Confessor
description: An essay on second-person address in James Mulhern's poetry collection Crossings — the reader as an accidental confessor.
text: The Reader as Confessor: Second-Person Address in the Poetry of James Mulhern — James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On Second-Person Address The Reader as Confessor In the Poetry of James Mulhern — how “you” addressed to the dying and the dead turns the reader into an accidental listener, present for words meant for someone else. Abstract The essays already devoted to Mulhern’s confessor figures — grandmothers, priests-by-implication, children entrusted with secrets — have examined confession as a structure between characters, staged within scenes. This essay looks at a related but formally distinct phenomenon that occurs almost exclusively in the poetry of Crossings : a narrator who turns away from third-person recollection and addresses a “you” directly, mid-poem, as though the dead or absent addressee were suddenly, briefly, present to receive what is being said. Where the fiction’s confessions pass between characters who share a scene, these poems collapse the distance between speaker and addressee entirely, making the reader an accidental witness to an act of direct address that was never meant for a general audience. The effect is to turn the reader into something like a confessor by proxy — present for words that are grammatically aimed at someone else, someone who, in nearly every case, cannot answer back. I. A Different Kind of Listening The essays already devoted to Mulhern’s confessor figures — grandmothers, priests-by-implication, children entrusted with secrets — have examined confession as a structure between characters, staged within scenes. This essay looks at a related but formally distinct phenomenon that occurs almost exclusively in the poetry of Crossings : a narrator who turns away from third-person recollection and addresses a “you” directly, mid-poem, as though the dead or absent addressee were suddenly, briefly, present to receive what is being said. Where the fiction’s confessions pass between characters who share a scene, these poems collapse the distance between speaker and addressee entirely, making the reader an accidental witness to an act of direct address that was never meant for a general audience. The effect is to turn the reader into something like a confessor by proxy — present for words that are grammatically aimed at someone else, someone who, in nearly every case, cannot answer back. II. “We’d Scrape the Rocks”: Address to the Living Who Will Not Live Long The collection’s grandmother poem stages its second-person address at the level of the whole poem’s grammar, not merely in scattered lines. From its opening movement, the poem speaks past its ostensible occasion (a visit, a bath) directly to the grandmother herself: “When Mom and I arrived, / you hid a donut behind the frame. / I stared at an old photograph, / gray-yellow as your skin.” 1 The poem never once refers to her in the third person; every observation is delivered as something said to her face, even the ones she could not have overheard, such as the closing image of the bathwater itself: “Behind the door, / bathwater swayed, / Clew Bay in an old white tub, / Brigid’s rock gleamed / in sour-salted steam.” 1 The address does not falter even when the speaker is physically excluded from the room — sent to “Grandpa’s chair” to recite prayers while his mother bathes Nana behind a closed door — which means the poem’s “you” persists past the point where any literal listening is possible. This is the device’s central paradox: the more intimate the address becomes, the less capable the addressee is of receiving it, so that by the poem’s final image the “you” has become almost entirely rhetorical, sustained by the poem’s grammar rather than by any scene of actual communication. III. “The Crosswalk” and “Piano”: Address to the Dead Two of the collection’s most emotionally exposed poems direct their “you” at addressees who are already dead by the time of speaking, converting second-person address into something close to prayer. “The Crosswalk” recalls a father’s hands on the speaker’s shoulders at a family party, misremembered by another relative as belonging to a different son — “I heard you say, / ’Remember when Danny and I built the shed?’ / But it wasn’t my brother who cut wood / and hammered nails with you” 2 — before the poem’s final stanza reveals the addressee is being spoken to across the threshold of the casket itself: “It was on the table by your casket. / Your hands on my shoulders. / One moment, framed.” 2 The poem’s grammar refuses to shift into elegiac third person even at the moment of the father’s death; the “you” that was corrected mid-poem over a misremembered anecdote is the same “you” addressed at the coffin, collapsing living conversation and posthumous address into a single unbroken grammatical relationship. “Piano” performs an even starker version of the same move, addressing an act of domestic violence directly to its perpetrator: “That gray day, you took an axe to the Steinway… You shattered the shiny veneer… I thought of my mother, / the day she moved out, / how you changed the locks.” 2 Here the second person does something confession’s usual structure cannot: it accuses without requiring the accused to be present to hear it, staging a confrontation that could never have occurred safely in life, made possible only by poetry’s willingness to speak to someone who is not, and perhaps never was, listening. IV. “Brother Mark”: Address as Refusal to Let Go The collection’s elegy for a brother figure uses second-person address to enact, formally, the psychological refusal at the poem’s center — an unwillingness to accept that the addressed “you” is gone. “Your arm on my shoulder, / your face orange from flames… I loved the circle of flickering flames and logs. / Sometimes in the blackness of my room, / a fire blazes. / I see our faces. / Hear our voices.” 3 The poem’s closing lines make the temporal confusion explicit rather than incidental: “I wish we’d stayed, / never stepped into the snowy light. / Our time together— / perpetually that night.” 3 The word “perpetually” is doing exactly the same structural work here that second-person address does throughout the collection: it converts a single, finite, past occasion into something ongoing, present-tense, still addressable. To say “you” to someone who is gone is already to perform, grammatically, the wish the poem states outright — that the moment never end, that the addressee remain reachable by speech regardless of what has actually happened to them. V. The Reader’s Involuntary Position None of these poems announce that they are being overheard, and that is precisely the source of their force. A reader encountering “you hid a donut behind the frame” or “you took an axe to the Steinway” has no grammatical position available except that of an unaddressed third party who happens to be present for a communication meant for someone else — structurally identical to Billy in “A Bath,” listening through a closed door to sounds he is not meant to interpret, or to Jimmy in “Assumptions,” entrusted with a confession that exceeds a child’s proper role. The poems do not invite the reader in the way a third-person elegy invites a reader to sympathize from outside; they position the reader as an accidental confessor, present for testimony that the “I” of the poem needed to say aloud regardless of whether the “you” could hear it, and regardless of whether anyone else was meant to hear it either. This is the sense in which the essay’s title should be taken literally rather than metaphorically: the reader of these poems is not asked to judge or absolve, only to have been present, which is exactly the function Mulhern’s fiction elsewhere assigns to its designated child-confessors. VI. Conclusion: Grammar as the Last Confessional Second-person address in Crossings accomplishes formally what the fiction’s confession scenes accomplish through plot: it creates an occasion for saying the otherwise unsayable by constructing, however fictively, a listener. The difference is that the poems’ listeners are almost always unavailable — dying, dead, or physically sealed behind a door — which means the “you” of these poems survives its addressee’s absence purely as a grammatical commitment, a refusal on the speaker’s part to downgrade the address to memory’s usual third person. Read alongside the corpus’s confessor figures, this reveals a consistent underlying conviction: that being heard, in Mulhern’s imagination, does not strictly require a listener capable of hearing. It requires only the grammatical act of address, sustained past the point of reasonable hope, which the reader — present by accident, absolved of nothing, asked only to have listened — receives in the listener’s place. — Silver Current Press Notes 1.
