title: The Religious Architecture of James Mulhern’s Work — A Study
heading: The Religious Architecture of the Work
description: A current critical study of James Mulhern's religious architecture: 1,096 catalogued passages and observations on Assumptions, care, Irish folk belief, and naming.
text: The Religious Architecture of James Mulhern’s Work — A Study ← Back to The 2601 Salon A Study · Literary Criticism The Religious Architecture of the Work The religious architecture of James Mulhern’s work — a current concordance of 1,096 catalogued passages across two novels, three story collections, the poems, and twenty-eight online publications. “You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you.” — Song of Solomon 4:7, epigraph to “Assumptions” The Case in Brief The religious architecture of James Mulhern’s work can be described with some precision. A line-by-line concordance across two novels, three story collections, the poems, and twenty-eight verified online publications has catalogued 1,096 passages , of varying relevance. The point of the count is not to turn reading into arithmetic. It is to establish that the Catholic, folk-Catholic, biblical, liturgical, and literary material is neither an occasional mood nor an inherited prop. It is a recurrent compositional resource, differently handled from book to book. The method is usually quiet. A loaded noun sits inside a plain sentence; domestic action carries an older ritual or scriptural pressure without ceasing to be domestic action. Suntan oil can recall anointing, a towel can recall a mantle, a shaken hand can recall blessing, and a work of care can retain its practical meaning while acquiring a second register. The recurrent effect is not allegory with its labels attached. It is a realist surface that permits more than one kind of attention. The Story: “Assumptions” “Assumptions” remains the keystone text because its title, day, epigraph, and ending are placed in unusually close relation. The action occurs on August 15, the Feast of the Assumption. Its epigraph, Tota pulchra es, amica mea, et macula non est in te , is not simply a line of love poetry borrowed from the Song of Solomon. It is the Marian antiphon Tota Pulchra Es , proper to the feast the story occupies. Its crucial word is macula : stain. The red stains at the ends of Peggy’s sleeves therefore answer a liturgical promise of unstained beauty before the plot has begun to explain itself. The adult narrator places dogma, art, and childhood memory beside one another rather than fusing them into a single voice. The movement from the child’s search for “flying Mary’s” to the later account of Pius XII’s definition is explicit; the return from Titian to the prospect of a roller coaster is deliberately bathetic. That doubleness is a formal resource. A private remembered life is allowed to bear the pressure of public doctrine without being reduced to an illustration of it. What the story’s form does — and does not do The newer formal work makes one important correction. The story does not sustain the Order of Mass, the Glorious Mysteries of the Rosary, the Stations of the Cross, or a novena as a governing macro-form. Those frameworks supply local vocabulary and useful analogies, but the narrative arranges their elements out of sequence and moves by irregular memory-blocks. The beach scene may gather images of water, rising, food, and service; it does not become a disguised liturgy. The closest formal analogue is instead a qualified saint’s life: origin, humiliation, hidden charity, death, and retrospective glorification. Even that description must be modest. There is no cult, relic, shrine, or public petition. The story’s canonization is literary and private, performed by a remembering witness. Its most exact structural supports are the braided time frames, the repeated verbs of remembering and helping, the recurrent laughter, and the final shift into a present tense in which Peggy “rises” again. Patterns across the books The concordance confirms recurring material without making every recurrence an identity claim. The Assumption feast, the sea cure, the wet silvery scalp, the dove, the chalice, the phrase “Up you go. On the count of three,” and the vocabulary of goodness and uselessness return as altered situations. Across the collections, recurrence works through doubling and revision: a later scene changes the moral pressure of an earlier one rather than merely repeating it. The Weight of Small Mercies provides the clearest corrective to a romantic account of this system. Its practical ministry falls chiefly to women and families: they intercede, touch, wash, anoint, transport, feed, protect, and keep silence for the vulnerable. But ordained men are not absent. They bless, heal, read scripture, and lead acclamation. Their ceremonial functions simply do not bear the pastoral weight that the household carries, and the book refuses to treat any cure — clerical, medical, charismatic, or domestic — as complete. Give Them Unquiet Dreams supplies a second necessary limit. It takes Catholic consolation, prayer for the dead, and communion across death seriously, but its ghosts are not purgatorial souls awaiting Masses or release. Second sight is hereditary; the good dead return to complete relational work; and the hostile presence is the Irish folk pooka, not a Christian demonology. The book borrows religious language without allowing that language to flatten its folk otherworld. Molly Bonamici makes the same layered practice visible in names. Molly is a nickname joining Margaret and Mary, so she carries Mrs. Muldoon’s Margaret Mary Alacoque association from the first page; Bonamici means “good friends,” an irony the novel places inside a damaged family. Its final chapter draws Dantean, Marian, and domestic material together without making belief a simple reward for good conduct. What It Amounts To The poems test the same system in miniature, and they answer differently than the prose. They do not inherit religious form: the verse is free, governed by syntax and breath rather than by the hymnal metres, and where a poem looks devotional it usually declines the actual shape — no invocation, no petition, no doxology. What survives is analogical. A catalogue of animals behaves like a creation litany; a repeated word of care behaves like an invocation; a commendation of a student carries a benediction’s cadence while blessing no one in particular. The endings make the argument plainest, closing on a small action, a sentence-stop, or a question rather than on assurance. Hope in the poems is a matter of restraint, not of doctrine. A more modest conclusion is neither that the work is a devotional tract nor that every object has one correct key. Mulhern’s books make religious language answerable to bodies, failed cures, ugly rooms, compromised caretakers, and forms of attention that do not secure salvation. The sacred is structural because it repeatedly changes the terms in which a damaged life is seen; it is not a mechanism for cancelling damage. That is why the Assumption remains central. The Marian antiphon is not used to deny Peggy’s stains, sickness, dependency, or death. It creates a pressure under which the narrative asks what it would mean to speak beauty of a body already judged otherwise. The answer is not catharsis, which purges. It is a literary act of attention that refuses to let the last word belong to contempt. title: Revision as Theology — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: Revision as Theology
description: An essay reading the genetic evidence inside James Mulhern's collected work — the same bath scene redrafted from poem to story, and a jetty passage duplicated within a single collection.
text: Revision as Theology — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On Genetic Criticism Revision as Theology Recurrence, Redrafting, and the Genetic Evidence Inside Mulhern’s Collected Text. Abstract Genetic criticism classically works from an archive of successive drafts. No such archive survives here, but the published work offers a different kind of evidence: the same scene, redrafted, appearing more than once in Mulhern’s finished corpus — once as a poem, once as a story, and, within a single collection, twice in near-identical prose. This essay considers that internal recurrence alongside the theology of recurrence Mulhern’s own essays describe: redrafting as a possible form of devotional repetition rather than correction. I. A Note on Method Genetic criticism classically works from an archive: successive drafts, marginal deletions, a writer’s crossed-out and reinstated lines, held up against the published text to reconstruct the labor of composition. No such archive of dated drafts survives, or has been made available, for the stories examined here. The published corpus does, however, allow a reader to observe the same scene, the same images, and in places the same sentences at more than one point — once as a poem, once as embedded short fiction, and, within the fiction itself, twice within the same collection in near-identical prose. This essay treats that internal recurrence as one possible, if unconventional, form of genetic evidence. Where classical genetic criticism reads a manuscript’s revisions to infer the author’s evolving intention, this essay considers Mulhern’s practice of redrafting a single memory-scene across multiple finished, public forms — verse, then story, then story again — as evidence of a compositional habit in which returning to and rewriting one’s own material may be a form of devotional repetition rather than simply correction, in keeping with the theology of recurrence his essays and interviews describe. II. The Same Bath, Twice: “Scrape the Rocks” and “A Bath” Mulhern’s poem “Scrape the Rocks” and his short story “A Bath” both stage a nearly identical domestic scene: a grandmother being helped into a bathtub by her daughter, while a grandchild waits nearby, and a framed photograph on the wall triggers a memory of Ireland — specifically, a girl wading toward a boulder at Clew Bay to gather “sea lettuce” for food. In the poem, the moment is compressed into a few couplets: You were pushing dark water aside to reach a boulder in the crashing foam… “I was gathering food. Sea lettuce, we called it. We’d scrape the rocks and then make stew… ‘Twas all the food we had and needed, but it was good, and we were happy.” 1 The scene ends with the grandson relegated outside the bathroom door: “As she eased you into the warm water, / I listened through the door.” 1 The short story “A Bath” relocates a similar photograph, Clew Bay identification, and listening-through-the-door structure into an entirely different narrative frame — a different grandson (Billy, not Jimmy), a different immediate occasion (concealing a boyfriend’s violence rather than a hidden donut), and a different emotional register (crisis and confession rather than tender routine). The image cluster is closely related: “Just outside Peg’s door, my grandmother stopped us…” becomes, in the later story, “‘That was Clew Bay in County Mayo. The photograph, I mean.’ I listened through the door. There was no conversation. I heard splashing and my grandmother’s sighs as my mother rubbed her back.” 2 The story also retains the poem’s gesture of the listener imagining, rather than witnessing, the bathing scene’s real content — “I suppose they were preoccupied by memory. I imagined my grandmother was thinking about an ocean three thousand miles away.” 2 What is significant here is not merely thematic recurrence (grandmothers, bathing, Ireland, listening at doors are documented elsewhere as recurring motifs across the corpus) but structural redrafting: an entire scene — its blocking, its central prop (a photograph), its emotional mechanism (a memory unlocked by physical care) — has been composed once in verse and recomposed in prose, with the surrounding plot and stakes rebuilt around it each time. This is revision in the genetic sense, except that instead of discarding the earlier version, Mulhern has published both, allowing the reader to witness the redrafting directly rather than inferring it from a private manuscript trail. III. The Jetty Passage: Self-Quotation Within a Single Collection Another case of internal genetic evidence occurs within Mulhern’s assembled Collected Stories and Poems (forthcoming), where a single paragraph — describing a walk to a fishing jetty, the discovery of “a lonely starfish, a shiny stone, or a clam with a secreted pearl,” the startling of a mourning dove, and the simile “the waves glimmered like sparks from an unquenchable fire” — appears twice, nearly word for word, at two separate points in the collection, embedded in two tellings of a similar beach outing (Nonna, Mrs. Muldoon, and the narrator at the shore for the Feast of the Assumption). 3 The first instance reads: “I got up and walked towards the end of the beach, where it was less crowded, near a fishing jetty and several clumps of boulders. I explored the spaces in between the rocks, looking for a lonely starfish, a shiny stone, or a clam with a secreted pearl, and unearthed small crabs in the sand. At one point, I startled a mourning dove that sped from its cleft into the bright sky… The waves glimmered like sparks from an unquenchable fire.” 3 The second, appearing later in the same manuscript in a parallel retelling, is a close paraphrase with only minor lexical substitution: “I explored the spaces in between the boulders, looking for a lonely starfish, a shiny stone, or a clam with a secreted pearl. I unearthed small crabs that scampered across the sand… The waves glimmered like sparks from an unquenchable fire.” 3 The phrase “sparks from an unquenchable fire” is worth pausing on, because it also supplies the title of the first essay in Mulhern’s critical series, “ Unquenchable Fire .” The duplication may be an editorial oversight in assembling a career-spanning collection, but it may also show an image — starfish, jetty, dove, unquenchable fire — that Mulhern returns to and reuses when the narrative revisits a related emotional coordinate: a beach ritual involving an aging, vulnerable woman and a witnessing child. The sentence functions less like local color than like a recurring formula: a pre-composed unit brought back when the scene-type recurs, akin to a remembered liturgical response. IV. Redrafting as Devotional Practice The theological register is relevant to this reading. Mulhern’s stated poetics — expressed in the essay “ A Working Philosophy ” and the “ Credo ” — describes his compositional method in terms of “recurrence” and “the ordinary as sanctuary,” language that regards repetition as a possible spiritual discipline rather than simply a limitation to be edited away. The evidence assembled here suggests this may be more than a thematic claim: it may also describe an aspect of how the work was assembled. A liturgical calendar returns, on the same feast day, to the same readings, allowing repetition under changed circumstance to produce new meaning. The Feast of the Assumption itself — the occasion of both the jetty passage and its parallel — offers this kind of repeating structure: a fixed date revisited each year. Mulhern’s reuse of the jetty and bathing scenes in more than one finished, published context can be read as drawing on a similar logic of return. The “unquenchable fire” is not merely an image used about Peggy Fleming’s assumption into glory; the sentence containing it returns in a second telling. V. Implications for Reading the Corpus This has a practical consequence for how the collected fiction might be read. Passages that might otherwise be flagged by an editor as redundant — the near-verbatim jetty paragraph, the migrated Clew Bay photograph — can also be read as possible through-composition, suggesting that the collection may be more connected than an anthology of discrete, once-drafted pieces. Genetic criticism ordinarily asks what a writer removed on the way to a final text. This corpus invites another question: what does a writer choose to keep drafting, in public, more than once? One answer is that revision, for Mulhern, may be a form of return related to the “ habit of return ” described in other essays — composition that permits the same thing to be said again. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. James Mulhern, “Scrape the Rocks,” in The Collected Stories and Poems of James Mulhern (Silver Current Press, forthcoming). ↩ 2. James Mulhern, “A Bath,” in The Collected Stories and Poems of James Mulhern (Silver Current Press, forthcoming). ↩ 3. “Myra Bocca” and related Molly Bonamici material, in The Collected Stories and Poems of James Mulhern (Silver Current Press, forthcoming). ↩ Works Quoted Quotations are drawn from “Scrape the Rocks” and “A Bath,” and from the “Myra Bocca” and related Molly Bonamici material, all collected in The Collected Stories and Poems of James Mulhern (Silver Current Press, forthcoming). title: The Sacramental Economy of Food: Communion, Poison, and Inheritance in the Fiction of James Mulhern — James Mulhern
heading: The Sacramental Economy of Food
description: An essay on food as sacrament in James Mulhern's fiction — communion, inheritance, and the cyanide cookies of Mia Bambina.
text: The Sacramental Economy of Food: Communion, Poison, and Inheritance in the Fiction of James Mulhern — James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On Food and Communion The Sacramental Economy of Food In the Fiction of James Mulhern — how cookies, candy, sugar, and whiskey carry love, obligation, and at last poison through the same trusted hands. Abstract Mulhern’s own introduction to All We Ever Needed mentions food alongside water among the collection’s recurring concerns: the stories are populated by “a bath drawn for an aging parent, a ride to the beach, a call answered, a gift misunderstood” — ordinary gestures of care that the introduction says “do not erase suffering” but “reveal the stubborn human wish to be known and cared for despite everything.” 1 The stories also invite a reading of food through a sacramental analogy: something prepared by one person is consumed by another and may carry care, obligation, or intention. This essay considers whether recurring food scenes do more than mark domestic tenderness, and how the collection’s two poisonings complicate that pattern. I. A Eucharistic Logic Beneath the Kitchen Table Mulhern’s own introduction to All We Ever Needed mentions food alongside water among the collection’s recurring concerns: the stories are populated by “a bath drawn for an aging parent, a ride to the beach, a call answered, a gift misunderstood” — ordinary gestures of care that the introduction says “do not erase suffering” but “reveal the stubborn human wish to be known and cared for despite everything.” 1 The stories also invite a reading of food through a sacramental analogy: something prepared by one person is consumed by another and may carry care, obligation, or intention. This essay considers whether recurring food scenes do more than mark domestic tenderness, and how the collection’s two poisonings complicate that pattern. II. Cookies as Grace: The Ordinary Sacrament A basic form of the pattern is maternal and grand-maternal feeding, especially visible in “Mia Bambina.” When Nonna sends Molly away to college, she sends cookies with a note that combines nutrition, threat, and blessing: “Here are some cookies for the sweetest cookie in my life. You must swear to eat them all yourself!… A curse on you if you don’t eat every last one of these cookies yourself. I want you to be fatter the next time I see you… Nonna loves mia bambina.” 2 The note’s swing from endearment to curse and back suggests that feeding a child is, for Nonna, an obligation with real stakes. The demand that Molly “swear” to eat them “yourself,” excluding the dormitory roommate, also marks the cookies as a private exchange rather than a general kindness. III. The Same Vessel, Weaponized: “Sure, mia bambina. What’s one more ingredient?” The horror of “Mia Bambina” is structural rather than merely plot-driven: Mulhern does not introduce a new, sinister object to carry out the murder. He reuses the exact vessel of tenderness already established — Nonna’s cookies — and simply adds an ingredient. When Molly needs to eliminate her roommate Ashley, she goes to the same grandmother, using the same register of family favor: “Getting the cyanide from Mr. Scarfone, a mobster friend of my grandmother’s, was easy. She was always saying she would do anything for her ’precious granddaughter,’ so when I asked her to bake the special cookies, she said, ’Sure, mia bambina. What’s one more ingredient? Not a problem.’” 2 The line’s horror is entirely in its syntax: “what’s one more ingredient” treats cyanide as continuous with flour, sugar, and chocolate chips, a domestic addition rather than a moral rupture. Nonna’s willingness collapses the distance between nurture and murder into a single unbroken gesture of love — she is not persuaded to kill; she is asked to bake, and baking is what she has always done for this particular granddaughter. The novel’s closing image confirms the sacramental register explicitly: Molly plans to “compliment her on the effectiveness of her wording in the note,” noting that Nonna “would be happy to know that Ashley had died for her sins and that her cookies were a perfect hit” 2 — the phrase “died for her sins,” borrowed intact from the vocabulary of atonement, recasts a poisoning as a kind of liturgical justice administered through food. IV. Peppermint as Absolution and as Weapon “Peppermint Candy” performs the identical operation in miniature and in reverse order — the poisoning precedes, rather than follows, the story’s use of candy as ordinary comfort. The narrator, a teacher retaliating against a student’s humiliation, prepares the weapon with clinical, almost priestly care: “I thought of the care I had taken to lightly rub Visine onto the candy before rewrapping it,” 3 language that treats the rewrapping — restoring the candy’s innocent appearance — as part of the ritual’s completion, not an afterthought. The story’s final line performs the same collapse “Mia Bambina” performs: after poisoning one student, the narrator writes, “I retrieved the peppermints from my desk drawer and placed them in my satchel. I would share them again another day,” 3 restoring the candy immediately to its ordinary, communal function of being shared. The peppermint does not stop being a treat because it has also been a poison; the story insists these are the same object serving the same social function — a small gift passed from an authority figure to a dependent — regardless of what has been added to it. This mirrors “Assumptions,” where peppermint candy first appears innocently, “enjoying the deliciousness of peppermint candy, swinging our legs together,” establishing the object’s baseline sweetness before the collection later corrupts it — the reader is trained, across the arc of the book, to receive peppermint as tenderness, which is precisely what makes its later weaponization effective rather than merely shocking. V. Whiskey, Sugar Cubes, and the Communion of the Table Not every food exchange in the corpus curdles into violence, and the essay’s argument depends on the fact that most do not: the sacramental logic is visible precisely because most transmissions remain benign, making the poisoned ones legible as corruptions of a norm rather than a separate category of event. In “Assumptions,” Peggy Fleming passes the young narrator a sugar cube “that she kept in her pocketbook in case her insulin dropped suddenly,” accompanying it with reassurance about a lost dog — “We saved Scruffy’s life, sweetheart… Sometimes that’s the way it has to be, my love” 4 — a moment in which a diabetic woman’s emergency medical supply becomes, in the same gesture, a token of comfort passed to a grieving child. The child is in turn taught to “pour her whiskey sours,” his grandmother supervising the dosage (“Not too much, sweetheart”) 4 — establishing a lineage of controlled substances (sugar, whiskey, later peppermint, later cyanide) moving hand to hand between generations, each transfer carrying both practical risk and emotional intention. The meal itself, not just its contents, repeatedly does theological work: the family’s habitual gathering around food and drink is explicitly a site of confession, testimony, and communal absolution, as when the whole extended family sits for “meatballs,” whiskey, and unresolved grievance in the “Myra Bocca” and Molly Bonamici material — food is the occasion under which secrets surface, not incidental to it. VI. Conclusion: Feeding as the Family’s Native Grammar Read across the collection, food can function as a recurring grammar — a set of gestures (prepare, offer, insist on consumption, receive) through which family members express what they do not say directly. Love, obligation, grief, and murder can all appear through feeding, an action that is direct and physical. The cyanide cookies and poisoned peppermints thus complicate a pattern readers have already seen associated with care. Mulhern’s introduction calls naming “a kind of devotion” and describes his stories as “prayers.” 1 The food scenes suggest that a family’s care and its capacity for harm can emerge from the same kitchen and the same familiar hands. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. James Mulhern, “Peppermint Candy,” in All We Ever Needed (Silver Current Press, 2026). ↩ 4. James Mulhern, “Assumptions,” in All We Ever Needed (Silver Current Press, 2026). ↩ Works Quoted Quotations are drawn from “Assumptions,” “Mia Bambina,” and “Peppermint Candy,” all collected in All We Ever Needed (Silver Current Press, 2026). title: The Sacred in the Shabby — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: The Sacred in the Shabby
description: An updated essay on the sacred and ordinary in James Mulhern's work: how feast-day liturgy, domestic care, folk belief, and attention meet without becoming allegory.
text: The Sacred in the Shabby — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon A Literary Essay · On the Governing Method The Sacred in the Shabby How the ordinary — a housedress, a bottle of suntan oil, a classroom of restless teenagers — can take on sacred associations in James Mulhern’s work. “The sacred is stated in the register of the shabby, and the narrator never once points at it.” One recurring approach in James Mulhern’s work is more specific than the claim that the sacred is merely hidden in ordinary things. A concordance of 1,096 catalogued passages traces associations across the fiction, poems, and online work: a plain domestic action remains plain, yet may press against a second vocabulary drawn from scripture, liturgy, folk Catholicism, art, and song. The result is not a code in which every object has one fixed answer, but an ordinary world whose objects invite more than one form of notice. “Assumptions” is the clearest instance. Its epigraph, “You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you,” is not simply a love-poem quotation from the Song of Solomon. In the story’s liturgical setting it is Tota Pulchra Es , the Marian antiphon proper to the Feast of the Assumption, the very day on which the action takes place. The word macula , stain, makes the first close description of Peggy’s sleeves — marked with spilled juice — more than incidental detail. The story places a feast-day promise of unstained beauty against a body already exposed to mockery, illness, dependence, and death. That pressure does not turn the story into a disguised Mass, Rosary, Stations, or novena. Recent formal work has tested each of those analogies and found that none governs the narrative as a whole. The story’s memories leap across years; the dove, rising, doctrine, and crown arrive in non-devotional order; the adult’s learned explanations interrupt rather than arrange the child’s experience. What endures is a local, cumulative pattern: washing, anointing, carrying, covering, feeding, helping, and remembering are allowed to suggest sacred forms without being stripped of their practical, awkward, or comic reality. This is why the grandmother’s care matters more than a claim that she is covertly administering a sacrament. Helen can be loving and cruel in the same exchange; Peggy receives assistance and also protects the children; a failed physical cure still yields laughter, touch, and a hand extended in the water. The work’s recurring question is not whether a domestic action can be certified as holy. It is whether dignity can survive when no one involved is fully worthy, competent, or kind. The pattern travels. In Useless Things and Other Stories , bathing, lifting, rubbing ointment into a heel, feeding, making a safe path, phoning, and asking another person to speak form the book’s actual care catalogue. The collection makes no lasting cure out of them. Attention creates value; it does not reverse decline. In The Weight of Small Mercies , women perform much of the practical ministry, yet ordained men still bless, heal, read scripture, and lead acclamation. The distinction is not between a female Church and an absent male one, but between ceremonial authority and the continuing work of carrying a family. The newer reading of Give Them Unquiet Dreams adds another restraint. Its dead are not purgatorial souls waiting to be released, and its danger is not a Christian demon. Second sight is hereditary, the dead return under rules of kinship and unfinished relation, and the hostile force is the Irish folk pooka. Catholic consolation and Irish folk belief coexist without being collapsed into one system. Mulhern’s own classroom essay gives the method its plainest statement. In “Teaching at Fifty-Six,” he names “a sacred self” and calls teaching “communion.” The phrase does not make the classroom an altar. It makes attention to another person’s interior life a serious, daily practice. The fiction and poems make the same claim in more oblique forms: the sacred does not wait for good conditions, and it does not remove the shabby conditions in which it appears. One paratext states this inheritance more directly than the stories do. Crossings , published by Silver Current Press, carries a dedication to a woman remembered by four things: “your crooked toes from shoes / passed house to house, / your rosary and Daily Missal / that sit on my desk, / your accord with all that life brought, / your devotion to God.” The sequence places poverty, devotional objects, temperament, and belief together — and locates the rosary and missal not in a church but on a writer’s desk. The lines offer a compact image of devotion inherited as an object, kept where work happens, and honored through attention rather than assent. title: Second Sight Against the Celtic Twilight: Yeats, Folk Belief, and the Making of Aiden Glencar — James Mulhern
heading: Second Sight Against the Celtic Twilight
description: A comparative essay on second sight in Give Them Unquiet Dreams against W. B. Yeats's Celtic Twilight and Irish folk belief.
text: Second Sight Against the Celtic Twilight: Yeats, Folk Belief, and the Making of Aiden Glencar — James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On Irish Folk Belief Second Sight Against the Celtic Twilight Aiden Glencar’s second sight read against W. B. Yeats and The Celtic Twilight — what Mulhern keeps from the folk tradition, what he discards, and what he invents. Abstract W. B. Yeats spent the early 1890s doing something that looks, on its surface, like fieldwork: traveling through Sligo, transcribing the testimony of tenant farmers and old women about banshees, pookas, and the “wee folk,” and publishing the results as The Celtic Twilight (1893), a book he described as an attempt to build “a little world out of the beautiful, pleasant, and significant things” of a fading oral culture. Yeats’s collecting stance is famously double: he wants to preserve peasant belief ethnographically while also, at moments, affirming it personally — “No matter what one doubts, one never doubts the faeries,” he writes, a line that refuses to resolve whether he is reporting a superstition or confessing one. James Mulhern’s Give Them Unquiet Dreams draws on related material — banshees, second sight, and the porousness of the dead and the living — within a realist, first-person American novel rather than a folklore anthology. Reading Aiden Glencar’s gift alongside Yeats’s Sligo material may help distinguish elements that echo the tradition from those the novel develops differently. I. Two Collectors of the Same Material W. B. Yeats spent the early 1890s doing something that looks, on its surface, like fieldwork: traveling through Sligo, transcribing the testimony of tenant farmers and old women about banshees, pookas, and the “wee folk,” and publishing the results as The Celtic Twilight (1893), a book he described as an attempt to build “a little world out of the beautiful, pleasant, and significant things” of a fading oral culture. Yeats’s collecting stance is famously double: he wants to preserve peasant belief ethnographically while also, at moments, affirming it personally — “No matter what one doubts, one never doubts the faeries,” he writes, a line that refuses to resolve whether he is reporting a superstition or confessing one. James Mulhern’s Give Them Unquiet Dreams draws on related material — banshees, second sight, and the porousness of the dead and the living — within a realist, first-person American novel rather than a folklore anthology. Reading Aiden Glencar’s gift alongside Yeats’s Sligo material may help distinguish elements that echo the tradition from those the novel develops differently. II. What Mulhern Keeps: The Taxonomy of the Uncanny Aiden’s grandfather transmits the family’s supernatural inheritance to the boy using vocabulary associated with folk taxonomies Yeats catalogued. The banshee appears by name and in a role resembling descriptions Yeats records — a wailing spirit whose cry is a portent of death, heard collectively by an entire household the night before a tragedy: “On the night before, she heard banshees calling out to her. What’s a banshee? A type of fairy or spirit… And there were three knocks on the door, which means someone is going to die.” 1 This account shares features with Irish oral tradition as recorded by Yeats and his contemporaries: a supernatural messenger rather than an active agent of harm, whose appearance is diagnostic rather than causal. The pooka receives a similarly taxonomic treatment: “A pooka is an evil spirit not to be trusted… If she is a pooka, she can change her form into a variety of animals — a cat, a goat, a horse, even an eagle. A shape shifter, the Irish call them… Often, pookas relay veiled messages about your future.” 1 Yeats’s Sligo informants describe the pooka in comparable terms — a shapeshifting, often equine trickster spirit whose favor or wrath depends on how a household treats the land it disturbs. Mulhern’s grandfather also voices an anxious epistemic posture, hedging between literal belief and interpretive caution — “I haven’t ruled out the possibility of ghosts or second sight. But believing those things makes life too complicated” 1 — that echoes Yeats’s uncertainty about how literally to take what he is told. III. Second Sight as a Documented Folk Category, Not an Invention An important continuity between Mulhern’s novel and Celtic Twilight traditions is that “second sight” is not simply the novel’s invention or a metaphor — it is a widely attested folk category in the Irish and Scottish Gaelic world, which Yeats encountered within his own family. Yeats’s cousin Lucy Middleton, visited at Rosses Point near Sligo, was said to possess second sight and to have described “amazing experiences” of it; Yeats’s brother Jack, too, “had heard mysterious sounds and seen mysterious sights,” and the young Yeats, by his own account, felt no impulse “to doubt the invisible.” Mulhern gives Aiden’s grandfather a related genealogical framing — the gift as a family inheritance, traceable through named female relatives, not a general psychic capacity available to anyone: “Second sight has been in your family for years… Your grandmother’s ma had the gift, and she, too, was demonized.” 1 The detail that the gift’s transmission is matrilineal and exposes its bearers to social punishment rather than admiration has parallels in folkloric accounts. Yeats’s informants describe seers as figures who are often pitied or feared by their neighbors as well as consulted; second sight in the tradition can be a burden as much as a power, as Aiden experiences it: “To me ’second sight’ was a curse, a burden.” 1 IV. What Mulhern Discards: The Land, the Fairy Rath, the Collective One difference from the Celtic Twilight material is setting. Yeats’s fairy world is inseparable from a specific rural Irish landscape — raths, fairy forts, particular fields and roads near Sligo where the supernatural is understood to reside in the land itself, encountered by whole communities who share and cross-verify one another’s sightings. Mulhern relocates the inheritance to Irish-American Boston, where it survives inside a single family’s bedroom, without the same geographic anchor or communal verification. In Give Them Unquiet Dreams , Aiden’s blood relatives are the main people who take the supernatural claims seriously; where Yeats reports “there are some doubters even in the western villages,” Mulhern’s Boston presents a more skeptical default. Martin’s “Aiden, she was acting crazy” 1 represents ordinary skepticism, against which Aiden and Laura’s inherited belief is isolated and stigmatized. The fairy fort is replaced by a psychiatric hospital; the shared village epistemology by a diagnosis. The novel thus relocates the taxonomy of the uncanny from a folk-communal world, where such claims are debatable in good faith, into a clinical-modern setting with stronger institutional ideas about what counts as real. V. What Mulhern Invents: The Metaphysics Yeats Never Supplied Yeats’s Celtic Twilight material is local and anecdotal — individual encounters, spirits, and portents — and does not offer a unified theory of time or consciousness underlying the phenomena it records. Mulhern’s grandfather offers a broader metaphysical account, and here the novel moves away from its folkloric source: the “block of wood” speech, in which all of time is said to exist “all at once,” with consciousness merely a “flashlight” moving across an already-complete block of past, present, and future, has no clear analogue in Yeats’s fairy lore. 1 It may recall modern philosophical eternalism or aspects of the visionary systems Yeats later developed in A Vision , rather than the folk collecting of The Celtic Twilight . The novel brings a time-metaphysics to folk-taxonomic materials, giving the family a framework for considering prophecy, grief, ghosts, and inherited guilt. VI. Conclusion: Inheriting the Twilight, Not the Village Aiden Glencar may be read not as a modern retelling of a Yeatsian fairy-seer but as a figure shaped by emigration and secular psychiatric authority after the village context has changed. Mulhern uses elements of the taxonomy — banshees, pookas, shimmerers, and three knocks on the door — in a way that engages with the tradition rather than merely gesturing toward “Irish mysticism.” The novel removes these elements from their communal ground and gives them a private metaphysical framework. Aiden has no broad audience for his inheritance. It survives, when it survives at all, in a single bedroom, transmitted by a single ghost and believed by a single boy: a public folk cosmology narrowed to one family’s private and increasingly unverifiable faith. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. James Mulhern, Give Them Unquiet Dreams (Silver Current Press, 2019). ↩ Works Quoted All quotations are drawn from Give Them Unquiet Dreams (Silver Current Press, 2019). title: Second Sight as Narrative Technology — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: Second Sight as Narrative Technology
description: An essay on how Aiden Glencar's second sight in Give Them Unquiet Dreams functions as a structural solution to foreshadowing, temporal compression, and point-of-view limits.
text: Second Sight as Narrative Technology — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On the Novel Second Sight as Narrative Technology Prophecy and Temporal Compression in Give Them Unquiet Dreams . Abstract Aiden Glencar’s “second sight” in Give Them Unquiet Dreams is usually read as theme — an inheritance of Irish folk belief, a metaphor for difference. This essay considers it instead as craft: a device built into the novel’s ontology that can support foreshadowing, compress three generations of family history into scenes a child narrator can plausibly witness, and convert an epistemological claim about the supernatural into the engine of the novel’s practical plot. I. A Craft Problem Disguised as a Theme Critics who encounter Aiden Glencar’s “second sight” in Give Them Unquiet Dreams are tempted, reasonably, to read it as thematic material: an inheritance of Irish folk belief, a metaphor for queerness and difference, a register through which grief for the dead stays commutable with love for the living. All of these readings are available in the text and none of them is wrong. But treating second sight only as theme risks missing what it is doing at the level of craft. Aiden’s visions, his conversations with his dead grandfather, and his intermittent access to other people’s thoughts are not simply content the novel is “about” — they are a device the novel uses to address a structural problem common to any first-person coming-of-age narrative: how does a single, temporally bound consciousness gain access to information — future outcomes, other people’s interiority, events before its own birth — without breaking the rules of its own point of view? This essay considers second sight as one answer to that problem: a license, built into the ontology of the novel’s world, that can support foreshadowing, compress decades of family history into scenes a child narrator can plausibly witness, and loosen the boundary between past, present, and future that a strictly realist first-person narration would otherwise have to respect. II. The Block of Wood: A Novel’s Time-Theory Made Explicit Mulhern does something unusual for a literary novel: he has a character state the book’s temporal logic outright, in terms nearly indistinguishable from a physics thought experiment. Aiden’s grandfather, appearing as a ghost at the foot of the boy’s bed, produces an image: “Look at this block of wood… The front represents the future; the middle is the present; and the back part… is the past.” When Aiden asks what this means, his grandfather explains: “That’s life. Eternity. There is no division between the past, present, and future; there is rather a single existence. Our brains can’t handle everything happening at once.” 1 This is, functionally, a statement of eternalism — the “block universe” view in which all moments of time are equally real and equally present, and where a mind capable of surveying the whole block, rather than experiencing it serially, would have no privileged “now.” The grandfather makes the narrative payoff explicit: “your consciousness is like a small flashlight that can only shine on one part of the block at a time.” 1 This account of time functions as an operating rule for the novel. Once a reader accepts that Aiden’s grandfather — and, by extension, Aiden and Laura, who share “the gift” — can shine that flashlight on parts of the block a normal consciousness cannot reach, the novel can move between the traumatic Irish backstory of Catherine’s mother’s death by drowning in a well, decades before Aiden’s birth, and the present-tense Boston narrative of Aiden’s own adolescence, without a framing device, an omniscient narrator, or a structural break. Second sight thus acts as a point-of-view exception, allowing a first-person child narrator to carry material ordinarily beyond that vantage. III. Foreshadowing Without Cheating: The Shimmerer and Hope Gallagher The craft risk of any foreshadowing device is that it can feel like authorial intrusion — the writer visibly arranging dominoes rather than the character perceiving them. Here the foreshadowing is diegetic: it happens to Aiden inside the story rather than arriving through narratorial hindsight. When Aiden asks his grandfather’s ghost about a “blond lady” he has glimpsed at school, the grandfather answers within the novel’s established supernatural taxonomy: “We call her a shimmerer. A good soul who has passed. Before she completes her journey, she has something she wants to accomplish.” Aiden immediately connects her to a living classmate: “Hope Gallagher?” “Yes, son.” “Why does she need to watch over her?” “You’ll find out.” 1 The scene does two things simultaneously that a conventional realist narration cannot do at once. First, it plants a Chekhov’s gun (Hope Gallagher will matter later) without the narrator needing to signal narratorial awareness of the plant — Aiden is genuinely puzzled, not knowingly withholding information from the reader for effect, because the “gift” gives him fragments, not full sight. Second, it dramatizes the withholding as the grandfather’s choice (“You’ll find out”) rather than the author’s, converting an authorial technique (deferred revelation) into a character trait (a ghost who teaches by riddle, in the tradition of the seanchaí or folk storyteller). The device recurs throughout the novel: Aiden sees “a vision” of “a girl… wearing a green pinafore, her scarf caught on a branch,” 1 long before that image’s significance to the family’s Irish history is unpacked; Laura’s obsessive drawing of the “ghost man” precedes, by chapters, the revelation of who he actually is. In each case, the information arrives to Aiden — and therefore to the reader — as partial, uninterpreted sense data, exactly the epistemic position a reader wants to occupy in a mystery structured around inherited trauma. IV. Compression: Three Generations in One Boy’s Bedroom Second sight also solves a scale problem. Give Them Unquiet Dreams is, among other things, a three-generation family history — Sinead’s death in Ireland, Catherine’s guilt and immigration, Laura’s breakdown and institutionalization, Aiden’s own adolescence — compressed into a roughly 264-page novel narrated by a teenager. A conventional realist novel attempting this scope would need either a multi-generational omniscient narrator (sacrificing the intimacy of first person) or extensive exposition delivered through dialogue (risking inertness). Mulhern instead uses the grandfather’s nightly visitations as a compression device: each visit delivers, in a few pages of dialogue at the foot of a child’s bed, information that would otherwise require entire chapters of backstory. The story of Sinead’s death by the well — the novel’s foundational trauma — is delivered twice, once by the grandfather in Chapter Two (“A horse startled her and she fell into a well… before, she heard banshees calling out to her”) 1 and once later, with more emotional detail, by Rita in the Public Garden. 1 The doubling is deliberate: the ghost’s version is folkloric and compressed (banshees, púcas, a horse “with golden eyes”), suited to a bedroom visitation that must also cover cosmology, family history, and moral instruction in the same scene; Rita’s version is naturalistic and detailed, suited to a scene whose purpose is emotional reckoning rather than world-building. Second sight allows Mulhern to deliver the same core information twice, in two different registers, without redundancy — because the first telling is doing structural work (establishing the supernatural rules and compressing the timeline) that the second telling, freed from that burden, does not need to repeat. V. The Epistemological Wager: Protecting the “Rational” Story The novel’s central practical plot — Aiden and Martin’s campaign to get their mother Laura released from the psychiatric hospital — depends entirely on a distinction the grandfather names explicitly: the difference between what is true and what is permitted to look sane. “If Laura does something that others think peculiar, you must protect her. Make her actions seem rational,” the grandfather tells Aiden. “They’re afraid when things don’t fit their idea of reality… their vision is limited.” 1 This line does triple duty. Thematically, it names the novel’s argument about the social construction of madness — Laura is not unwell, she is unwitnessed, surrounded by people whose “vision is limited” in the ordinary sense, in ironic counterpoint to Aiden’s literal second sight. Structurally, it hands Aiden — and the reader — a concrete dramatic task (protect Mom by managing her presentation) that converts an abstract supernatural gift into stakes-bearing plot machinery. And technically, it lets Mulhern write scenes of apparent domestic realism (family therapy meetings, a school suspension, a hospital visit) that carry a second, ironic layer of meaning available only to readers who share Aiden’s privileged knowledge that the “crazy” version of events is the accurate one. Margie’s blunt affirmation late in the same sequence — “I think she sees things that other people don’t” — voiced by a minor character with no supernatural stake in the matter, quietly seeds doubt into the “rational” consensus from the outside, confirming that Aiden’s technology of sight is bleeding, plausibly, into the ordinary world. 1 VI. Conclusion: Second Sight as Formal Solution To call Aiden’s second sight a narrative technology is not to diminish its thematic weight — grief, inheritance, and the stigmatization of difference are not incidental to the device but are what the device is built out of. The claim is rather that Irish folk cosmology offers the novel a structural way to address problems that a purely secular realist novel narrated by a fourteen-year-old might handle through an omniscient narrator, flashback chapters, or expository dialogue. Second sight lets the novel foreshadow through the character’s own uninterpreted perception rather than the narrator’s hindsight; it lets three generations of Irish-American history compress into bedside conversations with a ghost; and it converts an epistemological claim about the reality of the supernatural into the engine of the novel’s practical plot, the fight to bring a mother home. The device is both the novel’s most fantastical element and a formal choice with practical narrative effects. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. James Mulhern, Give Them Unquiet Dreams (Silver Current Press, 2019). ↩ Works Quoted All quotations are drawn from Give Them Unquiet Dreams (Silver Current Press, 2019). title: Services — Mentorship, Tutoring & Publishing with James Mulhern
heading: Services
description: Manuscript coaching, English & writing tutoring, AP English Language & Composition exam preparation and consulting, adult literary seminars, curriculum design, campus visits and faculty support, MFA and college application coaching, journal submission strategy, and professional publishing services from author and educator James Mulhern.
text: Services — Mentorship, Tutoring & Publishing with James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Invitation Services Ways to work together on writing, reading, teaching, and preparing books for readers. Choose the service that fits your needs. A Note from James Eight Ways We Might Work Together I am a novelist and poet, a Kirkus-starred author, an Oxford writing fellow, and — for more than thirty years — a teacher of English and writing at the high-school and college level. The services below draw on that experience. Each one states what is included and what it costs. If something here is close but not quite right, write to me and we can discuss an appropriate arrangement. Service 01 · For Writers Book Mentor & Manuscript Coaching Have you been carrying a novel, a memoir, a poetry collection, or a book of stories — and need a steady reader to work through it with you? We can meet page by page to discuss the manuscript. What you are purchasing One-to-one editorial mentorship from a novelist. In each hour, I read your pages in advance and meet you in person to offer feedback on: Structure, pacing, and scene shape Voice, point of view, and prose-line craft Character development and dramatic logic Revision strategy — what to cut, what to grow, what to leave alone A clear, written next-step plan after every session For writers in the middle of a manuscript who want sustained feedback and a regular reading partner. This is not a copy-edit or proofread; for those services, see Silver Current Press below. Single Hour $95 per hour Six-Session Arc $525 six hours · save $45 Full Manuscript Mentorship $2,800 flat · ~30 hours over 4–6 months Typical timeline: Weekly or biweekly in-person sessions. Single hours can be booked one at a time; the six-session arc runs over six to eight weeks; the full mentorship spans four to six months from first reading to final pages. Begin a Conversation Service 02 · For Students English, Writing & Standardized-Test Tutoring Is there a high-school or college student in your house who could use a patient, experienced reader? Whether it is a college essay, an AP exam, the SAT, or a stubborn paragraph, we can work on it one hour at a time. What you are purchasing One-to-one tutoring from a teacher with thirty years in high-school and college English classrooms, and a former AP English Consultant for the College Board and the National Math & Science Initiative. Sessions cover: Essay writing — analytical, argumentative, personal, college-application Grammar, sentence craft, and revision habits Close reading of literature (novels, poetry, drama, nonfiction) AP English Language & Composition exam preparation SAT and ACT Reading & Writing sections, plus the essay Study skills, annotation, and how to plan a long paper Sessions are 60 minutes, held in person. Parents are welcome to sit in on the first session. One-on-One $75 per hour Small Group $35 per student, per hour · min. 4 10-Hour Package $675 flat · 1-on-1 · save $75 Test-Prep Bootcamp $825 flat · 12 hours over 6–10 weeks Typical timeline: One 60-minute in-person session per week. Many tutoring plans run six to eight weeks; AP, SAT, and ACT preparation generally runs eight to twelve weeks ahead of the exam. Inquire About Tutoring Service 03 · For Curious Adults Adult Small-Group Literary Seminars Would you and a few friends like to spend a season inside a great book, a strange poet, or the craft of writing itself? Gather four or more — round a kitchen table — and I will lead the seminar. What you are purchasing A privately convened seminar for your group, designed around whatever you want to read or learn. I prepare the syllabus, the discussion questions, and any short writing prompts. You bring the curiosity and the wine. Sample seminars I have led or designed: A close reading of one major novel — Beloved , Middlemarch , The Great Gatsby A poet in depth — Yeats, Bishop, Heaney, Plath, Dickinson The personal essay or memoir, as a writing workshop Short-story craft for new and returning writers "How to read a poem" — a four-session crash course Any topic in literature or writing you would like to design with me Minimum four participants. Typical seminar runs four to six weekly sessions of 75–90 minutes. Custom topics welcome. Adult Seminar $65 per person, per hour · min. 4 Four-Session Series $220 per person, flat · four 90-min sessions Private Single Talk $400 flat · one 90-min session for the whole group Typical timeline: One 75- to 90-minute session per week. A four-session series runs about a month; a six-session deep-dive runs about a season. Syllabus and reading list delivered one week before the first meeting. Gather Your Group Service 04 · For Schools & Teachers AP English Language & Composition Consulting Are you a department chair, an AP Lang teacher, or a school leader reviewing your program? I have spent decades working with AP English Language & Composition; we can look at your course together. What you are purchasing Consulting from a former AP English Language & Composition Consultant for the College Board and the National Math & Science Initiative, and a two-time English & Social Studies Department Chair. Engagements focus on the AP English Language & Composition exam and may include: AP English Language & Composition course audit and redesign Rhetorical analysis, argument, and synthesis-essay pedagogy FRQ scoring norming and rubric calibration for teachers Multiple-choice strategy and stimulus-text selection Mock-exam design and post-exam data review Vertical-team planning that feeds AP Lang from grades 9–11 Coaching sessions for new AP Lang teachers Available remotely or, for schools within reach, on-site. Half-day and full-day flat rates available on request. Consulting Hour $185 per hour Half-Day PD $1,450 flat · up to 4 hours · whole department Full-Day PD $2,400 flat · up to 7 hours · whole department Annual Coach Retainer $4,200 flat · 24 hours over the school year Typical timeline: Single consulting hours scheduled within two to three weeks; PD days delivered on a date you choose, with planning calls in the prior four to six weeks; annual retainers run August through May with monthly touch-points. Request a Consultation Service 05 · For Programs & Educators Curriculum Design Do you have an English course, a creative-writing program, or a humanities sequence that needs to be built from the ground up or revised? We can design it with clear learning goals, a coherent sequence, and appropriate materials. What you are purchasing Custom curriculum design drawing on experience as a novelist, English teacher, and former Department Chair. Deliverables typically include: A semester or full-year scope-and-sequence document Unit plans with essential questions, texts, and assessments Reading lists curated for your students and your aims Sample lesson plans and signature assignments Aligned rubrics for writing, reading, and discussion Optional teacher-facing pacing guide and PD session Available for independent schools, public-school departments, homeschool co-ops, and adult learning programs. Project-rate quotes are available after a free 20-minute scoping call. Design Hour $150 per hour Full Unit Plan $1,100 flat · 3–4 week unit Semester Course $3,800 flat · full semester scope & sequence Full-Year Course $6,800 flat · year-long course with PD Typical timeline: Unit plans delivered in five to seven weeks; semester courses in ten to fourteen weeks; full-year courses in fourteen to eighteen weeks, with a midpoint draft review and one round of revisions included in every flat-fee project. Start a Project Service 06 · For Authors Publishing & Editorial Services Have you finished a manuscript — or nearly so — and need editorial guidance? Manuscript evaluation, developmental editing, line editing, copyediting, and proofreading are available through my imprint. What you are purchasing Editorial services through Silver Current Press , the literary imprint I founded. Each project is read by an editor, with feedback tailored to the manuscript and its agreed scope. Starting at $650 for a full manuscript evaluation, with developmental editing, line editing, copyediting, and proofreading priced per word. Full deliverables, inclusions, and exact rates for every service are kept current on the Silver Current Press site — the single source for pricing, so you always see the same number in both places. Detailed scope, exact rates, and a free quote are available on the Silver Current Press site. Visit Silver Current Press → Service 07 · For Departments & Faculty Campus Visits & Faculty Support Are you building a reading series, supporting a teacher, or finishing a book of your own? Campus visits and faculty support can include teaching, readings, and manuscript discussion. What you are purchasing Time on your campus, or in your department's meeting room online, from a writer and former classroom teacher with more than thirty years of experience. Every engagement is planned with the chair or program director and can include: Semester-long or year-long mentoring for one teacher, meeting monthly A visiting craft workshop for your students, sixty to ninety minutes A department craft lecture or reading, with real time for questions A four-session seminar series for an MFA or graduate cohort A close read of a colleague's book proposal, with revision notes A full editorial pass on a journal article before it goes out Available on campus or remotely. Travel within the Philadelphia region is included; beyond it, we agree on costs before anything is booked. Teacher Mentoring · Semester $1,650 flat · 14–16 weeks · monthly sessions Teacher Mentoring · Full Year $3,200 flat · 9–10 months Visiting Craft Workshop $650 per session · 60–90 minutes Department Lecture or Reading $550 per session · 45 min. + Q&A MFA Cohort Seminar Series $1,850 flat · 4 sessions · up to 12 students Book Proposal Review $725 flat · full read + revision notes Journal-Article Review $475 flat · single article · full editorial pass Typical timeline: Craft workshops and lectures need four to six weeks of lead time; seminar series and mentoring engagements are planned a semester ahead. Book proposals come back in three to five weeks, journal articles in two to four. Invite Me to Your Department Service 08 · For Students & Emerging Writers Mentorship, Applications & First Publications Are you applying to an MFA, sitting the AP exam in May, or trying to place your first poem? I can help you prepare materials and plans for these next steps. What you are purchasing One-to-one attention from a writer who has read thousands of student pages and placed his own work in more than three hundred journals. Depending on the scope, an engagement may include an essay, portfolio, submission list, or a revised manuscript plan. A three-month craft mentorship, meeting every other week Preparation for the AP English Language or Literature exam, with materials College admissions essays, from the first idea to the final draft A complete MFA or graduate application — statement, writing sample, and school list A submission strategy for literary journals, with a ranked list and cover letters A poetry chapbook selected and sequenced, ready to send out Sessions run in person in Philadelphia. Every engagement begins with a free conversation, because some of these you may not need at all — and I would rather tell you so. Three-Month Mentorship $1,150 flat · 12 weeks · bi-weekly sessions MFA Application Package $895 flat · statement, sample & school list AP Exam Preparation $595 flat · 6 sessions + materials Journal Submission Strategy $520 flat · 4 sessions + submission plan Admissions Essay Coaching $495 flat · 3 sessions + 2 rounds of edits Chapbook Curation $425 flat · selection & sequencing consult Typical timeline: The mentorship runs twelve weeks. Exam preparation and application packages want eight to ten weeks, so count backward from your deadline and write to me early. Admissions essays take four to six weeks, submission plans six to eight, and a chapbook consult three to five. Start With a Free Conversation An Honest Word About Rates These rates reflect the preparation, reading, and meeting time involved, along with more than thirty years of teaching, two department-chair roles, an Oxford writing fellowship, a Kirkus-starred novel, and work as a College Board consultant. If a rate is genuinely out of reach and the work matters, write to me anyway. We can discuss what may be possible. text: Submissions — CLOSED — Silver Current Press ← Back to The 2601 Salon Currently Closed Submissions & Contests Silver Current Press is not accepting manuscripts, contest entries, or queries at this time. Future reading periods will be announced here. Important Notice Submissions & the Silver Current Prize Are Closed Silver Current Press is NOT accepting manuscripts, contest entries, or queries at this time. Please do not send work for review. The pages below describe our standards and the next reading period will be announced here — please check back. Closed for Submissions · Closed for Contest What We Read Three Doors — One Standard We consider work in three genres. In each, we look for careful sentences, purposeful lines, and pages that invite continued reading. I. Fiction Short stories and novellas in the literary realist tradition, including work with the faintest paranormal or speculative seasoning. We are partial to interior, character-driven prose with patient sentence-making. II. Poetry Free verse and received forms alike. We read for image, music, and the particular pressure of a finished line — work that rewards a second and third reading. III. Nonfiction Personal essay, literary criticism, and craft writing. We are especially interested in essays that treat reading itself as a moral and intellectual practice. ⚫ The Silver Current Prize is currently CLOSED. Please do not submit entries. ⚫ Annual Contest The Silver Current Prize Our annual prize for an unpublished short story, poem, or essay. Open to writers of any nationality, writing in English, at any stage of career — when the contest is open . Prize $500 plus publication Entry Fee $15 per submission Reading Period Sept — Dec open annually Judge James Mulhern founding editor The winning piece appears in the Silver Current Press annual anthology. Two finalists receive honorable mention and publication consideration. All entries are read blindly by the founding editor. The Practical Submission Guidelines Length Fiction and nonfiction: up to 7,500 words. Poetry: up to five poems per submission. Send your strongest, not your longest. Format Double-spaced for prose. Single-spaced for poetry. 12-point serif. Number your pages. Your name should appear on the first page only; we read blind beyond it. Originality Unpublished work only. Simultaneous submissions are welcome — please notify us promptly if the work is accepted elsewhere. Response Time Eight to twelve weeks. If you have not heard from us after twelve weeks, you are welcome to query at the address below. Rights First serial rights for the print edition; first electronic rights for any digital edition. All other rights revert to the author on publication. Where to Send Use the form below, or write directly to submissions@silvercurrentpress.com with your manuscript attached as a single Word or PDF document. title: Teaching as Vocation and Trap — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: Teaching as Vocation and Trap
description: “Peppermint Candy” and “Drenched to the Bone” read as a diptych about pedagogical burnout, drawing on James Mulhern's own three decades in the classroom.
text: Teaching as Vocation and Trap — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On the Classroom Stories Teaching as Vocation and Trap “Peppermint Candy” and “Drenched to the Bone” read as a diptych about pedagogical burnout, moral compromise, and a biography spent in the classroom. Abstract James Mulhern has spent more than thirty years teaching. This essay reads “Peppermint Candy” and “Drenched to the Bone” as a matched pair of classroom stories, narrated by teachers whose competence and corrosion are closely related. It considers the stories in light of Mulhern’s classroom experience, while not treating their events as autobiographical. I. A Career Inside the Material The editorial introduction to The Collected Stories and Poems of James Mulhern (forthcoming) establishes a biographical fact relevant to two of the volume’s stories: Mulhern “has taught for more than thirty years, has served for over a decade as an AP curriculum consultant for the National Math and Science Initiative, and has read AP English Language exams for the College Board for more than five years running,” and the introduction goes on to observe “a teacher’s exactness in this work, a refusal to let a scene end a beat too late.” 1 This essay considers how “Peppermint Candy” and “Drenched to the Bone,” read together, portray the American teaching profession through institutional details such as incident reports, I.E.P. paperwork, vending-machine break-ins, and fire-drill choreography. The two stories share a structure worth naming before turning to either individually: both are narrated in the first person by a veteran teacher facing a disruptive incident inside the classroom, both incidents escalate into administrative process (an incident report, a suspension), and both stories end with the teacher alone, driving, privately reckoning with something the day’s official paperwork cannot capture. Where the two diverge is in what that private reckoning discloses about the narrator’s own moral condition — and it is in that divergence that the diptych does its most interesting work. II. “Peppermint Candy”: Competence as Camouflage Mr. Darnell, the narrator of “Peppermint Candy,” is introduced entirely through professional competence. When a student, Helen, vomits during a reading of Poe, his response is immediate, calm, and correctly sequenced: he grabs napkins, dispatches a student for the nurse, redirects the class, and manages a chaotic sequence of adults — a nurse, a janitor, a principal, a secretary — with unbroken procedural fluency. 2 The story’s middle section is, in effect, a documentary of institutional process: the incident report’s categories (“Burn, dislocation, puncture, concussion”), the secretary Valerie’s cynicism about the form’s real function (“No one looks at these things anyway. They get filed away in some drawer”), and the school principal’s pointed review of Helen’s I.E.P. and her allegation that Darnell called the student “a ‘rat’ and her mother… ‘a pain in the ass.’” 2 Darnell does not deny the remark; he defends it: “That sounds accurate… I believe my assessment is spot on.” 2 This is the diptych’s first thesis about the profession: institutional competence and personal contempt for the people the institution serves are not opposites but can coexist within the same well-regarded teacher, the same calm hands that managed the vomiting emergency. The story’s final movement makes the coexistence literal and lethal. Darnell’s offer of a peppermint to the principal — “Would you like a piece of candy before you go?” — immediately precedes the story’s procedural reveal: he retrieves Visine from his desk drawer, reviews “the poisonous effects from tetrahydrozoline,” and confirms, in the same flat diction he used to complete an incident report, “the care I had taken to lightly rub Visine onto the candy before rewrapping it… I retrieved the peppermints from my desk drawer and placed them in my satchel. I would share them again another day.” 2 The vocation and the trap are, in Darnell, the same set of skills: the meticulousness that makes him an effective first responder to a medical emergency is identical to the meticulousness that makes him a careful poisoner, and the story offers no seam between the two. III. “Drenched to the Bone”: Burnout Without a Villain Jack, the narrator of “Drenched to the Bone,” is a gentler and more self-aware case of the same professional exhaustion, and the story is careful to root his classroom fatigue in a specific, undramatic personal collapse: a marriage ended not by betrayal on his part but by his wife Kate’s verdict that he has become unreachable — “You don’t ask me anything. You don’t listen… I don’t know who you are anymore.” 3 He relocates to Florida and begins teaching at a new school, and the story’s central set piece — a ransacked vending machine, a fire alarm triggered by roofing tar, a psychotic break by a student named Mary Grace — unfolds as a single day’s accumulation of institutional chaos that Jack narrates with the weary, precise cataloguing of someone who has seen every version of this chaos before: “Bags of Lays potato chips, Doritos, Starbursts, Cheetos, Skittles, and other assorted healthy foods that we provide for our students… lie on the floor in a jumbled mess.” 3 Where “Peppermint Candy” ends on cold competence, “Drenched to the Bone” ends on something closer to genuine reckoning, precipitated by the very student whose breakdown has just disrupted his classroom. Mary Grace, mid-collapse, delivers an assessment of Jack that the story does not allow him to dismiss: “You’re no better than Turd, Mr. McCarthy. I know you think that because you’re a teacher you know everything, but you don’t!” 3 Sitting afterward at his desk, Jack allows the accusation to land: “Mary Grace, as deranged as she had acted, uttered a truth about me. I did think I knew a lot. I did keep to myself… I sit at my desk… preoccupied by what Mary Grace said, reflecting on my arrogance and self-centeredness.” 3 The story’s closing gesture — Jack calling his ex-wife from a rain-drenched parking lot to say, simply, “I’m sorry. I should have paid more attention to you” — converts a day of classroom disaster into the occasion for a marriage’s belated postmortem, with the Bob Dylan line that gives the story its title (“the waters growing around you… you’ll soon be drenched to the bone”) arriving as the closest thing to grace the story permits its narrator. 3 IV. The Diptych’s Argument Read separately, “Peppermint Candy” is a chilling character study and “Drenched to the Bone” a melancholy one; read together, they make an argument about the teaching profession that neither story alone fully states. Both narrators are competent, even exemplary, in the specific, narrow, institutional sense that their schools reward: they file the correct paperwork, manage classroom chaos with practiced calm, and say the things administrators want to hear. Both narrators are also, by the story’s end, revealed to be profoundly cut off — Darnell from any recognizable moral feeling for the students in his care, Jack from the wife and the interior life he spent two decades failing to attend to. The stories differ crucially in whether that cutoff is presented as fixed or reversible: Darnell’s closing line, “I would share them again another day,” forecloses any possibility of change, while Jack’s apology to Kate, however belated, at least gestures toward the attention he has just relearned how to pay. 2 What gives the diptych a biographical context is its attention to institutional process — the vocabulary of incident reports, I.E.P. meetings, and AP curriculum jargon. Mulhern’s teaching experience may inform these details, without making the stories a record of classroom life. In both stories, teaching is more than a backdrop for private crisis: paperwork, procedure, and performed patience provide structures in which Darnell can hide and Jack can lose himself by attrition, until a student’s breakdown prompts an uncomfortable recognition. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. Introduction, The Collected Stories and Poems of James Mulhern (Silver Current Press, forthcoming). ↩ 2. James Mulhern, “Peppermint Candy,” in The Collected Stories and Poems of James Mulhern (Silver Current Press, forthcoming). ↩ 3. James Mulhern, “Drenched to the Bone,” in The Collected Stories and Poems of James Mulhern (Silver Current Press, forthcoming). ↩ Works Quoted Quotations are drawn from “Peppermint Candy” and “Drenched to the Bone,” both collected in The Collected Stories and Poems of James Mulhern (Silver Current Press, forthcoming), and from the volume’s Introduction.
