title: Give Them Unquiet Dreams: A Comprehensive Study — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: Give Them Unquiet Dreams
description: A close reading of Give Them Unquiet Dreams — structure, dual geography, family inheritance, the psychiatric plot, and the novel's place in Mulhern's body of work.
text: Give Them Unquiet Dreams: A Comprehensive Study — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon A Close Reading · On the Novel Give Them Unquiet Dreams A full-length study of the Kirkus-starred novel — its structure, its dual geography of Boston and Achill Island, its architecture of inherited trauma, and its place in James Mulhern’s body of work. Abstract Give Them Unquiet Dreams (Kurti Publishing, 2019; a Kirkus Reviews Best Book of 2019 with a Kirkus Star) develops concerns that recur in Mulhern’s work: the sacred disclosed inside the ordinary, inherited trauma made legible across generations, and first-person narration extended, through the device of second sight, to carry history beyond a single fourteen-year-old’s direct experience. This essay reads the novel as a whole — its two-generation, two-continent structure; its central plot, Aiden Glencar’s campaign to free his institutionalized mother; its treatment of psychiatric authority and gendered credibility; and its critical reception — and situates it alongside companion essays on this site that examine its narrative technique and folkloric inheritance in more specialized detail. Contents I. A Novel Built on a Double Inheritance II. Structure: Two Continents, Three Generations III. Aiden Glencar and the Ethics of the Gift IV. Laura’s Diagnosis: Credibility, Gender, and Institutional Power V. Catherine and Sinead: The Well at the Center of the Book VI. The Pelican and the Sacramental Ordinary VII. Reception and Place in the Corpus VIII. Conclusion: What the Title Means I. A Novel Built on a Double Inheritance Give Them Unquiet Dreams asks a fourteen-year-old boy to carry two inheritances at once: a family history of loss stretching back to rural Ireland, and a diagnosis — his mother Laura's psychiatric commitment — imposed by a Boston medical establishment with no interest in that history. The premise sounds, described this way, like a case study, but the novel withholds the tools that would let a reader safely resolve the case. Aiden Glencar, the narrator, shares with his mother a family “gift” of second sight — visions, a dead grandfather's nightly visitations, flashes of other people's thoughts — that the novel never confirms or debunks. The reader is asked to hold the same undecidable question the Boston child-welfare and psychiatric systems refuse to hold: is Laura ill, or is she simply the bearer of a perception her culture has no diagnostic category for? This premise places the novel squarely inside Mulhern's larger project, described in the site's other essays as an insistence that the sacred survives disguised as the ordinary and that inherited trauma persists as a kind of family cosmology rather than a resolved plot event. 1 What distinguishes Unquiet Dreams from the short fiction that shares its methods is scale: it is Mulhern's only long-form treatment of the Glencar-family material, and the additional length lets him build out consequences — institutionalization, family fracture, a child's improvised campaign against an indifferent bureaucracy — that a story's compressed form cannot fully dramatize. II. Structure: Two Continents, Three Generations The novel's architecture moves constantly between two geographies and three generations: the rural Irish past of Aiden's great-grandmother Sinead, who dies falling into a well after hearing banshees call to her; the immigrant generation of Catherine, Aiden's grandmother, who carries guilt for her mother's death across the ocean to Boston; and the present-tense 1970s narrative of Aiden and his brother Martin, fighting to bring their mother Laura home from a psychiatric hospital. Companion essays on this site examine in detail how second sight functions as the mechanism that lets these three generations compress into a single first-person narrative without an omniscient frame, 2 and how Mulhern's Boston bedroom visitations depart from the communal, geographically anchored folk belief recorded in Yeats's The Celtic Twilight . 3 What matters for a whole-novel reading is the effect that compression produces: a book in which the past is never background. Sinead's death by the well and Catherine's decades of unspoken guilt are not exposition delivered once and set aside; they recur, retold in different registers by the grandfather's ghost and later by Rita in the Public Garden, 4 until the reader understands that for this family, no death is ever fully in the past tense. The novel's two-continent structure enacts, at the level of plot geography, the same claim its supernatural apparatus makes at the level of metaphysics: nothing is over. III. Aiden Glencar and the Ethics of the Gift Aiden narrates the novel from an adult retrospective vantage, looking back at his fourteen-year-old self, and the gap between those two ages does real work in the book. As a child, Aiden receives instruction from his grandfather's ghost in explicitly practical, almost tactical terms: “If Laura does something that others think peculiar, you must protect her. Make her actions seem rational,” the ghost tells him, adding that the adults around her are afraid “when things don't fit their idea of reality… their vision is limited.” 5 The instruction converts Aiden from a passive witness of family crisis into an active manager of his mother's public presentation — a fourteen-year-old assigned the job of curating, for a hospital and a court system, what version of his mother's inner life is permitted to be called sane. The novel is careful not to let this responsibility resolve into heroism without cost. The adult narrator admits, late in the book, that he spent much of his adult life trying to “ignore my second sight, the flashes of intuition, and telepathy,” 6 a confession that reads simultaneously as proof the gift was real — why suppress an invention? — and as the testimony of someone who has spent decades uncertain whether to trust his own perception, a companion essay on the site's unreliable-narrator readings terms this “the child narrator's unreliability and the adult narrator's unresolved doubt… the same problem restated at two ages.” 7 The gift, in other words, protects Laura and costs Aiden something the novel never fully quantifies: a lifetime of not knowing whether his own mind can be trusted. IV. Laura's Diagnosis: Credibility, Gender, and Institutional Power Underneath its supernatural apparatus, Give Them Unquiet Dreams is a novel about who gets believed. Laura's visions and Aiden's visions are, within the text, the same category of perception, inherited through the same family line — yet only Laura is institutionalized for hers. The distinction the novel draws is not between true sight and false sight, but between a child's private, containable version of the gift and an adult woman's version, which disrupts a marriage, a household, and eventually draws the attention of a medical system built to pathologize exactly the kind of disruption she causes. Martin's flat verdict on his mother — “Aiden, she was acting crazy” 8 — voices the ordinary, unremarkable modern consensus the novel sets against the Glencar family's inherited belief, and the minor character Margie's late, unprompted observation that “I think she sees things that other people don't” 8 quietly seeds doubt into that consensus from a source with no stake in defending Laura. The novel does not resolve this tension by proving Laura sane in a courtroom sense; it resolves it, if it resolves it at all, by making Aiden's protective performance — managing what other people are permitted to see — the actual mechanism of Laura's freedom. That is a bleaker resolution than a conventional redemption plot would offer: Laura is not vindicated by the medical establishment recognizing her gift as real. She is freed because a child successfully stage-manages her presentation until the institution loses interest in scrutinizing her. The novel's quiet suggestion is that this is how belief and credibility actually get distributed inside families and institutions alike — not through truth prevailing, but through someone taking on the exhausting, permanent work of translation between a person's reality and what power is willing to accept as real. V. Catherine and Sinead: The Well at the Center of the Book If Laura's crisis is the novel's present-tense engine, Sinead's death by drowning in a well, and Catherine's lifelong guilt over it, is its buried foundation. The grandfather's ghost delivers the story to Aiden in compressed, folkloric terms — “A horse startled her and she fell into a well… before, she heard banshees calling out to her” 9 — and a companion essay on this site details how that telling and Rita's later, more naturalistic retelling in the Public Garden function as two registers of the same information, one suited to cosmology and one to reckoning. 9 What deserves emphasis in a whole-novel reading is what the doubled telling implies about guilt's half-life across generations: Catherine carries her mother's death as unspoken guilt for decades, crosses an ocean without resolving it, and dies without fully unburdening herself of it, leaving Aiden — who never met Sinead and was not alive for most of Catherine's guilt — to inherit the obligation of closing the account on her behalf, delivering Catherine's gratitude to Rita only after Catherine herself has died. 10 The novel's argument, made structurally rather than stated outright, is that family guilt does not expire with the generation that incurred it; it is simply handed forward, disguised as inheritance, folklore, or a boy's strange gift, until someone is finally in a position to set it down. VI. The Pelican and the Sacramental Ordinary Mulhern's fiction, across the corpus, tends to locate the sacred inside deliberately unglamorous objects and creatures rather than inside conventional religious iconography, and Unquiet Dreams supplies one of the clearest instances of the pattern: a pelican, functioning within the novel's argument as a sacrament administered without a priest, standing alongside a classroom communion scene and a family beach trip elsewhere in Mulhern's work as evidence of the same recurring conviction. 11 The choice of a pelican specifically — an awkward, unglamorous bird rather than a dove or any more conventionally sacred creature — is consistent with the novel's larger refusal to let its supernatural material harden into tidy religious allegory. Second sight in this novel is never simply a metaphor for Catholic faith; it survives, like the pelican, as something ungainly and specific, closer to inherited family fact than to doctrine. VII. Reception and Place in the Corpus Give Them Unquiet Dreams was named a Kirkus Reviews Best Book of 2019 and awarded a Kirkus Star; Kirkus's own assessment called it “a luminous, beautifully told fairy tale grounded in history and elevated by spirit.” 12 The novel also won the Readers' Favorite Book Award, was named a Notable Best Indie Book of 2019, and received a Red Ribbon (highly recommended) designation from the UK's Wishing Shelf Book Awards. 12 A comparative study elsewhere on this site discusses the novel alongside Molly Bonamici and notes points of contact with Alice McDermott's family chronicles, William Kennedy's ghost-haunted Albany fiction, and William Trevor's tragedies of overlooked lives. 13 Selected material from the novel was later adapted into short fiction gathered under Aiden and Laura's shared second sight. 14 VIII. Conclusion: What the Title Means The novel's title, Give Them Unquiet Dreams , reads, after a full engagement with the book, less like a curse than like an inheritance the Glencar family has decided to accept rather than refuse. A quiet dream would be one undisturbed by the dead, by inherited guilt, or by a perception that will not resolve itself into a diagnosis anyone else can confirm. The Glencars do not get quiet dreams, and by the novel's end, the withholding of that peace reads less as tragedy than as fidelity — to Sinead, to Catherine, to a family history that insists on being felt rather than settled. Aiden's second sight, Laura's visions, and the ghost's nightly visitations are, in the end, the mechanism by which this family refuses to let its dead, or its guilt, or its own reality, go quiet. That refusal is the source of the novel's suffering and, in the same measure, the source of its grace. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. title: Unreliable Child Narrators and the Limits of Innocence — James Mulhern
heading: Unreliable Child Narrators and the Limits of Innocence
description: An essay on the child and adolescent narrators of Molly Bonamici and Give Them Unquiet Dreams — how affect withheld, rather than perception failed, shapes unreliable narration.
text: Unreliable Child Narrators and the Limits of Innocence — James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On Narrative Technique Unreliable Child Narrators and the Limits of Innocence In the Fiction of James Mulhern — how affect withheld, not perception failed, produces the unease of Molly Bonamici and Give Them Unquiet Dreams . Abstract The unreliable narrator is usually discussed as a problem of concealment. Child narrators complicate that taxonomy: they introduce a third condition, a narrator who reports what she sees accurately while lacking the interpretive frame — or the willingness — to say what the seeing costs her. This essay reads Molly Bonamici and the child-Aiden sections of Give Them Unquiet Dreams through that third condition, considering innocence as a craft position rather than a character trait. I. Two Kinds of Not-Knowing The unreliable narrator is usually discussed as a problem of concealment: a narrator who knows more than she tells, or who tells what she believes while the text arranges evidence against her. Child narrators complicate this taxonomy because they introduce a third condition, neither concealment nor delusion: a narrator who does not yet possess the interpretive frame required to understand what she is reporting, even as she reports it accurately. James Mulhern’s fiction — especially the novel Molly Bonamici , but also the child-Aiden sections of Give Them Unquiet Dreams — explores this third condition. His child and adolescent narrators are rarely naïve in the sentimental sense; they can be more perceptive, articulate, and emotionally guarded than the adults around them. What they lack is not perception but consequence: they see accurately and feel — or claim to feel — strangely little, and it is the gap between accurate seeing and absent feeling, rather than any failure of perception, that constitutes the unreliability this essay examines. Both novels are narrated from an adult retrospective vantage looking back at childhood, which means the “unreliability” can operate on two temporal tracks: what the child character did not understand in the moment, and what the adult narrator, looking back, does not fully explain. II. Molly and the Toad: Affect Withheld as Narrative Style Molly Bonamici opens with its title character, sixteen, retreating to the back steps after witnessing her father choke her mother in the kitchen. Within the space of a single page, Molly’s attention detaches from the domestic violence she has just witnessed and fixes instead on a sick toad: “I searched the backyard for several minutes until I found a large rock. I walked over to where the toad sat, lifted the lid of the trashcan until he fell onto the cement pad, where he continued to croak and shake. To put him out of his misery, I smashed the rock against him a few times and watched his guts smear across the concrete. Then I sat on the bottom step for at least twenty minutes.” 1 The prose registers no shock, interpretive frame, or causal link between the violence indoors and the violence Molly commits on the animal; the narration juxtaposes the two acts with similar flatness. This is one of the novel’s notable technical choices: rather than filtering the abuse scene through visible childhood trauma (crying, fear, a shaking hand), Mulhern displaces affect onto an ostensibly unrelated action and lets the reader make a connection. The killing of the toad may function as displaced violence, an assumption of the father’s power by proxy, but Molly’s narration offers no such gloss; she reports the act with the same declarative calm she uses to describe pouring a glass of orange juice a paragraph later, “I added some vodka from my stash hidden in the closet, and took a few sips.” 1 The novel names this flatness through another character rather than through Molly’s self-awareness: it is Aunt Bianca, not Molly, who diagnoses the problem. Watching Molly’s unmoved reaction to a chaotic kitchen accident, Bianca says, “The girl doesn’t seem human sometimes. It’s like she doesn’t feel things… Always so cool, so cold… It’s not normal. I tell you it ain’t right.” 1 Molly’s response is to turn the accusation into a joke — “I come from another galaxy. I am an alien… My people are planning an invasion” — delivered, the narration specifies, “completely straight-faced.” 1 The joke may illustrate the novel’s unreliability mechanism: Molly deflects an observation about her emotional detachment by performing a more extreme version of it, treating her alleged inhumanity as deadpan comedy rather than a claim to defend or deny. The reader is left to decide whether the joke is a child’s defense mechanism, evidence that Bianca is right, or both at once, while the retrospective adult narrator does not settle the question. III. The Retrospective Frame: What the Adult Narrator Still Withholds Both Molly Bonamici and Give Them Unquiet Dreams are narrated by adults recalling adolescence, and Mulhern uses small temporal markers to remind the reader that a gap exists between the experiencing child and the narrating adult, without collapsing that gap into full explanation. Molly’s opening chapter is dated with unusual precision for a first-person memory narrative — “I was sixteen, a senior in high school; the year was 1980” 1 — a specificity that signals documentary intent even as the content that follows (killing a toad, mixing a screwdriver alone in a dark bedroom) resists documentary neutrality. Later in the novel, discussing the discovery of a neighbor’s decomposed body, the adult narrator makes the retrospective frame explicit: “It wasn’t until many years later that I learned the source of the friction between the two of them, and when I did, I was the one who was shocked.” 1 This sentence is doing careful work: it confirms that the adult narrator possesses information the child character did not, which technically resolves one kind of unreliability (withheld information becomes, eventually, available information) — but it withholds that resolved information from the reader in the same breath, reporting only that a shock occurred, not what caused it. The adult narrator is thus unreliable in a second-order way distinct from the child’s flat affect: she curates her own retrospective disclosures, telling us that understanding eventually arrived while declining, at that exact narrative moment, to share it. The same passage extends Molly’s affectless register into a meditation on the macabre that borders on clinical: describing public curiosity about a corpse, adult-narrator Molly writes, “I found it a strange paradox then, as I still do now, that most of us don’t want to think about death, our own mortality… Yet, when we hear about someone else’s death…” 1 The construction “then, as I still do now” collapses the distance between the sixteen-year-old and the narrating adult that the novel has otherwise been careful to maintain — suggesting that the coldness Aunt Bianca diagnosed in the child was never a phase Molly outgrew, but a durable feature of the consciousness narrating the entire book. This is a significant interpretive fork: readers who assumed Molly’s childhood detachment was trauma-response, likely to soften with age, are told directly that it did not soften. The unreliability is not a temporary distortion to be corrected by adult hindsight; it is the narrator’s permanent temperament, present in both the remembered child and the remembering adult. IV. Aiden and the Ambiguity of the Gift Give Them Unquiet Dreams deploys a structurally different but related form of narrative unreliability through Aiden Glencar, whose first-person narration is complicated not by withheld affect but by an unverifiable claim to supernatural perception. Aiden reports his grandfather’s ghostly visitations, his mother’s visions, and his own “second sight” with the same declarative confidence Molly uses to report killing the toad — the prose style does not flag these episodes as delusion, dream, or metaphor, and the reader has no external narrator to corroborate or debunk them. This creates a distinct variety of unreliable narration: not a narrator concealing what she knows, but a narrator whose reported perceptions cannot, by the nature of the material, be adjudicated as true or false from within the text. Aiden’s own uncertainty about how to read his mother’s visions — “Maybe those visions she was having were true?” he asks his brother Martin, who answers, “Aiden, she was acting crazy” 2 — stages the interpretive problem inside the plot itself, so that the reader’s uncertainty about Aiden’s reliability mirrors Martin’s uncertainty about Laura’s. Mulhern refuses to resolve this ambiguity even at the level of adult retrospection: the novel’s frame narrator, an adult Aiden looking back, confirms in a late passage that he “tried to ignore my second sight, the flashes of intuition, and telepathy” as an adult, 2 which reads simultaneously as confirmation that the gift was real (why suppress something imaginary?) and as the self-account of someone who has spent a lifetime uncertain whether to trust his own perception. The child narrator’s unreliability and the adult narrator’s unresolved doubt are, in this novel, the same problem restated at two ages. V. Conclusion: Innocence as a Craft Position, Not a Character Trait What unites Molly’s affectless deadpan and Aiden’s unverifiable second sight is that both may withhold interpretation rather than information. Neither narrator obviously lies to the reader in the classical unreliable-narrator sense of misrepresenting events. Both report scenes — a strangled mother, a smashed toad, a ghost at the foot of a bed — without the emotional or moral scaffolding an adult narrator might ordinarily supply, producing unease for the reader. Mulhern’s “limits of innocence,” then, need not be a matter of children failing to perceive the adult world correctly; the child narrators often perceive it sharply. The limit is interpretive: these narrators see clearly and refuse, or are unable, to tell the reader what the seeing costs them, leaving that cost to be inferred from displaced acts (a toad, a joke about aliens) or from the frame narrator’s incomplete hindsight. The technique leaves much of the moral judgment with the reader and draws on an unsentimental tradition of childhood narration rather than a more redemptive arc. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. title: The Unreliable Confession — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: The Unreliable Confession
description: First-person justification in “Peppermint Candy” and “Mia Bambina,” situated against Nabokov's Humbert Humbert and Highsmith's Tom Ripley.
text: The Unreliable Confession — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On Narrative Voice The Unreliable Confession First-person justification in “Peppermint Candy” and “Mia Bambina” — the plain, procedural diction of the reasonable criminal narrator, after Nabokov and Highsmith. Abstract Vladimir Nabokov’s Humbert Humbert and Patricia Highsmith’s Tom Ripley exemplify a narrative type: the first-person criminal narrator whose prose remains reasonable, articulate, and unbroken by guilt even at the moment of confession. This essay considers related rhetorical choices in two James Mulhern stories — the poisoner-teacher of “Peppermint Candy” and the self-described sociopath of “Mia Bambina” — and examines how plain, procedural diction can carry violence without the narration signaling alarm. I. The Reasonable Criminal Narrator Vladimir Nabokov’s Lolita offers a well-known instance of a narrative problem: a first-person narrator, Humbert Humbert, whose ornate, seductive, allusive English prose becomes a moral obstacle for the reader, who may be charmed by the sentence even as she recoils from what it describes. 1 Patricia Highsmith’s Tom Ripley, introduced in The Talented Mr. Ripley , approaches a related problem from a different stylistic direction: plain, practical, almost affectless prose that narrates murder with an even tone, as Ripley might describe packing a suitcase. 2 Together, Nabokov and Highsmith offer two approaches to the criminal narrator whose voice does not supply the moral alarm a reader might expect. James Mulhern’s “Peppermint Candy” and “Mia Bambina” use plain, procedural, unornamented diction for confessions their narrators do not treat as remarkable. The stories substitute professional or clinical vocabulary for moral vocabulary when violence is confessed, so that a sentence describing a poisoning can resemble one describing a lesson plan or form. II. “Peppermint Candy”: Confession in the Language of a Safety Data Sheet Mr. Darnell’s confession in “Peppermint Candy” is delivered in the register of product information. Having decided to poison a student’s candy, he does not narrate deliberation, guilt, or hesitation; he narrates procedure: “I took the Visine out of my drawer. I found the paper listing the poisonous effects from tetrahydrozoline, the active ingredient in the eye drops. If swallowed: difficulty breathing, nausea, vomiting, and coma, among other effects.” 3 The sentence resembles a safety data sheet because it draws on that kind of language. Mulhern has Darnell narrate his criminal method using a bureaucratic register also used for incident reports and I.E.P. reviews. The confession that follows maintains the register: “I thought of the care I had taken to lightly rub Visine onto the candy before rewrapping it. Then I searched through the trash barrel for Helen’s wrapper. I placed it in the zipper pocket of my satchel with the printout about the drug.” 3 A notable feature of the passage is the absence of verbs of feeling. Darnell does not report satisfaction, anxiety, or triumph; he reports actions in sequence — took, found, thought, searched, placed — in the syntax of a procedural checklist. The story’s final line extends the pattern: “I retrieved the peppermints from my desk drawer and placed them in my satchel. I would share them again another day.” 3 “I would share them again” is grammatically a statement of simple future intention, much like one used to describe returning library books; the horror depends on the context the reader supplies, since the narration does not name it. In this respect, the story draws on the broader tradition of withholding moral vocabulary and leaving the reader to provide it. III. “Mia Bambina”: The Sociopath Who Names Herself “Mia Bambina” performs a variation on the same technique with one crucial difference: where Darnell never uses the word that would indict him, Molly Bonamici names her own condition outright, and the naming becomes, paradoxically, part of the same procedural flattening. Having engineered a roommate’s death by lacing cookies with cocaine, obtained from a family associate, to trigger a genetic heart condition she has learned of in confidence, Molly narrates the method with the same checklist precision as Darnell: “I knew Ashley loved sweets during her workouts, and I had placed the cookies on top of my dresser, the direction she faced while doing her ‘fitness dancing.’ I also knew that whenever she paused or was interrupted, she ate a cookie.” 4 The reasoning is presented as competent tactical planning, indistinguishable in its syntax from a coach describing an opponent’s habits. Molly’s explicit self-diagnosis differs from the more oblique approach often associated with Nabokov and Highsmith: “One of the perks of being a sociopath is that you learn how to quickly gather necessary information by manipulating people, using their weaknesses to your advantage… Ironically, Ashley and I had something in common—a genetic inheritance. I guess you could say we both had heart conditions. Of course, mine was more useful. Sociopathy wouldn’t kill me.” 4 The passage supplies moral vocabulary but converts it into a wry piece of self-description — “a perk” — rather than a confession requiring justification. Molly has already used the word a reader may have been considering, which can make the sentence register as confidence rather than confession. The story’s final movement continues the procedural register with grim comedy: Molly’s grandmother Nonna, asked to add the lethal dose to the cookie batch, agrees in the same domestic register she would use for a recipe request — “Sure mia bambina. What’s one more ingredient? Not a problem” — and Molly plans to “call to thank her, and remark on the effective wording in her note,” reframing murder as a collaborative project between grandmother and granddaughter. 4 The story’s closing sentence, reporting that “the chocolate chip cookies were a perfect hit,” uses a pun on baking success and a lethal strike, with a deadpan flatness that may recall Highsmith’s handling of Ripley. 4 IV. Two Confessions, One Rhetorical Machine Placed beside each other, Darnell and Molly show variations within a related technique. Darnell withholds the word for his own condition, leaving the reader to supply it; Molly supplies the word herself and may thereby defuse some of its power to indict her, converting confession into something like a professional credential. Both narrators treat the reader as an audience whose moral reaction is not their concern, while the prose remains clear and sequential regardless of what it describes. These stories locate their confessions in a public-school classroom and a Boston University dormitory, settings of ordinary American adolescent and professional life rather than Humbert’s motels or Ripley’s European high society. The comparison suggests that an unreliable confession can be staged through a desk drawer, a mixing bowl, and a narrator who describes both without raising her own voice. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. title: Water, and What It Carries — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: Water, and What It Carries
description: A literary essay on water imagery in the work of James Mulhern — baptismal tides, mourning rain, and the humble waters of caretaking.
text: Water, and What It Carries — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon A Literary Essay · On Recurring Imagery Water, and What It Carries Tears, rain, tide pools, and the unglamorous water of the sickroom — the element that carries mercy through Mulhern’s fiction and verse. “The damp leaves shimmer like tears, not many, that drop on the yellowed grass.” — “Leaves,” The Galway Review Water in James Mulhern’s work is almost never grand. It does not part or flood or drown anyone in a single dramatic stroke. It arrives instead as a tide pool by a “bony cliff,” as tears mistaken for dew on a fall afternoon, as rain tapping a windowpane while someone falls asleep, as the indignities of a body that can no longer hold its own water. It is, in other words, an element associated less with spectacle than with care in his fiction and verse. The clearest instance of water asked to do theological work is the beach trip at the center of “Assumptions.” The family drives to Nantasket for one reason: “the cure Helen dragged everyone to Nantasket for.” Two women walk into the sea to be healed, in the plain, unexamined faith of people who have always gone to the shore when something in the body needs fixing. The story lets the reader believe, briefly, that the water is where the miracle will happen — that this is a baptism in the ordinary sense, immersion as cure. Then it quietly withdraws that promise. “The cure… does not come from the water. It comes from the Son, after death.” The sea does not fail the family so much as it clarifies what water is actually for in this world: not the site of the miracle, but the place you go while waiting for one, the ritual that dignifies the waiting. Mulhern’s poems keep the water at a more intimate, unglamorous scale. In “Leaves,” the wet ground of a childhood chore — “smell of earth and wet decay,” a flashlight hunting the last stray leaf — returns, stanza by stanza, as the wet ground of a grave. The poem does not announce the shift. It repeats the same physical sensations, the cold air and the visible breath, until “the damp leaves shimmer like tears.” Water can be read here as memory’s medium: the thing that returns, involuntarily, disguised as weather. In “Honeymoon,” water turns domestic and tender at once. A speaker rubs ointment into a mother’s calloused heel while “the rain outside taps a pane” and an old photograph glows on the end table. “I think of how far these feet have walked, / the tenderness at the bottom of her sole.” The rain does no plot work; it keeps time, marking the room as a place where care is being paid out in small, unglamorous installments. And in “Moving Forward,” Mulhern includes water at its least dignified: a dying dog’s “bloody urine,” the diapers that keep “falling off,” an aging mother’s failing eyes and a body “filled with metal.” The poem’s conclusion — “All of the living are broken, inside and out… it’s how we care for others… that helps us become whole again” — follows this physical, humiliating material. A related pattern appears in the fiction: care is administered by unreliable, embarrassed, exhausted people through undignified materials. Taken together, the tide pool, the rained-on windowpane, and the incontinent old dog suggest a shared use of water in this body of work. It is not the medium of the miracle so much as the medium of tending — a substance encountered where illness, mourning, and love intersect. Water carries meaning here without much dramatic emphasis. A tear that might be dew, a tide that might be a cure, a rain that is only rain until you notice what it is falling on: this reticence shapes the technique. Unlike the fire, the water in these pages does not announce itself. title: Women Who Perform Belief — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: Women Who Perform Belief
description: Lady Jane and Myra Bocca read against the American literary tradition of the confidence woman — Melville's The Confidence-Man and Sinclair Lewis's Elmer Gantry.
text: Women Who Perform Belief — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon An Essay · On a Recurring Character Type Women Who Perform Belief Charlatans, healers, and con artists in James Mulhern’s fiction — Lady Jane and Myra Bocca, read against the American literary tradition of the confidence woman. Abstract This essay examines Lady Jane, the storefront faith healer of “Useless Things,” and Myra Bocca, the New Age shop owner of the story that bears her name, as instances of an American literary type: the confidence woman who monetizes belief itself. Reading both figures alongside Herman Melville’s The Confidence-Man and Sinclair Lewis’s Elmer Gantry , the essay considers how Mulhern’s fiction leaves the charlatan’s fraud and apparent accuracy unresolved rather than moving directly to unmasking. I. The Confidence Woman as American Type The confidence man is one of American literature’s oldest exports, and Herman Melville gave the type its founding text in 1857: The Confidence-Man: His Masquerade , in which a shape-shifting swindler works a Mississippi riverboat, adopting whatever persona — philanthropist, herb doctor, cosmopolitan — will best extract money or trust from his marks, while the novel itself declines to ever confirm which, if any, of his identities is real. 1 Sinclair Lewis extended the type into organized religion with Elmer Gantry in 1927, whose title character rises through the American revivalist ministry on pure showmanship, his gift for simulated conviction indistinguishable, to his congregations, from the real thing. 2 Both books share a structural commitment: the confidence figure’s fraudulence is never fully separable from a kind of genuine gift, and the reader is left uncertain whether unmasking the con would actually explain away everything the con has produced. James Mulhern places two women in a related lineage, translated into a female and late-twentieth- and twenty-first-century American register: Lady Jane, the Tremont Street faith healer of “Useless Things,” and Myra Bocca, the Wilton Manors New Age shop owner of the story bearing her name. This essay does not identify earlier readings of these figures alongside the Melville-Lewis tradition, but both can be read through its central ambiguity: each appears fraudulent while also providing information the fiction does not simply dismiss. II. Lady Jane: The Twang That Slips Lady Jane’s fraudulence is built into her introduction with unusual specificity: she speaks with “a fake British accent with a hint of Georgia twang,” a vocal costume that keeps slipping under pressure — by the story’s climax she is “speaking completely in her Georgia twang,” the performed Englishness abandoned entirely. 3 Her healing technique is theater rather than method: “circular motions with her hands,” a “crisscross” gesture over the heart, an “ostensibly sacred language” that two skeptical listeners both hear degrading into the word “pussy.” 3 Every visible signal the story provides argues for pure grift: the parlor beneath a printing company, the line of “desperadoes” extending around the corner, Lady Jane’s youth and showgirl costuming (“busty,” “white ballerina slippers with a flower pattern of red gemstones,” “untied” laces) so at odds with Mrs. Muldoon’s expectation of a wise elder that she immediately judges her “a tart that’s trying to make a few extra bucks before she goes to her other job in the Zone.” 3 Yet one piece of information Lady Jane provides within this discredited performance has consequences beyond the scene. Told to look at twelve-year-old Molly, Lady Jane says: “I see gruesome deaths in your future… You have the unlucky fortune of being someone who will either find dead people or be with them when they die, sometimes in violent situations. I guess you might say, ‘You’re an Angel of Death.’” 3 A reader who has met Molly Bonamici elsewhere in the collected volume — where she narrates, in flat procedural prose, her own poisoning of a college roommate — may find the prophecy difficult to dismiss. Rather than explain Lady Jane’s apparent accuracy, the story leaves the relationship between fraud and perception unsettled. III. Myra Bocca: Psychic Patter as Diagnostic Instrument Myra Bocca performs the confidence type’s comic register more fully than Lady Jane, her shop “Sacred Ashes” stocked with “incense sticks… tarot cards, essential oils, prayer flags” and her patter built from stock New Age vocabulary — chakras, “universal force,” “awakened spirit” — that the story’s narrator, Molly, dismantles in real time: when Myra claims psychic insight into Gabe’s home state, he corrects her immediately, “It was the way that you pronounced ‘dear’ that clued me in. You dropped the ‘r.’” 4 Every one of Myra’s claimed psychic perceptions has a mundane, deducible explanation available in the same paragraph, which is precisely how the confidence-woman genre is supposed to work: the mark, or in this case the skeptical narrator standing in for the reader, is always one step ahead of the performance’s mechanics. Myra also appears to read something accurately about Molly on their first meeting — “Did someone die recently?” — a question Molly refuses to answer honestly (“Lots of people experience death. That’s not psychic”) even though her aunt has, in fact, just died. 4 Molly’s retrospective analysis of the encounter poses the essay’s central question: “Maybe the black stones had nothing to do with grieving and she was making it all up, just a good reader of people, a con. In her business, you had to be.” 4 The passage suggests that con artistry and perceptiveness need not be opposed skills. Myra’s eventual theft of Molly’s credit card, charged toward “a television and some pornographic DVDs,” establishes her dishonesty without fully settling the question of her perceptiveness. 4 IV. Two Charlatans, One Family Resemblance Placed side by side, Lady Jane and Myra Bocca share more than a profession. Both are physically described in terms that undercut their claimed spiritual authority — Lady Jane’s youth and showgirl costume, Myra’s “receding chin and… wrinkled prune face” that the narrator explicitly, if uncharitably, contrasts with her own grandmother’s beauty. 4 Both are placed by the text in implicit comparison to the story’s actual matriarch: Molly notes that Myra’s eyes “reminded me a bit of my Nonna’s,” and Nonna herself is present as a skeptical chaperone throughout the Lady Jane scene, her running commentary (“Cut the crap!”) establishing her as the story’s implicit standard of authentic, unpaid, familial spiritual authority against which the professional healer is measured and found wanting. 3 Both women, that is, are shadow versions of the grandmother figure examined elsewhere in Mulhern’s corpus: unlicensed authorities who claim access to hidden knowledge, except that where the grandmothers’ authority is familial, sacrificial, and free, Lady Jane and Myra Bocca’s is commercial, performative, and, in Myra’s case, outright criminal. Mulhern’s use of the confidence-woman type differs in one respect from the Melville and Lewis works discussed here: the stories do not move directly toward unmasking. The Confidence-Man and Elmer Gantry can be read as allowing readers to see behind the performance, even if their fictional communities do not. In Mulhern’s stories, Lady Jane is fled from rather than exposed, and Myra Bocca is implicated in theft without an arrest scene. Both women leave their stories still performing, with fraud and apparent accuracy unresolved. The twenty-first-century charlatan, in this reading, need not be caught to be believed and need not be believed to be, on occasion, right. — Silver Current Press Notes 1. title: Writing as Communion — An Essay by James Mulhern
heading: Writing as Communion
description: James Mulhern on writing as an act of communion — between writer and page, writer and subject, and a page and a reader it will never meet.
text: Writing as Communion — An Essay by James Mulhern ← Back to The 2601 Salon On Craft · In the Author’s Own Words Writing as Communion On the sacrament hiding inside the sentence — between writer and subject, page and reader, the living and the dead. “This is communion, and teaching will be the pond that I bathe in each morning, every new day.” — “Teaching at Fifty-Six” , The Font: A Literary Journal for Language Teachers I have said before that teaching can feel like communion — that a roomful of unconvinced teenagers and one exhausted teacher, meeting honestly for fifty minutes, can take on a seriousness not unlike a sacrament. I have come to believe something similar may be true of writing itself, and I only ever discovered it backwards, sentence by sentence, the way a person discovers most things they already half-believed. A sentence, when it is working, is not a message sent from a writer who already knows something to a reader who does not. It is closer to a shared table. I sit down not entirely certain what I mean, and the sentence, if I am patient enough with it, tells me — the way a good conversation tells both people something neither of them arrived already knowing. That is the first communion: between the writer and the page, two parties neither of whom fully controls what gets said. The second is between the writer and the subject — and here I mean subject in the oldest sense, the person or memory or ordinary object being written about. I cannot write about a grandmother anointing a bald scalp with tanning oil, or a mother’s calloused heel, or a housedress with roses on it, without in some sense sitting with that person again, at that table, in that weather. Writing does not preserve the dead so much as it reopens a chair for them. Every essay, every poem about a person now gone is, whether I announce it or not, an act of company kept past the point company should be possible. My family members are my prayers. I wrote that once and meant it more literally than the sentence lets on. To write about a person with enough attention to get their gestures right — the exact word they used, the exact slant of light in the kitchen when they said it — is to hold them in mind the way a prayer holds its subject in mind: not to fix them, not to improve them, only to keep them present a little longer than memory alone would manage. The third communion is the one I have the least control over and perhaps trust most: the one between the finished page and a reader I will likely never meet. A poem written out of one family’s grief may become, on a stranger’s late-night reading, a poem about their own. I do not think this is a failure of the poem’s specificity. It is one reason to write something down rather than simply feel it privately — an offer of company, extended blind, across however many years and rooms the page happens to travel through. A writer who finishes a book alone at a desk at midnight can only hope that a reader may later find something of use in it. None of this requires the reader to share my faith, and very little of it announces itself as faith at all. It looks, on the page, like craft: revision, patience, the refusal to look away from an ordinary detail until it begins to disclose more of itself. Craft, practiced with patience, need not be separate from communion. It can be one way of approaching it. The sacred, if it appears at all, may emerge through attention to the shabby, the overlooked, and the nearly forgotten rather than through declaration alone. This is why I no longer think of writing as expression, a word that suggests something already complete inside the writer, waiting only to be let out. I think of it as a place set at a table — for the subject, for the reader, for whichever version of myself will need this sentence back someday and will not remember writing it. Teaching was the pond I said I bathed in each morning. Writing may be another part of the same current, with more uncertain room for connection. Editorial Note · On the Craft Notes on the Craft These samples show three recurring habits. The first is a willingness to slow down — to let a chipmunk dart across a patio, a blue jay shake water from its wings, a scent of roses reach the nose before the dialogue resumes. The second is a habit of placing the ordinary and the unspeakable in the same paragraph: a teacup poured, a lie confessed; a hand on a child's forehead, a diagnosis of schizophrenia. The third is attention to what a character cannot yet say aloud. These pages gather a handful of openings and finished poems, with links to the journals where they first appeared. Read them as you would the first pages of a book in a shop. If a piece interests you, more work is available on Amazon, in a back issue, or at the local library. First Pages From the Fiction Short Story · An Aiden Glencar Story Arise and Go Now A companion piece to Give Them Unquiet Dreams . I arrived at Rita's house about noon. Her blue eyes widened when she opened the door. She patted the sides of her red hair and smoothed her pleated cotton nightdress, a pattern of honey-bees. She was always donning unusual clothing or changing the color of her hair, which was ash blond a month ago. "Aiden, I'm a mess. I fell asleep on the couch. Come in." She held a book entitled Audrey Rose . She saw me looking at the cover. A girl in a red dress stood in front of a grave. The ground was on fire. "Junk. I hope you're reading better things in school. Let's sit in the backyard. It's such a lovely day." We walked through the hallway and kitchen to a brick patio covered by a pergola. She led me to a black wrought-iron table. Sunlight glimmered through the red cedar lattice above us, dappling her face. The air smelled grassy and pungent. Cat urine? Then a scent of roses reached my nose. "Will ya have a cup of tea?" She pulled out a rusted chair. "Sure." "Sit here. I'll be back in a jiff." A blue jay lapped the greenish water of a fluted cement birdbath, then shook its wings, cawed, and flew away. Along one side of the patio, potted plants moved in the breeze; a few swayed in macramé holders — lush ferns, the yellow and green spider plant, the wandering Jew with its purple and green heart-shaped leaves, and others I could not name. Children laughed on the other side of the tall hedge. "Come grab the door." Rita elbowed the screen door. She held a small tray with a teapot and two cups. As I hurried towards her, a chipmunk darted in front of me. "Thank you, Aiden." When we were seated, she said, "Isn't this peaceful?" She looked around. "Sometimes I sit here from morning until evening, watching the birds lift their wings or listening 'til the crickets sing." She laughed. "That rhymed. I'm a poet." She poured tea into a cup with milk and sugar. "Here you go." Then she poured her own. A small pot of azaleas cast a purple glow under her chin. "I want to apologize," I said. "For what?" She sipped and looked at me over her tea. "Nanna and I lied to you." "And when did you do that?" "I don't have leukemia." "I know that, Aiden," she said matter-of-factly. The story continues Read the full story at Impspired Essay · The Teaching Life Teaching at Fifty-Six A nonfiction piece on the classroom, salvation, and synchronicity. Inspired by the words of Thoreau, Whitman, Emerson, Dickinson, and other patron saints of American literature, I tell my students, in whatever ways I can, they contain multitudes, that nothing is at last sacred but the integrity of their own minds, and the real business of life is to live in the present, find eternity in a moment. We dwell in possibilities, I say, and possibilities are endless. As a teacher of American literature, I want my students to use the literature as a way to make connections and find meaning. Explore the circumference of your life. Write about your experience. Celebrate yourself! I urge. My students answer, This ain't math, Mr. , or say under their breaths, Mr. Mulhern be on crack, He be trippin' , or That's so gay. I teach poor inner-city kids, children of immigrants, immigrants themselves, kids who are struggling with many issues that I never dealt with in my Boston Irish Catholic upbringing, but sharing many of my issues as well: insecurity, perplexity, longing, nanosecond cycles of optimism and pessimism, but always, hope eternal. To live is so startling for them, it leaves little time for anything else. I begin my American Literature course by asking students to answer the questions, Who am I? Why am I like I am? What do I believe is true? They have to write an essay and read it to their peers. Most of them cringe at the thought of writing an essay, especially one that needs to be read aloud. My hope is that they start to see beyond the surface of themselves, their adolescent identities, and begin to know a sacred self deep inside, what Emerson calls the infinitude of the private man . Literature, as I see it, is the ladder hanging close to the side of the schooner, this assignment is the first rung, and I want my students to get wet. Telling students that they are schooners and that my sincere hope is that they get wet leads to all sorts of exchanges. Fuck you, for example. Mr., I ain't getting wet for nobody , or perhaps the definitive, That's nasty. My methodology is more precise. I give them a handout with specific, concrete directives, and have them read it first to themselves. Then I or a student reads it aloud, then I paraphrase each point several times, then I am repeatedly interrupted by Sasha, Makeba, Latitha, Tim, or Mark, who asks if she or he can go to the restroom, then I forget what I was in the middle of explaining, then I begin all over again, then somebody in the back says, What the fuck is he saying? , This sucks , I feel sick , or It's too hot in here. The image of literature as “the ladder hanging close to the side of the schooner” borrows and repurposes a line from Adrienne Rich’s 1973 poem “ Diving into the Wreck ,” where a diver descends a wrecked ship’s ladder in search of what the wreck, and the myths built around it, still have to tell. Here the schooner becomes the student rather than the vessel to be salvaged — an act of homage as much as an image. The essay continues — on synchronicity, Langston Hughes, and what teaching saves Forthcoming in collected nonfiction · Silver Current Press Four Poems From the Poetry Selected work from journals including The Galway Review and Sparks of Calliope . Mulhern has been shortlisted for the Aesthetica Creative Writing Award and nominated for Best of the Net . Leaves First published in The Galway Review That fall day we raked leaves from behind the shed. Smell of earth and wet decay rose in the cold air. We could see our breath. Worms and beetles scattered through a fence. I saw dirt and thought we had finished. "Not yet," you said. The gray sky grew darker and the wind chilled. When your flashlight showed not a speck of leaf, You said, "We're done." Today I look at the wet leaves below. I kneel and clear your grave. Again, I smell the earth and feel the biting cold. The damp leaves shimmer like tears, not many, that drop on the yellowed grass. "We're done," I hear you say. I say a prayer, cross myself, and rise. I see my breath and imagine I see yours. I should leave, I think, but not yet. Honeymoon First published in Sparks of Calliope She asks me to put bacitracin on her heel. "Do you see a small cut?" I nod and rub the ointment against the crack. Her feet are calloused and rough. "That feels good." She sighs. I see her honeymoon picture on the end table. My mother and father could be my children. Waving from the past, bright eyes and lips, she resembles Elizabeth Taylor in a hat. Both dressed in fine apparel, expectant, happy, apprehensive expressions. "What you looking at?" She glances to the side. "Oh, that," she says softly. I rub Aveeno into her feet. Tilting her head back, she closes her eyes and smiles. The room darkens. The rain outside taps a pane. I think of how far these feet have walked, the tenderness at the bottom of her sole. Kneeling, I'm thankful to ease one hurt. Her chest rises and falls, and soon she will sleep. Someday later, I'll hold the photograph and remember this night — the rain and the darkening eve. I will see my mother waving to me. Maybe I will feel the cut of pain, a sigh of love, or nothing at all. Moving Forward First published in The Galway Review Mornings I injected insulin into my dog and made sure she had enough water in her bowl. To see her in the yard, wobbling as she peed bloody urine, pained me. Ethel's pain was greater than mine though, especially the times she collapsed onto the cold tile or bumped into walls and furniture because of her thick cataracts. One day she could no longer hold her urine, so I bought diapers for her, which always managed to fall off. I began carrying her when she had that look, helping her get quickly to the yard. My mother said, "Can't you put her to sleep?" I said, "So when you become incontinent, I should do the same?" "Guess not," she answered. I'm my mother's healthcare proxy. Eventually I had to euthanize her, Ethel that is. As I left the office, the young woman at the desk said, "Sorry for your loss." I bent over my steering wheel and cried for a long while, then drove out of the lot. My mother, eighty-two, is losing her sight. She tells me she depends on audio books and the largest fonts for her texts. Her body is filled with metal — multiple surgeries on her spine, hips, and leg. Someday she will die and I'll visit the empty space of her apartment. I will remember her resolve to move forward when I see the walker beside her chair. How she listened to me, standing tall, and told me through dim blue eyes, "I love you, sweetheart." All of the living are broken, inside and out, and the problems continue to accumulate. It's how we care for others, show love, and move forward that helps us become whole again. Session's End First published in Sparks of Calliope One day there is no news. The anchors stare at empty teleprompters, Eyes wide and twitching, lips quivering, they look into the camera. We change channels. See black screens or people scrambling on sets, Passing blank papers and whispering. We do not hear what they say, and we do not care. We are too tired to move. Through the living room windows: trees and sky. The wind blows and birds fly. Somewhere snow falls and thunder booms. But not here. There is no weather. No drama, conflict, or story. No wars, crimes, or political crises. No empty talk. No sound and fury. In a forest, high on a pine, a wood thrush sings. Deep in a dark-water cave, the Emperor angelfish knocks. A judge's ruling: session's end. Someone shuts a door.
